A YOUNG lady who was blamed for allowing her glove to be discovered in a young man's pocket, stated that she had no hand in it. ON the recent yacht cruise around Newport, one "watch" was made up of young ladies, and it is charged that they made a very pretty mess of it. THE Sun says the mu,ic of the campaign has begun. The Michigan papers relate that the Democrats of that State have made overtures to the Greenbackers. This confirms the Sun's state- ment. A MAN who invented an electrical apparatus by. which a man could lie in bed and fish, was informed that there was no need of such an invention, as an amateur fisherman can lie any- where. AN old miser in a country village being asked for a subscription towards repairing the fence of the graveyard, declined, saying, "'I subscribed towards improvin' that buryin'-ground nigh on to forty years ago, and my family hain't had no benefit from it yeti" " rat a plumber 1" answered a burglar who was discovered in a chamber in a house in Cincinnati at midnight, and the owner turned over in bed with the remark: "Oh, I was in hopes it was a burglar, and that he might leave me something." A GEq'TLEMAN noticing that his wife's bonnets grew smal!er and-smaller, and the bills larger and larger, calmly said: "I suppose this thing will go on until the milliner will send nothing but the bill."

A GENTLEMAN was examining an umbrella and commenting upon its fine quality. "Yes," said a person present, "he fancies everything he sees." "And," added, a third party, is "inclined to seize everything he fancies." "I saw the glibbest-tongued lawyer I ever heard stuck for a word once," said the clerk of a co,,rt in Arkansas. "How did it happen ?" asked the stranger from New York. "Why, you nee," responded the clerk, "the lawyer said that Colonel Crane was a li•.r, and the word was no sooner out of his mouth than the colonel whipped out his bowie-knife and stuck him. An' he never spoke after that."

Clergyman : "Alt, -wow you see my meaning. Why should I feel :sorry ?" Boy : "Please, sir, cos you was ketched." One little girl held up her hand, and the inspector told her to answer the question, upon which she replied : " When nobody does nothing, and everybody goes telling of it every- where." THINGS TIIAT NEVER WILL BE SETTLED —Ent neer says that among things tat never will settled are the following : Whether a long screw- driver is better than a short one of the same family. Whether water wheels run faster at night than they do in the daytime. The best way to harden steel. Which side the belt should run next the pulley. The proper speed of line shatts. The right way to lace belts. Whether compres- sion is economical or the reverse. The principal of the steam injector. A WELL KNOWIq actor had a most resplendent coat made wherewith to embellish a new piece; and after the play had been running for some weeks, the player went to the tailor to order a new suit, when the latter remarked that the aforesaid coat had made both gain and fame for him. "Indeed," said the customer. "Oh, yes, sir," , quoth the tailor. " Why, I had another order for one of the same sort to-day." "From an actor !" asked the customer. "No, sir," replied the tailor, "from a gentleman." "Is there not something you wanted, madam ?" a shoedealar queried, as a lady was going out of the store. Lculy—" Why, I came in for a pair of shoes, and I've waited twenty minutes and no one has come near me, yye got tired." "Wait just one minute," he whispered. "I've spent twenty-five minutes with this lady with the big feet, but it won't take five minutes to fit your little two's with something nice." Although she wore fives, she smiled and sat down to wait. Fou HEADS AND TOOIII. —David G-- was well i known in a certain village n P.erthshire for his netny quaint, wise, and witty sayings. He always went about with his chin resting on the top button of his waistcoat, which gave to his head a medita- tive pose. Meeting the head gardener of the big house, who was a pompous individual, and carried his head well above the perpendicular, he was accosted with—" Hoots, Dauvit, I wormer a man like you wud gae shoot wi' his held hinging like that—haud up your heid, min." Dauvit took up with a sly twinkle in his eye. "Ay, min, thee ye wonner at that? Just you tak' a look at that field o' barley there, an' ye'll notice that a' the fou beide are hinging doom, an' a' the toom tines are staunin' up." It is rumoured that Professor Huxley is to be the litomanes lecturer next year. If this be so the dis- course will be strangely different from that with which Mr. Gladstone delighted his undergraduate audience in the Sheldonian. It'will not conclude as Mr. Gladstone's did, with a eulogy of theological studies.

The old manor house known as Myrtle Grove, Youghal, county Cork, built in the fourteenth cen- tury, is still in the market. The building was ori- ginally the residence of the clergy of St. Mary's, Youghall, and stands next to the church, a door still existing between the fortress tower of the church and the grounds of the house. Sir Walter Raleigh having assisted Sir Humphrey Gilbert to put down the rebellion in Ireland, settled down at Myrtle Grove, which afterwards became rich in historical incidents. Here Sir Walter carried the poet Spen- ser into the presence of Queen Elizabeth to read his "Faiirie Queene." Here, too, Sir Walter interested her Majesty in his sea-roving adventures.

The principal loom was Sir Walter's study. It is beautifully panelled in dark oak, and in one corner is a fine picture of the Virgin Queen. There also still remains the ingle nook where • the gallant knight sat and smoked, and the old oak chairs and table are yet preserved. In the garden, too, are shown the spots where the potato and tobacco plant first brought to Ireland were planted. In later days Cromwell visited the house, and is said to have preached in the church: That sturdy Quaker, George Fox, also stayed in this fine old house.

Studley Castle, the Warwickshire seat of Mr. J. T. Eades Walker, whose bankruptcy is announced, is one of the stateliest homes in that leafy county. It was once the property of Sir Francis Goodricke, but was purchased from him by Mr. T. Eldes Walker, the son of a famous midland ironmaster, who left an immense fortune many years ago. The castle stands in a park of eight hundred acres, and is sur- rounded by a large estate of exceptional loveliness, with many tenants wi.o are naturally anxious as to what the future of the estate is to be. Mr. Walker is related to .the Allsolips. Another Warwickshire estate concerning which speculation is busy just now is that of Melcombe, which was left by Mr. Needham Phillips, a rich Manchester merchant, to his grandson, Sir George Trevelyan's second son, who is evidently not indisposed to part with it.

It is said that the result of the first year's work- ing on Lord Carrington's allotments in Lincolnshire shows an average net profit of £6 Sa. per acre to the allotment holders. This is the return upon labour in hours which might otherwise have been passed in enforced idleness, and is a striking proof of the truth of the arguments advanced during the 'recent agitation for the more general extension of the allotment system. Lord Carrington's tenants, who bold one acre each, pay a rent of 835., and have obtained a far higher return from the land than the large. farmers in the neighbourhood. The lowest yield was from an acre of barley, and the highest from an acre of potatoes; but more valu- able results still were obtained from tile plots cul- tivated for home consumption rather than for sale. Most of the men, however, are selling their produce arid putting the money into a common fund, with a view to the accumulation of sufficient capithl to take more land under the Small Holdings Act.

Wednesday was a very joyful day at the Palace of Fredensberg, where the Ring and Queen of Denmark are staying at present, for it was the anniversary of the birthday of their son-in-law, the Prince of Wales, of the marriage of their daughter the Czarina, and of the birthday of the Due de Qhartres, the father of the Princess Walde- mar of Denmark. These anniversaries were all celebrated joyfully but quietly, for the deaths of the Duke of Clarence and the Grand Duchess Paul of Russia (Princess Alexandra of Greece). the grandchildren of the Ring and Queen of Denmark, are yet comparatively recent. On that day the Prince of Wales was fifty-one years old, the Czarina had been married twenty-six years, and the Due de Chartres was fifty-two years old. With their healths were drunk the health of Princess Victoria Alelita of Edinburgh, who was sixteen that day, and who is connected with the Danish Royal Family doubly by marriage,

Mr. Balfour has recently returned to his place in Haddingtonsbire, where he is entertaining a party of friends this week. Winningham House lies at the head of a long and winding sheet of water in the lowlandparts of Haddingtonshire, and within easy reach ot the North Beswick golfing links,which no doubt add to its attractiveness. The mansion which has taken the place of one that bore marks of great antiquity, was erected at the beginning of the present century by Jame* Balfour, the first 4,f the family who owned the property. It is of light- coloured sandstone in the Grecian style, and has undergone some considerable alterations at the hands ot its present occupier. The grounds are very beautifully wooded, and are intersected by three tine drives, which approach the mansion. In one part of them there is still shown a venerable tower, carefully preserved, which is all that remains of an ancient fortress of- the Dnuglases. A very aged yew also exists,under the boughs of which the Bads of Douglas and Morton sat when they plotted Darn- ley's murder. Danes Castle, where Darnley and Mary resided for a time, is about two miles away.

By the Australian mail we, have an account of the colonial career of 11r. Robert Sutton Sevier, who recently married, under somewhat peculiar circumstances. Lady Mabel Bruce, sister of the Marquis of Ailesbury. It seems that Mr. Sevier, arrived in Australia in 1881, and immeliately started business as a " cash bookmaker," in Mel- bourne. Being " gifted with a fine baritone voice, and endowed with plenty of effrontery,' he did so large a business that he was compelled to employ three or four clerks. He set up a grand establish- ment in a fashionable Melbourne suburb, and kept his horses and dogs. But a fracas in a Melbourne public-house with Lord Deerhurst, son and heif of the Earl of Coventry, was the cause of his undoing. Lord Deerhurst, was at the time aide-de-camp to Sir Henry Loch, the then Governor of Victoria, who is now in London. Sevier and his lordship had a dispute about some betting transaction and came to blows. Police-court proceedings ensued and Sevier was sentenced to a term of imprison- ment without the option of a fine. Against this sentenae he successfully appealed, but the incident ruined his business as a " cash bookmaker."

" The news of his marriage with a titled lady is not viewed as very surprising by his Melbourne friends, as he had a peculiar fascination for the fair sex." So says the Antipodean narrator. One of the Melbourne dailies has a cynical comment on the recent unexpected marriage: 'When the cash book maker of Flemington (the principal Melbourne racecourse) is able to ally himself with one of the oldest and most aristocratic famalies of Great Britain, this surely is a circumstance which proves that the Australian turf is locking up whatever Australian funds may be doing."

The two principal candidates in the American Presidential election—General Harrison rep esent,- ing the Repuhlicans and Protection, and Mr. Cleve- land standing for the Democrats and tariff reform— are opposites physically as well as politically. Pre- sident Harrison is a little men, who leads a quiet life, caring nothing for society. He is a hard plod- ding worker, and has a keen eye for national in- terests. He bas a little of Mr. Blaine's Jingoism in his policy, and as much Protection as M'Kinley. He is not a good speaker, and is cold in manner. He is now sixty, and enjoys excellent health, lie does not fatigue himself with too much Presidential handshaking. Ile has recently lost his wife, who was a fine specimen of American womanhood; and his only daughter. Mrs. McKee, is now hostess at the White House. During the last Presidential campaign not much was heard of Mr. Harrison, but I a great deal of his illustrious ancestors. Their I phantoms were utilised as election agents. His grandfather was President, another paternal an- cestor signed the declaration of American independ- ence, and he is descended from the Commissioner Harrison who signed the decree tor the execution lof Charl,a I. Ile could have no better pedigree in I • America. lie has been a popular subject with the caricaturists, who generally represent him sitting under the shadow of his grandfather's hat.

Mr. Cleveland is a man of weight—politically and avoirdupois. He weighs eighteen stone, and he the most popular politician in the country. He is known as Grover, but he is also Stephen, his full Stephen Grover Cleveland. He has a slight moustache, and is double-chinned. largenam e g He is a fairly good speaker, and makes his state papers and messages forcible outspoken documents. Four years ego he was a long way ahead of his party on the tariff question,but now he lags behind, for tile Democratic House of Representatives and the Democratic Convention have both passed free.

trade resolutions while he has only accepted what is vaguely called tariff reform, Like Mr. Harrison, hais a lawyer by profession. He reads little, and takes no recreation, except going in tor angling, for which be has a passion. He is a first-class band shaker, and made apopular president. Mrs. Cleveland is a charming lady, who made an exem- plary hostess, and also led Washington society. The newspapers have a great deal to say about Mr. Cleveland's weight,and are much interested in Baby Cleveland. Mr. Cleveland is fifty-six.

The vice-presidential candidates are Mr. White- law Reid (Republican) and Mr. Adlai E. Stevenson (Democrat). Mr. Reid recently retired from being ' Minister to France. He is editor of the "New York Tribune"—the leading Republican paper—a man of fine presence, amiable manners, who for social purposes woad make a better President than Mr. Harrison. He is fifty-five. He is a native of Ohio, and after making a mark for himself as a journalist, made a marriage with a millionaire's daughter. He is a fairly good speaker and a better writer. Mr. Stevenson is a lawyer and a popular politician in the West. He pronounces his peculiar Scriptural name " Adlee," and so have his parents betore him. Harrison, Cleveland, and Stevenson are all of English Puritan stock. Reid is of Scotch Puritan origin. All four are Presbyterians.

This one is quite mooth and blue-coloured, whereas the other is brown and rough. The annealed is the smooth one. That is brought about by Pb cing the sheet to the furnace we have seen and baking it with the greatest heat we can raise." After this another journey through the yard was made to the Dallam Steel Plate Mills. The process of rolling steel plates here is, in principle,exactly like the one of rolling iron sheets, except that stronger machines have to te used. We remained here for a few moments and then proceeded to other departments,where merchandise iron of a miscellaneous character was being made. The first thing we saw was the manufacture of iron hoops for tubs and barrels. The hoop iron is made first in long lengths by a similar process to that of making steel wire. When the lengths are cool they are cut up and twisted by a machine into the size of hoop required. We visited several other departments, where different classes of iron articles were being made, by a similar process. As we passed another large department, which was in dark- ness, the writer learned that it was the engineering house. In this place alone there are employed some hundreds of men, and 200 apprentices. Some of the largest contracts in the country are carried out here. The ironwork for many of the largest bridges in the country were made here. What is considered to be the largest iron chimney in the world was manufactured in this department a few weeks ago. It was 250 feet high. What is the total number of men employed at the forge, the writer could not discover, but, he was told that a sum of £3,000 was expended in wages each week. Forty-five years ago the forge occupied but a few square yards in Bewsey, and now its size is appalling, being probably larger than any forge in the world. A great deal of this success is popularly at- tributed to the efforts of the chief partners, Messrs. Bleckley and the indefatigable manager, Mr. Thomas Morris, woo has been with the firm 29 years.

div.head: TUE BEWSEY FORGES.
div.p: TUE BEWSEY FORGES.
AN lINSCIENTIFIu DESCRIPTION. (conducted.)

That was so I said. I bad heard that Pearson and Knowles's works were about the largest on this revolving globe. But I said I was not aware that the men employed here were more fortunate than other individuals in town in receiving the benefits of sunshine. We were passing from the mill I des- cribed last week, through the yard to the plate rolling department. My friend continued " That is so. We enjoy the benign influence of sunbeams here when the sun is invisible to you. Its ruddy ;radiance heats our uorcelane frames both night and • day. No, don't interrupt, I'm not gammoning you. It's this way. -You know that coal consists chiefly of decomposed leaves and tree boughs, and other vegetable matter, and the heat which it gives is known to be the essence of the sun's heat which the plants and leaves absorb whilst growing. Fifty per cent of the heat given by coal is sunbeam. We use 1,000 tons of coal a day here. When that is put through a course of proper deductions it shows that most of our men enjoy an average of 600 of sunbeams per day." Only the sudden plash of our feet in the puddles broke the silence for a few moments. Then I said the company might augment their fortunes greatly. It was well-known that the crops for miles around had been practically ruined for the want of sun. Garden parties, &c., had been unmitigated failures through the funeral- like aspect of the weather. Now, if the company could only procure some inventive genius who could supply the necessary rudiments of the system they might make their fortunes in a couple of summers by supplying sunbeams to garden parties at so much an hour, or ripening corn at a profitable price per rood.

div.head: EIIiF.RT IRON ROLLING.
div.p: EIIiF.RT IRON ROLLING.

13y this time we had reached the sheet iron rolling department. This is a ponderous place. When the writer entered be felt he would have to fall back upon the hackneyed way of writing about a forge. .He would have to go to the library and take a plentiful supply of extracts from "he procPss of iron making. But eventually he decided not to, on account of the Copy- right Acts. Impressions given in this mill are excep- tionally strong. One of the men said that unless the rolling machines were capable of impressing the hot iron very heavily the sheets could not be manufactured But the spectator does not receive his impressions like the iron. If he did, the man said, they would be too much for him and he would probably die. This is not a joke. Some men who have put their hands under these machines have been positively useless and armless ever since. Upon entering the mill the visitor's attention is arrested by a series of clink cer-clinks, clink cer-clinks, which go on in rapid succession. This sound is caused by the iron plates entering and leaving the roll- ing machines. But it is better for him to start at the commencement of the process. In one part of the department there is a large fur- nace. Close by these is a stack of the blocks of iron which you saw welded into shape by the steam hammer. There are two men employed at the furnace. You go and stand by, and presently one of the men opens the large iron door. The other inserts his iron grippers and m a moment pulls forth one of the blocks of iron all aglow with a heat which has rendered it pli- able. For a moment he swings it in the air, then loosens his grippers. Whizz! It spins through the air, and falls with a bang upon the iron floor,causing a shower of sparks to fly around. Then another man comes with a pair of grippers, and taking up the iron places it between two

div.head: HEAVY REVOLVING IRON BOWIES,
div.p: HEAVY REVOLVING IRON BOWIES,

which seem to weigh about a ton each. The original length of this block of iron is about a foot and a half, and half a foot thick. When it emerges from between the rollers it is as long again but only half as thick. Quick as lightning, another man who stands behind the machine has caught the iron between a pair of grippers and carried it to a cutting machine, where the block is sliced into halves like a large fire cake. Close by there are two other rolling machines something similar to the one which the block has already gone through, and each having a man at both sides. To the first of those machines the two halves of the block are taken. One half is put between the rollers, . which receive it with a snapping clink ! like the luxurious expression of a satisfied shark in detaching a leg or other favourite joint from a human body. As the piece of iron comes out at the other side it is turned over the topmost roller and run between the cylinders again. It takes but a moment for this to be done, and the two men are kept constantly at work, one placing the iron between the rollers, and the other twisting it over the top roller back again. This goes on until the block has 13,en rolled into a sheet, pnibably two yards long, a yard in width, and the ith of an inch in thickness. Then it is thrown upon the iron fieor with other sheets. But it is by no means finished with yet. A very muscular gentleman known as a shearer comes along next, and takes the sheet in hand with a view to making it look respectable. Ile carries the sheet to a steam roller and cuts all the jagged and uneven edges off. After this he throws it on the floor, then another man comes along and says some- thing like this: " Hey Jemine. Hast getten my 'ammer and a chaw o' bacca tha con lend me till to-morrow ?" Presently he goes away after putting something in his mouth. But the amount of wind which he expended over the sheet didn't Seem to cool it much, because it was quite hot when another man seized it and took it away.

div.head: BEING ANNEALED.
div.p: BEING ANNEALED.

"That man," said my friend," is taking a sheet to the annealing furnace. This is a process which hardens the iron and takes off the brown rough surface which it wears now, leaving it quite smooth and slate-coloured. Come and see it." owe clambered over a heap of iron sheets, and came to another large furnace, the front of which was open. As we approached the heat became stronger and stronger, and when we were within a few yards of it the writer felt as though he was in a large oven. You coula absolutely see the heat in the furnace. It looked like one great mass of shimmering gauze. Every moment we stood there was like an hour of purga- tory. My friend was used to it and conversed plea- santly. The writer tried to look nonchalant. In a minute or two the perspiratien was teeming down his face like water from a duck's back. But he held on, turning his back to the furnace for relief, and kept up the conversation. In about twelve seconds he felt as though the akin was coming off his back. During the conversation he remarked, en peasant, that it was a trifle warmer inside than out. The other gentleman said "just a little," and then some men came by and smiled at seeing the writer dissolving by degrees and parting from himself in streamlets of perspiration. Although always in favour of ameliora- tion of the working man's lot, he felt that he himself was a prodigious "sweater," on this occasion. Inside of five minutes, however, he retired to a distance, under the plea that he could see better from there. But during the whole of this time, there had been a couple of men working at the very mouth of this annealing fur- nace, they wee strong sinewy men,all muscle and bone, without an ounce of superfluous flesh about them. They were attired in light duck pants and flannel singlets. They were preparing to bring out a sheet which had been annealed. As they stood in the glare of this terrible heat, with the sweat pouring off them, one unused to the sight realized the meaning of work as it falls to the lot of a forgeman. It seemed impossible that a human frame could battle so long with such fierce and cruel heat, which could make itself excruciating in five in teeto a person unaccustoned to it. And yet, the writer Was told that these men won their bread by fighting night after night, and week after week with it. It seemed incredible ! But when the writer turned to his friend and said "God knows, these men have a right to ask is life worth living," 'he was met with a smiling reply, " We shall see."

div.head: TRAINED TO TAN HAAT.
div.p: TRAINED TO TAN HAAT.

"How do you find this kind of work ?" "oh, all right," was the cheery reply. "Don't you find it hot ? " "Just a trifle."

are you able to stand it the hours you do ?" " Oh, it doesn't cope any harder to me than carrying bricks would to a builder; it is all a matter of use. I have be-n brought up to it, and don't suffer from the heat like you would."

div.head: "THE NOVEL AS SHE IS WROTE."
div.p: "THE NOVEL AS SHE IS WROTE."

Mr. Grant Allen, in lecturing under the auspices of the Tyneside Sunday Lecture Society, on " The Novel as she is wrote," said they had probably thought of fiction from the point of view of the unhappy people who had to read it, not from that of the more unhappy and unfortunate people who had to write it. But literature had become a trade, and, as one of the skilled operatives, he wanted to show how the trade was carried on—not the literary aspect, but the practical business of writing. There was a laudable desire—he supposed it was laudable—on the part of the public to know all about the inner management of this affair of hookwriting ; so lie wanted to cast an electric light upon the actual mode in which the modern novel was produced—not entirely from introspec- tive analysis. lie had conversed with most of the principal novelists, and had learned something of the way in which this article of manufacture was produced and placed upon the market. First, there was the " invocation of the muses." This now came in the shape of a type-written letter from the proprietors of some serial paper, asking the novelist to write a novel, describing the naturs of the story, its length, esc., and stating the price that was to be paid for it. The usual divisions of the novel were twenty-six chapters, and it would be found by novel readers that moat novels contained exactly the twenty-six chapters. This was in con- sequence of the method of syndicating—one novel running simultaneously in a number of journals— and was to suit the convenience of the newspapers. Most popular novelists had their books spoken beforehand ; and even if the novels were not spoken beforehand, the writer must prepare to meet the best market. Divine literature had gone to trade. In a novel, the hero and heroine were the ! most difficult people to deal with. They must he' always perfect, and a slight departure to either aide of the chalk line of rectitude came at once into prominence. There was only one orthodoxy, but there were many heterodoxies. The villain was much easier, because there were so many various kinds of villainy. The first thing to do, after the novelist got his.order, was to get a plot. Most novelists kept a number of plots in their note books, and the author, after he got his order, turned over the pages of his note book, and found what central idea was most likely to satisfy the particular person from whom the order emanated. , Then be proceeded to elaborate it, and to "flesh it 11 out" with the episodes and incidents Needed for the twenty-six parts. Everything was sacrificed to plots and episodes. Then the author talked it over with somebody. The married novelist generally talked it over with his wife—the ladies being the consumers—and he got directly at the intelligence : of the consumer. Robert Louis Stevenson had said ' that he got most of his plots from dreams. Most novelists were not so lucky ; they had beautiful ! dreams, but when they woke up the plot vanished ; or, if there was a little of it left, it turned out, on investigation, to be pure non- sense. The plot having been fixed and decided upon, the novelist began to write. Each had his ewn way of doing this. The most conscientious ' way—not many adopted it now—was te write a skeleton chapter, and to flesh it in as the scene gained clearness in the mind. The usual way seemed to be to write down the skeleton story first,and to make the additions for style after- wards, putting in those little touches which gave literary finish and literary character to the woik. Still, it could not be said that there was any best way. It was best for the novelist to read and re- read everything, to think over it carefully, and to say to himiself, "Is that how I could say it ?" This was necessary to get a flowing, colloquial style-,. The lecturer described the difficulties resulting from the syndicating,—h6w it was necessary to keep incidents suspended for weeks ; the difficulties coming from the arbitrary division into twenty-six parts, while the author had to keep an eye to the possibility of the story going into a maga- zine in twelve monthly parts, and to its final issue in the three-volume form. It was often asked how long it took to write a novel. One might as well ask how long it took a man to live. Every fellow had his own way of doing it, and n• fellow did it twice the same way. As a rule, a:novelist in the swing of the trade wrote two novels a year, but much of the time was occupied in correcting what had already been written. It was a good plan, in describing the appearance of characters,to pourtray people of one's own acquain- tance. The modern novelist should be possessed of encyclopedic knowledge: he should know law, medicine, art, and craft. It was desirable that he should have been a publio-schoolbey, a member of both universities, a colonel in the guards, called to the bar, and have taken holy orders. It was also well, if possible, that he should have committed a murder or twc, and lost a fortune at Monte Carlo. He should be able to speak all the dialects of Eng- land equally. When the novel had been written, and the love interest worked in, and the humour duly inserted, if possible, they would suppose that the novelist's work was at an end. The novelist knew a great deal better: it was only just beginn- ing. True, if the novel was bespoken the writer's work was nearly over. But he had to deal with the inexorable editor and his demands for alterations. The editor would not have any class, or sect, or section offended, and the novelist had to write or re-write certain chapters. Mr. Walter Besant said that he once made a sailor kiss a girl to whom he was not engaged. They all knew that sailors were not straight-laced persons, but an indignant father wrote and said that Mr. Walter Besant should pro- tect society against such .outrages. For his own part, he thought it best to Atop short at a gentle pre Rause of the hand, and, if anybody objected after- wards, it could be explained that the pieseure was purely nervous. 1 the novel was not bespoken, the writer had to go into the open market. Ha had recourse tc the middleman. But the modern author wa., an astute man of business, and knew the worth of his wares and the turn of the market about as well as the ordinary cotton broker. The middleman was called a literary agent, and he placed stories with the newspapers, who were the real customers. The literary agent got 10 per cent of the proceeds, and the author submitted to that exaction because the writ could do something which be could not do for himself ;he knew the ropes and pulled the wires. The, keynote ot the whole was that the newspaper paid the author three to one in propor- tion to the book-wright ; in other words, if a novel was worth, as a whole, one thousands pounds, the newspaper paid the author .£750, and the book- wright only paid him £250. He got. a little as well from America nowadays—.£4o or .£5O, perhaps, on the .£l,OOO. But Ames iea was a great cc.untry, and could not afford to pay for its literature. The cir- culating library had killed the novel commercially, and the novelist had become a journeyman labonrer in the pay of the newspaper. That was not an ideal life for a man of letters. The ideal was that the author should he able to write when he liked, what he liked, and to write it at. the length he liked. No writer during the last forty or fifty years had turned out first-class work unless he was a man of independent means; and it was re- grettable that the present system made high-class literature possible to only the moneyed class. The actuality was that literature had become a trade ; ' the author had to get his living and to meet the ! market. He believed, however, that the public was ready for far better work than most editors were ready to pat before it.

"You forget, sir," said Miss Carriscourt, indig- nantly, "that you are in a house of mourning. Such words, such actions ill become a gentleman." A derisive laugh broke from his lips. He turned upon her fiercely, crying, in hoarse excite- ment:

"This is all a sham; I feel sure of it. She never disappeared before the colonel's death. I say it was after it. She has long since made a confidant of you, in all probability, and you have hidden her away, now that the sword which was suspended above her head has been removed. But listen to my vow: I will search the world over for her but what I will find her. Tell her that. I come of a raca that knows no defeat."

CHAPTER XXIX. "THERE IS NO FATE SO CRUEL AS TO BE AN UNLOVED WIFE." Too indignant to reply to his accusation, Miss Carriscourt turned haughtily away. She would not bandy words with hiir, and a little later he left the house in a perfect fury of rage. As the colonel was widely known, all the leading journals of the metropolis paid glowing tributes to his memory. "Surely. lonie must see it, and return at once," thought Miss Carriscourt. Another day came and went. There were still DO signs of lonie. A month passed by, in which many ch4n;;es had been wrought. Still Joule came not. The house had been closed up shortly after the colonel's death, the servants paid off and dismis:ted, and the place had passed into the hands of those named as executors in the colonel's will. The disappearance of the heiress the week before her roarrittg.., to Mr. Lyons was a nine days' wonder among society people; then it died out. But there were two people who never for one moment forgot her. To Arthur Rochester bole's sudden flight had been a revelation. She, could not bring herself to marry Frank Lyons. But why, then, had she not requested him to release her? he wondered. The course she had taken was certainly not in accord. an" with her nature. IT he bad observed Elaine more closely, he would bays noticed that she was a changed person ever -

truth. My heart cries out for my old love. I have found that she was not as false as I believed her. Yes, I love her, Elaine, better than before, yet my word is pledged to you. You hold your fate and mine in your hands, Elaine. I leave it with you as to what the future will be." The words died away on his lips as he saw the marble-white face raised to his.

"Are you ill. Dame 2" he cried. "Great heaven! what is wrong? What is the matter? Have my words hurt you as much as that ?" "Your words have slain me, that is all. Arthur," she said, slowly. "Yes, it is wrong—a terrible wrong which I lay at your door. You have broken my heart." She looked so piteously at him that he was touched. He would have resented reproaches or passionate words; but when a lovely girl, like Elaine, tells a man that her heart is broken, and he knows that it is for love of him, what words can he find in which to answor her?

She had sinned so cruelly for this man's love. She had seen her rival go down in the dark waters from which she never rose—without one cry for help which could have saved her: but it seemed to her now, as she stood there, that in those ma Inents of horrible torture that she suffered tenfold fOr what she had done; yet, she told herself, she would never lose her lover without a desperate struggle. _ _
(To be continued.)

div.head: WORRY, DRINK, AND LUNACY.
div.p: WORRY, DRINK, AND LUNACY.

--- It is no new thing, says the " Lancet," to hear of the close connection between indulgence in alcohol and the development of insanity. Accordingly, we feel no surprise at a statement by Dr. Augustine Planus that a large proportion of the cases of lunacy registered in Paris of late years are attribut- able to this form of excess. Far more significant is his observation that drunkenness has increased very markedly in the French capital. The effect is, of course, due to the variety of causes. Among these one is of particular interest as bearing upon the neurotic aspect of the alcoholic dyscrasia. It is the pressure and worry of overwork, probably combined, as usual in the like circumstances, with irregular feeding and want of sleep. Though felt by all classes of workers, an important characteris- tic of its action as a cause of alcoholism is its in- creasing influence among those who labour with their brains. Artists, authors, and especially journa- lists—a group of persons by no means usually given to excess—are enumerated as having suc- cumbed to the subtle poison; and this result has, doubtless with truth, been attributed to the crav- ing depression of mental fatigue. Iris not difficult, indeed, to trace a connection here, and we may accept it ai a warning that forced labour is ever prone to become the natural parent of other and worse excesses. The best work, however hard, is always methodical enough to permit of timely rest and of regular nutrition, and the full recognition of this fact is a mere question of public utility which we hope to see more and more widely ad- mitted in practice.

div.head: ELECTION OF MAYOR
div.p: ThE ELECTION OF MAYOR

The annual meeting of the Town Council for the +election of the Mayor, deputy-mayor, aldermen,and committees, was held at noon on Wednesday. there were present the Mayor (Ahlarman Greenall), the deputy-mayor (Alderman Fralcomb')., Aldermen J. Harrison, C. J. Holmes, S. Chantlley, J. 11. Sutton, J. K.. Wright, and T. IL Sutton ; Councillors G. Blackhurst, J. Ashton, W. Bo9ton, A. Browne, J. Carmen, F. Dixon, J. Garner, T. Flood, J. 11. Fleming, J. S. Green, R. T. Fai relough J. Faircloug.e, J. Wilkinson, 'J. Smethurst T. Hutchinson, 11.1. Roberts, J. Hill, H. Heaton, L. Greening, F. W._ Monks, G. Plimpton, J. Muir, J. Elepherd, and W. Tinsley ; Mr. J. L. Whittle, tzwn clerk ; Mr. T. Longdin, borough surveyor; and Dr. J. H. :Garnall, medical officer. -There svas a large attendance of the public, including Mr. John. White, J.P„ Mr. W. Pierpoint, Mr. P. Davies, Mr John Hampton. Mr. T. B. Kiernan, Mr. James Bolton, Mr. G. P. V. White (deputy magistintes' clerk), Mr. John Evans, Mr. John Clayton, Mr. Chantry, Messrs. Rath bone. Hesketh, W. J. Shaw, and others. Alderman FIOLdiES said he 'had very great pleasure in proposing the re-election of the present Mayer. (Applakse.) He had supported his election that day 12 months, and the pleasure with which he now proposed him was enhanced by his having consented to accept office for another year. He must express his satisfaction at the manner in which he had conducted the business of the Council during the year that had passed. On behalf of the members Of the Corporation he had to say that he was very rntidll obliged to Mr. Greenall for 4consenting to undertake the onerous duties of his office for the coming year. Alderman CIIAVIDLIEV seconded the nomination. He said he could only testify to the very efficient manner in which the retiring Mayor had served them. He was exceedingly glad that be had consented,although reluct- antly, because it was the unanimous wish of the council to re-elect him. He felt confident that the gentlemen around the table had heard such frequent expressions indicative of liiwzeal and industry in the performance of his duties as Mayor, that it would be simply wasting time to add to what had been already said. Alderman StCrTON in supporting the resolution remarked that he had pleasure twelve months ago in proposing the election of Alderman Greenall as Mayor of the borough, and had now equally great pleasure in supporting the proposition for la re-election. He believed it to boa very wise and proper course to allow a mayor to have a second innings, because during a second year of office he was familiar with the work and duties of the Mayor, and it was a much easier task to perform them, and his re-election would be of consider- able benefit to the town He thought tnat they would all be agreed that the Mayor had performed his duties in a very creditable and satisfactory manner during the past year. He was quite satisfied that he would per- form the work even more successfully during the forth- coming year than in tke past. Councillor ROBERTS said that as one of the junior members of the Council he wished to join in the congra- tulatory remarks which had been made by other mem- bers with regard to the retiring Mayor, who was to be re-elected. He could say with confidence—and he knew that he was only representing the opinions of the rest of the members of the Council—that Ald. Greenall had made a very exemplary Mayor. During the past year of office he has dealt with them as liberally as it was pos- sible to do. He had given them every possible latitude,and by so doing he had very largely promoted the best ia- tereatsof the borough, because they had had discussions upon very important subjects that had been more thoroughly thrashed out than perhaps they would have been if the Mayor had stuck to the strict letter of his duty, as the chief officer of that Corporation. Alderman FRANCoMB supported the resolution. He said he had great pleasure in endorsing everything that had been said by the previous speakers. Aid. Greenall had tried to the very utmost to do his duty, and he was quite certain that he had been very successful. (Ap- plause.) He then put the resolution, which was carried unanimously with hearty acclamation. Alderman GREENALL said it was the source of consid- erable pleasure to him to have been asked to stand again as Mayor for the ensuing year. That pleasure was the more increased by the kindness which he had received from the Council, and the kindly words which had been said outside the Council with regard to himself and wife, who had been of the greatest assistance to him. He was on the eve of a very troublesome year, and he wanted all their support. He hoped there wonld be no bickering in the 'iouncil, and that all their energies would be centred in the most serious question with which they had to deal at present. He trusted every support would be given to the committee which had to deal with the question. No ono knew what difficulties he had had to encounter ; how he had been hampered— he would not say bullied—during the past few days. There had been no committees or chairmen, and he lied been forced to take into his own hands the dealiag with certain matters. He trusted the Council would endorse his actions, and admit that tie steps which he had taken were for the benefit of the town. As he had been elected Mayor, he looked •to them to support him in con- ducting the business of the town. (Applause.) Be would do his best this year at least. (Renewed ap- plaus .)
DEPUTY-MAYOR.
The MAYOR appointed Alderman Francomb Deputy- Mayor.
CHAPLAIN.
The Rev. F. W. Willis was appointed by the Mayor as his chaplain for the ensuing 12 months.
ELECTION OE' ALDERMEN.
The election of aldermen was then proceeded with. The retiring aldermen were Messes. John Burgess, Joseph Harrison, Charles John Holmes, and Thomas Hindmarsh Sutton.

A rush was now made for the ballot papers by the Councillors, who having filled them up commenced to hand them up to the Mayor, but this was only done with a considerable amount of difficulty. All the Coun- cillors endeavnured to reach the Mayor at once, and consequently caused a considerable amount of turmoil. In the midst of this Councillor Shaw-Green facetiously remarked to the Mayor that the Councillors at the end of the table were compelled to mount thd chairs. Messrs. Sutton, Harrison, and Holmes were at this time in the ante-room, and Mr. Burgess was not present. Mr. Blackhurst retained his seat in the Council Chamber during the voting. The MAYOR eventually declared the result as follows : —Holmes, 22 ; Harrison, 29 ; Sutton, 29 ; Blackhurst, 16 • Burgess, 7. He then added : I declare that Messrs. Holmes, Harrison, Sutton, and Blackhurst are duly elected aldermen of this borough. The following is a summarised analysis of the voting. Councillors Plurnpton, Monks, Browne, Fleming, Shaw Green, Flood, Blackhnrst, Bolton, Wilkinson, Muir, I Roberts, Greening, Cannel!, Beaman, and Garner, and Alderman Wright plumped for Blackhurst. Total 17. Alderman Chandley, Alderman Greenall, Councillors R. Fairclough, J. Fairelough, Hepherd, Muir. and Smet- burst voted for Alderman Burgess. Total 7. Council- 1 lors Heaton, Tinsley, Hill, Smethurst, Ashton, Hutchin- son, and Alderman Francomb did not vote for either . Alderman Burgess or Councillor Blaukhurst. The whole ' of the 29 members of the Council who were present voted unanimously for the re-election of Aldermen tiuti,n and Harrison. There were 22 votes for Alderman Holmos'A re-election. . . .

Alderman Houtm, in returning thanks, as senior alderman said : I had looked forward to the 9t,h of November as a day of emancipation from the duties end responsibilities of office, but the Council have thought b right to give me another term. As they have done so, I thank them very much indeed for the honour they have conferred upon me, and I will do what I can in the future to serve the interests of the town. (Applause.) Alderman IlLacrtupasr : I thank you for the honour you have done me in electing me to this position, and I hope I shall so discharge the duties that will devolve upon me in such a manner that you will have no need to regret having done so. At the same time lam pained to have taken the position under the circumstances, but the office has been thrust upon me, as it were. I should have been more pleased if Mr. Burgess had retired from from the scene ; I should have been more pleased, and it would have given me a great deal more satisfaction, if I could have taken the office under more agreeable circumstances. I thank you for the honour you have done me this afternoon. (Rear, hear.) Alderman HAniusow : If custom and tunige did not oblige me to acknowledge the kindnees that I have just received at the hands of the Council, the amenities of life would prompt me to such an extent that to do so would be irresistible. I cannot conceal from myself, gentlemen., that you have again paid me a very high compliment. I believe this is the twenty-ninth time that I ought to have been present when th” Mayor was elected. Owing to an unfortunate circumstance, I was prevented from being here this morning.. Twenty-nine years is not so long—Alderman Holmes has served the Council much longer, and served it faithfully and well. (Applause.) Lam proud to be elected again, and I can only assure you that my conduct, so far as I can pos- sil•ly control it, shall be equal to the emergencies of the case and the position, whatever it may be. I thank you very sincerely for again reposing your confidence in me in electing me to what I consider a very great honour. (Applause.) Alderman Sums; :1 also beg to thank the Council for having elected me as an alderman of the borough, and I can only say that I shall endeavour to deserve their con- fidence. At any rate in my case, I must congratulate the members on their great discretion. (Laughter.) APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEES.

The followirut committees were appointed : Warcu.—The Mayor, Aldermen Chandley, Francomh, Greenall,Harrison,Platt,and Sutton ; Councillors Cannel!, Fleming, and Heaton. FlNANCE.—Alclertnen Holmes and Greenall ; Council- lors James Fairlough, Fleming, Shaw Green, Hepherd, Monks, Tinsley, and Walker. DISTRESS AMONGST THE JEWS OF LONDON. PROPOSED BAREFOOTED MARCH.

Mr. Lewis Lyons presided at a meeting of the Jewish Unemployed Committee, when is was decided that a letter should be sent to the Chief Rabbi, asking him to receive a deputation from the Committee to lay before hint facts concerning the great distress prevailing amongst the Jewish workmen of all trades in the East End of London. The letter went on to express the belief of the committee that the Chief Rabbi might use his great influence over the employers of labour, by asking them to reduce the hours of labour i order to absorb a portion, at least, of the Jewish unemployed. The committee also desire to consult him on the pro- posed barefooted march of the Jewish unemployed through the streets of London. There were at least 10,003 skilled Jewish workmen partly or wholly unem- ployed, and the dependents upon these, supposing each to have only one child, would be 20,000. Thus they had at the very lowest estimate 30,000 Jewish people of the East End of London on the verge of starvation.
THE STRANDED BRITISH WARSHIP.

The last reports from Ferrol are to the effect that ;he Howe rests on the rocks without any signs of breaking up, and the opinion is growing that the great ironzlad may yet be saved and repaired. Men-of-war with salv- age appliances on board are on their way from Ports- mouth to Ferrol. and private companies of salvors are affeady on the spot with their steamers. It is asserted that the Royal Sovereign, which was the leading ship, also touched the reef, and that the sudden change in the course of the flagship compelled the Howe te slacken speed just at the spot where the currant runs strongest, with the result that she lost her " way" and was swung on to the rocks.

div.head: RUNCORN :SCHOOL BOARD EVENING
div.p: RUNCORN :SCHOOL BOARD EVENING
SCHOOLS.

On Tnursday evening the certificates were dis- tributed to those students who successfully passed the examination in arithmetic in connection with the " Union ,of Lancashire and Oheshire Institutes." The examination, which took place in February last year, was superintended by Messrs. George Roberts and Peter Davies, and it is gratifying to report that out of the number who voluntarily pre- sented themselves for examination, 10 successfully passed first class, and:9 second class. Mr. Moulton, the head master, distributed the certificates as follows:

FIRST CLASS.—EI. Holt, J. E. Rowles, Jos. Percival, R. H. Bridges, T. H. Carruthers, Geo. Pennington, E. A. Ward, W. T. Howard, J. H. Houghton, Geo. McNorton. Swum) Cratss.--W. Cook, S. Miles, J. R. Brown, G. Kay, J. W. Brown, G. W. Holt, J. T. Rowland, J. H. Austin. _ _ .

Before the certificates were distributed, Mr. Moulton pointed out that a similar examination in arithmetic, and probablyin other subjects also, would be held in connection with the same institution during the present session, and.strongly urged all those present to sit for at least one of the subjects, and he trusted they would be as successful as those last session. On the same evening the Afghan and Egyptian wars were illustrated by means of the oxy-hydrogen lantern. The views were explained by the head master, and Mr. Rosser manipulated the lantern. History is one of the subjects taught in the Evening School this year, and in order to make the sub- ject thoroughly attractive and interesting, the lantern will from time to time be called into requisition. That th,s mode of teaching history is appreciated by the pupils, was amply preyed by the careful attention they gave during the whole of the lesson.

div.head: ST. EDWARD'S BRA.NCH OF THE LEAGUE OF THE CROSS, RUNCORN.
div.p: ST. EDWARD'S BRA.NCH OF THE LEAGUE OF THE CROSS, RUNCORN.

A magic lantern entertainment and concert in aid of St. Edward's League of the Cross Brass Band was held recently in the Catholic Schoolrooms, Mill Brow, and was largely attended by an appreciative audience. After a few preliminaries were gone through, Mr. I homae Cook was elected Chairman and master of ceremonies for the evening. The Chair- man, in opening the proceedings, alluded in laudatory terms to the great work performed by the League of the Cross, since its formation amongst the Catholic people of Runcorn, and wished the League success in the future. The first part of the programme consisted of some pretty and interesting views of Mount St. Bernard, and its famous Convent and dogs. The magic lantern Slides were worked by Mr. William Haxworth, and as each scene was thrown on the canvas, its nature and meaning was ably explained by Mr. Cook, to the satis- faction of everyone present. A short interval took place, 1 during which St. Edward's League of the Cross Brass Band discoursed some sweet music, under the con- ductorship of Mr. Ainsworth. Afterwards, Mr. James, ,at Widnes, sang with deep feeling and tenderness, that ever-green song," Our bands have met." He was accom- panied by the violin, played by Mr. Thompson, from Widnes. Mr. Cogley's concertina song,- in which he made that popular instrument imitate the female voice, called forth rounds of applause, and as an encore he played " When other lips." Having now finished for a while, with the sentimental, there was an excellent comic, in the person of Mr. Moran, whose rendering of the "Irish colleen," accompanied by a" rale ould Irish jig," drew down thunders of applause from every por- tion of the house. Encored, he gave " The Shannon's silvery stream," in which hie capabilities as an accom- plisheitstep dancer, were displayed to advantage once more. Mr. Hoxworth's Lancashire sketch was thoroughly enjoyed, being of a humorous nature. Mr. Edwardson, another Widnes gentleman, sang with feeling and taste Shat pretty Swiss air, " Up in the mountains so high," following which Mr. James sang a comic, entitled "There is no room for me," and he gave as an encore another favourite comic, entitled " Mr. Johnson." After this the stage was vacated in favour of Mr. Edwardson, whose rare song " Dutch girl Susannah," was well received. The violin solo of Mr. Thompson, "Killarney," held the audience spellbound, hut when the favourite of the evening, Mr. Moran, once more appeared on the boards, in his usual comic way, and treated the audience to another of his laughable productions, called a " Member of ould Ireland," the cheering was simply deafening. A few more magic lantern scenes, in which several prominent members of St. Edward's Branch of the League of the Cross, were thrown on the canvas, elicited well deserved praise. The playing of God save the Queen by the band, brought an enjoyable evening's entertainment to p. close.—Contributed.

div.head: TABERNACLE DIVISION. DR. PIERSON'S FIRST SERMON.
div.p: THE TABERNACLE DIVISION. DR. PIERSON'S FIRST SERMON.

The Rev. Dr. Pierson preached his first sermon since his recent arrival in England at the Metropolitan Taber- nacle on Sunday morning, the vast building being filled. The rev gentleman will occupy the pulpit for the next six months, and despite the divisions which have been witnessed in the congregaticn lately, his preaching is likely to preve a source of strong attraction, and to command large attendances. At the conclusion of his sermon, Dr. Pierson made a few personal remarks. He would rather drop dead there that morning than go on preaching to that congregation in any dependence on rhetoric or logic, poetry or philosphy. His only concern was how out of love to every man, woman, and child in that church, which with great unanimity had invited hint in June last to begin that ministry amongst them, he might represent not a part of the Church, but the whole of it.

div.head: PARIS FUND AND THE IRISH PARTY. MRS. PARNELL'S MONETARY AFFAIRS.
div.p: THE PARIS FUND AND THE IRISH PARTY. MRS. PARNELL'S MONETARY AFFAIRS.

The "Freeman's Journal" states that at a special meeting of the Irish Parliamentary party, on Monday, a letter was read from Archbishop Croke, in which he con- sents to act as one of the trustees in the matter of the Paris funds. He asks the leaders of the Irish party to come together inn friendly way to arrange for the nomi- nation of the other trustees, and says he will be pre- pared to submit to them the names of four gentlemen on whose honour and integrity Irishmen may implicitly rely. Messrs. Davitt and Dillon were appointed a com- mittee to meet his Grace and take the steps necessary. The London correspondent of the "Freeman's Jour- nal" is in a position to say that a receiving order has been granted in the Brighton Bankruptcy Court against Mrs. Catherine Parnell, 10, Walsingham-terrace, West Brighton, on her own petition. The date of the applica- tion was the 2nd of the present month, but no particu- lars have been disclosed. It is expected that this will have serious consequences on the release of the Paris funds. The Press Association has received a telegram from its Brighton correspondent confirming the statement that the order applied for has been made. The statement of affairs, however, has not yet been lodged, and will not be for two or three days.

div.head: FEARFUL OUTRAGE AND MURDER OF A LITTLE GIRL.
div.p: FEARFUL OUTRAGE AND MURDER OF A LITTLE GIRL.

A terrible crime was committed at Witton, Blackburn, on Tuesday, the victim being Alice Barnes, aged nine, daughter af a Witton farmer. At about one o'clock in the afternoon the child was sent to drive some cows to a field at Witten Park, and was not afterwards seen alive by her father. Within a short space of the time alter she left home the was found dead near Witton Park gates, with a handkerchief stuffed tigktiv into her mouth. The ground about the spot where the body was lying showed signs of a struggle having taken place, and there were evidences that the child had been sub- jected to the most brutal violence. Soon after the murder was discovered the police received from two sources description of a man who was loitering about near Witton Park gates at the time when the child was driving the cows, and for this man vigorous search was made, but up to a late hour on Tuesday it had not been successful.

Most important new evidence was obtained by the Blackburn police late on Tuesday evening. A lad named Riding, a son of General Feilden's gamekeeper, states that, as he was running down the lane, which is very steep, he came upon the murderer, carrying his victim through the park wicket-gate. He was so terrified at the sight that he ran back to another part entrance, where he gave the alarm. Another youth, named Riley, living in a house overlooking the lane, saw a man run- ning away, looking over his sheulder as he went, and the lad remarked to his father, who was dining at the time, that he looked like a man who had committed a crime. Other witnesses saw the man cross the main road and pass through a back road into Vauxliall-st. Here he went into a passage and took off his muffler, with which he wiped his bleeding and muddy face. Finding that Vauxhall-st. was a cul-de-sac, he returned, and, passing down another passage, jumped over a wall and ran off across the fields. A remarkable circum- stance is that when it was discovered that the child had been gagged, the finders of the body would not allow the handkerchief to be removed until the police arrived, although the body was quite warm. The police made two or three arrests on Tuesday night, but the prisoners were liberated after inquiry had been made respecting them. The inquest was opened on Wednesday afternoon, when evidence was given as to the finding of the body and as to a man having been seen loitering about and watching the child as she was driving cows into Witten Park shortly before the murder was discovered. The inquiry was adjourned until next Thursday. The police have not yet succeeded in gaining a clue to the whereabouts of the murderer of the child Alice Barnes. On Thursday two bloodhounds were taken to the scene of the crime, in the hope that they might, as in another notorious Blackburn case, assist in the cap- ture of the murderer ; but, as might have been expected considering that two days had passed since the murder was committed and that the place had in the interval been visited by thousands ol people, the trial was a failure. There were two or three cases oa Tleurs- day of arrest on suspicion, but they came to nothing.

div.head: GREAT COTTON TRADE STRIKE.
div.p: THE GREAT COTTON TRADE STRIKE.

80,000 'OPERATIVES IDLE. One of the greatest strikes of recent years in the Lan- cashiie cotton trade commenced on Saturday. The operatives, it may be said, deny that it is a strike at all, as they allege that when the ,masters enforce a reduction of wages by closing the mills against those who refuse to accept it it is a lock-out. The dispute of which this is the outcome began to take form as long ago as Easter. There was then a strike at Stalybridge, and in order to support the members of the Master Cotton Spinners' Federation there the whole of the members of the Federation locked theirmen out. At that time the cotton trade was known to be in a bad state, and there was more than a suspicion that the masters simply wanted to relieve the market by reducing the output. Prices im- proved to some extent,'but not very materially, and at the end of July the master cotton spinners made a demand for a reduction of 10 per cent, in wages. This was rejected by the operatives, and the employers also became divided upon the question of enforcing it. Im- mediately afterwards a five per cent, reduction was pro- posed. This also was rejected at a joint meeting, the operatives making a counter proposal that the produc- tion should be limited by means of short time. The employers then gave a month's notice of the reduction to the men's trades unions, and a week ago they gave individual notices. These notices expired on Saturday, and the strike or lock-out commenced. The operative cotton spinners on Saturday held a meeting in Man- chester, which was attended by delegates from all the four counties engaged in the cotton trade. It was then reported that 7,619 spinners would be locked out, and that 53,000 to 54,000 operatives Of one class or another would have to stop. At the same time it was stated that the lock-out had collapsed entirely at Stockport, and very nearly so in Bury and Rochdale. 'Oldham, therefore, will be the great seat of battle, as lit has been on previous occasions. It was decided that an extra levy of 4s. per week should be made upon the men who remain at work, and, as they constitute two-thirds of the whole, they will be able to maintain the union men who are out of work for for a considerable period, especially as the society has a large balance to its credit at the banker.. Of the 53,000 who will be thrown )ut of work, however, no fewer than 20,000 are non- unionists, and they will have nothing but their own re- sources to rely upon. Mr. Mawdsley, secretary of the Operative Spinners' Association, stated on Saturday that the workers were fully prepared for the struggle, and were now better supplied with funds. They would receive 10s. a week strike pay, and an allowance for each child, and grants from the local associations. Cardroom hands are not so well off, and if outside assistance is asked for, it will be on their behalf. In an interview with a Manchester correspondent on, Monday afternoon, Mr. Mawdsley, secretary of the Operative Cotton Spinners, said the position of the operatives in reference to the proposals for the settle- ment of the dispute by arbitration had been misunder- stood. They were as anxious as anybody to avoid the hardships and sufferings which a long-continued struggle—perhaps through the whole winter—might 'entail. They were quite ready to meet in conference either the Mayor of Manchester, the joint board of con- ciliation, or other person or body of persons who might be especially deputed to meet them by the masters' federation ; but they could not treat with anybody who did not directly represent the federation. That was the one condition they made. In Mr. Mawdsley's opinion the effect of the strike will be most severely felt at Mossley, near Oldham. In that village 750 out of 810 spinners are out of employment, and this means that 5,200 workpeople are stopped. 'The Oldham Masters' Association on Monday issued a return showing that over ten million spindles are repre- sented in the association, of which over eight millions are stopped. The total running and paying the penalty .is 1,560,000, and those working short time and paying are 156,000. THE COLLAPSE OF TIIE REDUCTION. MOVEMENT Al' STOCKPORT.

A Stockport correspondent writes that an extraordin- ary state of thine has tranipired at Stockport, where niany mills are connected with the Federation. It was decided at a meeting of the local association of masters to agree to the reduction, and the operatives expected that thsy would receive notice of the redaction. How- ever., a difference of opinion arose amongst the masters and the day upon which the notices should have been posted went by, and the only announcement made was at several of the mills, where notice was given that it was the intention of the masters to work short time. At these mills the operatives will only work about half- time, and it is stated that this will override the rule prescribing a penalty for working when the other mills are stopped. It is expected that in Stockport short time will be generally adopted.
INQUEST ON A CHILD Dl CEASED FLONI SMALLPDX.
EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT OF A JURYMAN.

On Saturday, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held in inquest at the Cemetery Inn, Warrington, concern- ing the death, on the previous Thursday, of Sarah Ann Moody, aged eight years, daughter of a forge- man, who had been removed to the smallpox hospi- tal, and who resides at 36, Pierpoint-et., the child having died, under circumstances pointing to neglect, and there having been no notification to the authorities of the fact that the child was suffer- ing from mallpox. Mr. J. C. Gilroy was: foreman of the jury. The juriors having been sworn, the Coroner explained that they would have to proceed with him to view the body, as the law compelled them to do this; but he had made arrangements by which, he believed they could comply with the law, and at the same time keep themselves free from infection. They would make their formal view at some distance off.—The Coroner and jury then proceeded to view the body, which lay in the cemetery mortuary. On their return Mr. Critchley, one of the jury, took d-bjection to another of them (Mr. Henry Welsby) being allowed to re-enter the room, on the ground that he had persisted in entering the mortuary while the other jurors remained outside.—The Coroner said he would excuse Mr. Welsby (who was down- stairs the inquest being in the large upper room) from attending.—Mr. Critchley asked Dr. Gornall, who was present as a witness, if he did not think it advisable that Mr. Welsby, in the interests of Mr. Allinson, should quit the premises.—The Coroner : Of coulee they must fight that out between themselves. I have asked Dr. Gornall, and he considers it was a very injudicious act.—Mr. Critchley asked the police who were present, to see that Mr. Welsby left the premises, remarking that he had no right to remain endangering those present at the inquest, as well as dr. Allinson.— Inspector Cox proceeded downstairs, to carry out the request.—The Coroner censured Mr. Welsby for his act. Be had, he said, unlocked the door of the building, in which the body was, and entered it to view the body, apparently out of pure bravado. Be closed the door after him, and none of them knew what he did inside. He would, for the safety of himself and the jury, excuse him from attending. He commented on the practice of viewing bodies as unnecessary, except in cases of mur- der, and as something that ought to be dispensed with by the legislature. The Coroner then pointed out to the jury the issues they had to consider.—Ann Moody, the deceased's mether, was then called, and gave formal evidence as to the name and address of herself and the child.—The Coroner pointed out to her that it was alleged that the child's death had been hastened by her neglect, and that if the jury found this had been so, they might send her for trial. She could either give evidence as to the cause of death, or keep her mouth closed, but whatever she said. would be put down in writing and might be used against her. He asked her if she wished to be examined as a witness.—Mrs. Moody, who appeared perfectly dazed : I have not anything to say, sir.—The Coroner : I don't think I shall examine you under the circum- stances. I don't think it is fair and right.—Witness : I will answer any questions.—The Coroner: But you are not legally represented. To had better sign your name. The witness then signed her testimony.—Annie Jones, Mrs. Moody's next door neighbour, deposed to being called on the Thursday morning about half-past ten into Mr. Moody's house by his wife, as the child was dying. She said she had been to see Dr. Adams, and she went again and saw the assistant who said he would come as quickly as possible. Dr. Gornall came first,however. The child died between 11 and half-past. The Coroner said if Dr. Adams had come he could not have done any good.— Witness said she did not know whether it was a fortnight or three weeks since Mr. Moody was taken to the hospital. The baby was removed on the Thursday night to the Small-pox Hospital. The deceased child was in a crib in the kitchen by the fire covered with clothes. She saw tea in a cup and grapes and biscuits which Mrs. Moody had bough: for the child, but no chicken broth or meat tea. She had slept in her house and nursed the child, and was up late at night with it. She was sober when witness went in to see the child. She saw nothing to lead her to suppose she neglected the child.—Dr. Gornall deposed that an Octo- ber 13th he visited the house and found a woman Mrs. Moody's sister in bed, suffering from a mild attack of smallpox, and she had recently had a miscarriage. She , had since been removed to the hospital. The house was In an indescribable condition of filth. The patient was under the influence of drink, and Mrs. Moody was maudlin drunk. The father was taken to the hospital suffering from smallpox on the 25th ult. He walked to the hospital, but by whose permission witness did not know. On the morning of the 26th the case of a child lin the house was notified, and it was conveyed to the hospital, where it still was. Witness again visitedllthe house on the evening of Thursday. He found on a " squab " in the kitchen the dead body of the child Sarah Ann Moody. It was evident it had died from smallpox. He saw no meat or drink, and no grapes, but there was no light in the kitchen. Mrs. Moody had had experience of other eases of smallpox, but she was in such an alcoholised condition that he did not think she would know it was smallpox. If she had been sober she would have known on the second day. He made a poet mortem examination, with the assistance of I his Ben that morning. The child had been allowed to scratch all the pustules off its face. The body was generally emaciated, but she had been a fine child. The organs generally were healthy, but there was complete absence of fat. The conditions were such as one would generally find in a case of smallpox. The girl had not been vaccinated ; as also was the other child now in the hospital. The deceased child, from the fact of being unvaccinated, had very little chance of re- covery. There was neglect to begin with. The child had had one of the worst forms of the disease. He cer- tainly thought the child would have lived longer if it had not been neglected,because the child in the hospital, though unvaccinated,was getting better. There was no food undergoing digestion in either the deceased's stomach or intestines. The child was covered with lice and filth. He should say there had been general neglect and inattention.—The Clroner asked Mrs. Moody if she had any questions to ask.—Mrs. Moody : As he has said it, let him stick to it. God above knows all.—ln reply to a juror, as to why the child Sarah Ann Moody was not removed at the same time as the father, since it was suffering about the same time, Dr. Gornall said he was not the private medical attendant of the family, and it was not notified to him that the child had small- pox, and probably Dr. Adams never saw it. The home was in such a state as not to be fit for even a private practitioner to go to.—Police-Sergeant Smith deposed to finding Mrs. Moody in a helpless state of drunkenness at her house on the Thursday. He spoke to her at the door but could get no answer, and started vomiting close into his face. He did not enter the house, as it was in such a filthy state, but got what particulars he could as to the child's death from Mrs. Jones.—Mrs. Moody denied that she was drunk, and said she never tasted spirits, and never had more than a gill of beer when she had been working hard. The Lord above knew it. She denied also that the house was in a filthy state, and suddenly burst into tears.—The Coroner then summed up. He explained to the jury that in dealing with the question of alleged neglect they must remember that evva if the child would not have recovered with proper care, it would be a criminal act on the part of the mother if she hastened its death. It might be that she had not money to provide ti e child with food; still in that case it would have been her duty to apply to the Relievinff Officer. He pointed that though the jury might coasider her not sufficiently culp- able to be seat for trial on a g raver charge, yet she might under recent legislation be brought up and fined for the minor neglect.

div.head: TFrE VERDICT.-DR. GORNALL PROTESTS.
div.p: TFrE VERDICT.-DR. GORNALL PROTESTS.

The jury having privately considered the evidence for about 20 minutes, returned the following verdict We find that the child died from smallpox, and that the case would be met by your administering a mild re- buke to the mother with regard to her neglect in not notifying the authorities at the time the child took ill. We wish also to add a rider that we consider the town authorities rather remiss in their duties in not looking after infected houses sufficiently."—Dr. Gornall : May I ask a question, sir; lam the responsible person. Does that mean a condemnation of my conduct? No one else is responsible except rayeelf•—The foreman : Then of course, you take all the brunt of it.—Dr. Gornall : I think it is the most absurd conclu- sion that has ever been come to, in the history of I British juries. I never heard such a thing in my life.- -The Coroner addressing Mrs. Moody, said she ought to have gone to the authorities, and told them that her child was suffering from smallpox. As she had already seem her husband, her sister, and her other child suffer- ing from the same complaint she must have known what was the matter with deceased. It was a most remark- able thing that after the 25th and 26th October, when her husband and child were removed, and the house and bed and bedding disinfected,the house got into the state in which it was seen on the 3rd November.--Dr. Gornall again expressed his astonishment that the jury should make the assertion they had.—A juror protested against Dr. Gornall making such observations.—The Coroner : The doctor has no right to comment upon your verdict.
