MEDICAL MALL, ABERDARE, WALES.
RECLAIMING A FALLEN WOMAN AY TITE POLICE COURT.

" She's about the worst case we have," said the Chief Constable "she will not keep away from the drink, but she has very respectable parents." Mr. Garnett and Mr. Guest, the two magistrates at court on Tuesday, had paused, at a loss to know what to do with the female prisoner before them. It was liodelia linockton, a young woman scarcely 21 years of age, but who had now made her 62nd appearance in court. Her life since she was about 17 has consisted of a consecutive running of one month in jail and one month out. The police know her as they know their helmets, and she is almost as regular an attendant in , court as Sergeant Chantler himself. In her more reck- less days she has appalled the bench by dancing in the- dock, and threatening to shy her clogs at them. On this occasion she was charged with being drunk and riotous the night before. But she appeared to have lost all her recklessness, and stood quiet and worn-out looking. There was an unbroken silence bra few moments. Then Mr. Garnett said kindly ;—" Arn't you getting tired of living this life p" Her head drooped, and , moved in the affirmative. " Wouldn't you like to reform ?" She held her head down, and scraped the floor with her clog, but gave no answer. "Surely you would like to lead a better life P" No answer. " I wish I could help you out of your terrible state ?" A deep silence in court only broken by Bodelia's clog scraping the floor. " Look here,girl, think of the filthy wretched life you are leading,and think of your age—your parents —the terrible future before you. Now, say, woulernt you like to go into some home and reform ?" The girl raised her haggard face. Sonic sensitive chord seetnsd to have been touched. A tear glittered in her eye and rolled down her cheek, and with a husky voice she said "I'll go home to my—my—father and mother." "No not to your father's home yet. Go with Mr. Taylor, the missionary, to one of the homes in Liverpool !" She paused for some moments, then looked Mr. Garnett in. the face and said :—" I will." Ihirin7 the afternoon Bodelia was taken by the court missionary- ta one of the Liverpool homes, where it is hoped she will have strength enough to mend her ways.

A CONSTABLE BRUTALLY MALTREATED AT LATCHFORD. On Monday, at the Warrington Borough Po/ice Court, before the Mayor (Alderman Greenell) and Aldermen Harrison and Francomb, Frederick Leonard, Thomas Clare, and Thomas Alfred Bell were charged with assaulting P.C. Jones whilst in the execution of his duty at Latchford on Saturday „night. The officer stated that whilst on duty in Knntsford-road at ten minutes to twelve on Satur- day night, he saw the three defendants in company with two more men coming from the direction of War- rington. They turned up Wash-lane, behaving in a very disorderly manner, shouting and singing. He overtook them opposite the church and cautioned them. They then behaved better, and presently another man joined: them. They took him over the bridge at the crossing,. and returned without him, and again became very dis- orderly. He once more cautioned them, whereupon Leonard struck him on the side of the neck. As there were five of them he struck him in return, and he fell.. The two other defendants and one of the other men get hold of him from behind and pulled him down, ant while on the ground they ticked him in a most shameful manner. He eventually got up, and took Clare into cus- tody. In struggling with him he VMS again thrown to the ground. and kicked unmercifully. Be at last managed to get up, and proceeded down Wash-lane, covered with blood and dirt. At the bottom of the lane he had to support himself against the rsilirigs. A man took him into No. 3, Wash-lane, He was in a dazed condition, and hardly knew what he was doing. Even- tually a sergeant came to him. From inquiries made it was ascertained that Leonard lived at 32, Frederick- street, and he was arrested there. They had great difficulty in getting him out of the house, and down to the police station. The other defendants had been arrested since.—When charged, Leonard replied that he left the other defendants at the bridge. Clare alleged that the constable struck one of them, and the other defendant said he knew nothing about the matter.—Bell now alleged that the officer was drunk.—F.S. Row- bothain, P. C. Almon and Inspector Spinks deposed that P.C. Jones was sober at different times on Saturday night.—Ainson said be met the defendants that night about 200 yards trona* the Warrington side of the Black Bear bridge; they s.ore shouting and he cautioned them. —ln answer to Clare lie now said if they had not been quieter he should have struck one of them to quieten him. The defendants were each sentenced to three months, imprisonment with hard labour. Joseph Borne, another of the gang, was chsrged on Tuesday with assaulting P.C. Jones on Saturday night, in Knutsford-road.—The officer now stated that Horne kicked him in the eye.—lnspecter Spinks inforined their worships that this gang of young fellows were a terror to the neighbourhood, a!!d scarcely any respectable person could pass by witleatt being assatiited. A TIMM seem tep( -he two classes of Contrast_ People who tuts deserving of the

cumemseration of a sympathetic public just. now. One class isethat of the unem- ployed, anclithe other is composed of American millionaires'. Their tribulations arise from differ- ent causes, he fact from diametricallye opposite causes. TS, put it in brief, the ,millionaires possess too much of this woeld's goodsewhile the unemployeelliave a good deal too little to ensure a comfortable existence. The unemployed are at the present tineepand especiaiDy in Londou,hringing their grievances and their needs 'under the notice of the autbovities by the familiar nietho&of demon- strations and. elepntations, and • there appears to be a pretty general acknowledgement- that there is but toownueb likelihood of the prevalence of a great amount ot distress in our large • towns dur- ing the coming winter.. The woes at the million- aire spring, largely oat of the. possession of an exceeteive amount of that wealth, of which so many of his fellow rneneare greatly;inneed. An American writer, writing in an Ameriean journal, tells. me that it is a eturprising and. distressing sight teewalkthrough the streets efothat part of New York which is devoted largely tomillienaires. Their rith•people, he sem. seem to live in prisons, or in houses which careenly be cerapaned to pri- sons. The lower windows are heavily barred with iron and the area doors are built of iron. The a-ent doors at thetop of the_ stepsopen with a rattle and clash, like doors ina,gaol, because they sea fitted with chains and. bolts and bars, besides the locks. %leer, warlike, .spike-pointed bits of iron fence areenade by the thousand to fit in the meter lower corner of each perlieur window, so that no burglar can step from the front-door stepeto, the windowsill to break thiough and steal. Inside the houses there is an elaborate arrange- ment of secret wins and burglar alarms, and the bed chenabers of the lord and lady of the house; are supplied 'with the calleboxes of the private, raessfeager companies. Aerich wine-Seller, it is said, has shown much ingenuity in guarding is mousy and his valuables against the wiles of the enterprising burglar. The -main staircase of his Ileum is so connected with bells and pistols that no one can ascend it without setting up sufeeient alarms to awaken the whole neighbourhood. The.. regular police ,have not the entire confidence.of the New York millionaireseeed therefore special watch— men are engaged, and these axe armed with clubs. and pistolteend paid by private contributions. The VANDERBE,ICs employ -a. special detective to guard the costly railing with whial4 with vulgar ostenta- tion, they have surrounded their Istlw, Xork palace ; and, it is said; theyrarely give a reception or a ball without having detectives mingling with their guests, and dressed in every wayflike them- selves, to see that nothing is stolen off the mantels and the buffets'. Such is one of the strange con- trasts produced by nineteenth century eivili- vation. On tha one hand great gatherings of un- employed clamouring for a bare subaiatence, and, on the other hand,, millionaires with, wealth beyond the "-dreams of avarice," and, yet ,oprived of-the full enjoyment of life by the, very vastness of their accumulations.
•MERE is something which strikes Architecture. one as perhaps partaking of the

character of ungenscions irony in the seleetion of architecture EiS the subject of the first coa-Zee 0 University Extensien Lectures in Warrington. If there is , a • town of any pretensions to commercial importance al to population in existence in Great Britain. in which there is necessity for inculcation of, the principles of architecture it is Warrington, Our local commerce, in the carrying out of that ambi- tious spirit of enterprise which has given our town the proud distinction,we believe,of having the larg- est number of industries possessed by any placu of its size in the kingdom, has destroyed "au cla, of the natural beauty f-a which Warrington waagenera- ' tions ago remarkable. But in exchange for the amenities of nature which have thus been sacrifi- ced by the ruthless Moloch of commerce, we have not had supplied any of those amenities of art, if we may so express it, in the shape of fine and sightly edifices which many towns 'nOt larger than Warrington can boast. Considering the destruc- tion of natural beauty that has been brought about

through the necessary progress of our industry, 1 the claims and necessities of Warrington to some- thing like aestheticism in its public buildings, are all the more imperative. Absorbed as the town is just now in the struggle with amalignant disease which is demanding the utmost energies of the authorities to cope with it,and seems some- times to threaten to overmaster theni, the present is hardly the most opportune time to broach the question of local architecture. The only phase of that subject with which the Town Council are likely to concern themselyee at all seriously, for some months to come, is the , architecture of a new smallpox hospital, which the ' exigencies of the apparently increasing epidemic, may possibly ere long demand. But the com- mencement of the course of lectures on architec- ture gives us some occasion for comment on the subject at, this time ; and the reading of a paper at the Liverpool Royal Institution on Monday evening by Mr. T. MELLARD READE, FILLBA., in which he dealt with archi- tectural matters furnishes us with an ad- ditional prompting for some remarks on the subject. It is satisfactory to have confirmed by Mr. Reade an impression that we have long had, that there is an in creasing disposition to employ architects, and that a great improvement is tak- ing place in the design of public buildings and in the appearance and beauty of the streets. Mn Reader in his paper remarked,censoriously on that architectural monster, the ierry builder, and his wretched productions, and concluded that even he in time would be reached by the higher level of 'intelligence which education would bring about. 'That class of houses of which the, Yankee said that if you leaned against the end of a row of them and laughed, you would bring down the whole , row, is too numerous ; and some legislation, such as that which in America holds the jerry builder responsible to a certain extent for his architec- tyr d iniquities, is most desirable in England, so that the shanties of habitations that disgrace our towns, may, at least in some degree, be placed uoticr the ban of the law. That advance in architecture which will ensure not only sightli- ners and beauty in our main streets, but also comfort and decency in the homes of the poorest, is the only true f civilisation in architecture, and it tis to be hoped that the time is fast approaching whew local authorities will begin to realize this fact.

•Soma people seem,to have anticipated The- Town ,‘ a scene" or at all events " some- ' Council. thing lively" at theWarrington Thwn Council meeting on Wednesday. What or where tbe scene was to originate from we do not know, b ut in any case, it is satisfactory_ to note that no " scene" Was enacted on this occasion. The meet- in g if not dull, was decorous,, and there was an absence of friction of any kind, which promises wwell for, the municipal year just entered upon. As everyone knew would be the case, Alderman tam*anLAwas unanimously re-elected mayor; and he enters upon his second year of office with the comnseiousness that the Council fully recognises hi 64 deeive, to act impartially, and to hold the balance, evenly between conflicting opinions and, interests.. Alderman BURGESS, who has for many- years played a conspicuous part, now disappears, from thestage of municipal affairs, and his place in the aldorrnanie seats is taken by Councillor. BLAckmunsr„ who received sixteen votes as. against seven east for Alderman BURGESS: They Sanitary,Committee, as the chairman of which the the lataAL:leirmart figured so prominently, and milita.ntly,-at trines; is also a thing of the past. It has been, broken up, a.-rditsduties have been distributed between two new committees—the Health Cemmittec, and the:Sanitary Works Cok ( mittee., It has been well known for a good while past that the old Sanitary Committee had more work thrown upon it thank could efficiently:per- form, and there is not the slightest fear that the twa new committees will find time to hang heavily ' on their hands. Indeed .each of them is /ace to face with a task which wilt test their administra,- tivecapacity to the utmost. Besides other duties. of 2,,ratiltifarious and important character, the- Health CommitteE. has,, at the very oatset, ,to' grapple with the epidemic which is giving the town. such an unenviable notoriety, and the ratepayers will expsort them to set about 1 thisi part of their work in a well-Jo,usideredi and a vigorous fashion The Sanitary Works Committee hays to. deal with that.. peren- nial problem which the Lartlord and intercepting depots involve—a preblern which is always on the point of being solved) and yet of which there is never a satisfactory solution, it will be seenfrom this that the now defunct Sanitary:, Committee leaves a legacy to its twin progeny which is, likely to keep them engaged for some timely come. Of the other Committees there is little, to be said. They were constituted very much on the old lines, and they will continue to discharge the same cunctions in the body corporate as they did, before.

THE Evicted Tenants Commission is proving to be a great thorn in the side of the Tories. They have evidently, from Lord SALlsisiakm and Mr. BALFOUR downwards, set themselves the task of bringing it into discredit even before it has well begun its work. They will not- suneeed, though their desine to do so springs,.from wery obvious,

causes. The Tory party is, above all else, a landr, lords' party,nnd it is already beginning to be seen that the Commission is a moat offeetive instrument,, for bringing to 'light some of the iniquities of Irish landlordism. It is sincerely to be hoped that Mr. Justice MATTHEW, the president of the Com- mission,, will not carry out his intimation that the 'press. would be excluded in case. the "golden rule of honourable journalism." was not observed, and coiSmarita made upon witnesses and the course of procedure. Already the most intemperate corn, moots have been made on everything connected with the Commission,„ both, by the Tory ress and Tory statesmen, and it is. not difficult tasee that, next to the dissolution of the Commission itself, ;nothing/would be more pleasing to the landlords' ;party than the closing di all the usual cliannas of publicity.

THE letter written by Mr. 11,taav Ftraxiss, which we publish in another column, helps us to see ourselves as others see us, with. regard to the smallpox., that prevails in the toavn. Mr. FURNISS had been engaged to give a lecture in Warrington on the 21st of this month, but he now writes to say that the accounts ha reads of the smallpox are "simply appalling," and he strongly advises the postponement of the 'fixture. The fact of his being a married man with a family would, he says, never allow him "to appear in a town which has brought this epidemic upon itself by stupidly refusing to comply with a preventative which all sensible people have adopted,' In pen- ning the sentence we have just quoted, Mr. Frramss was evidently under a misapprehension. We interpret tbe " preventative" he refers to, to 1

be vaccination, and he seems to have formed the-. impression that Warrington is an anti-vaccination centre. In that, of course, he is mistaken. War- ringtonians have generally, complied with the - law in that respect. Mr. Ftraxiss asks that the note which is sent to him by return of post should. be—disinfected. But he is a humorist, and no doubt, that was a flash of his humour. It will certainly be an awkward incidtait of the epidemic if outsiders begin to ex- pect their Warrington correspondents to put every missive they despatch through a trouble- some purifying process. At the same time all this should be an additional spur to the sanitary autho- rities to wipe away the reproach which the con- tinuance of this epidemic is to the town. To say the least, it is extremely damaging to that repu- ' tation for progress in sanitary matters which has sometimes been claimed for Warrington.

" KILLEmby Protection" is the epitaph, which may fitly be inscribed to the memory of the pre- sent Republican Government of the United States, Mr. CLEVELAND', the democratic candi- - date for the presidency, has swept everything before him to an extent that is not often witnessed in presidential contests.; and • there seems to be a general consensus of opinion in the United States that the main factor. in the great democratic victory was the reaction of feeling against the high protection of the Republican party, and par- ticularly that development of it known as the M`KlNLarr Tariff. The election shows, says a 'prominent member of the Democratic CarsPeige Committee, " that the producers of the country have determined that they will no longer be bur- • dened by excessive taxation for the benefit of the great monopolies." At the same time it would be a mistake to suppose that Protec- tion is at once to be discarded in the United States. Even the Democratic party is not Flee Trade party in the full meaning of the term; and, what is more, by one of those strange de', toral anomalies which sometimes tend to frustrate the carrying out of even the most decisively Pre' notinced public opinion,the victorious party do not seem to have secured a clear majority in the Senate. BLit; after making all allowances, the election of Mr. Cleveland is a most significant and valuable''"tory for the cause of freedom in commercial inter- course.. It will encoura-,e the Democrats to more boldly follow the path they have entered upon 6 yet somewhat timidly and tentatively; while it will, on the other hand,, convince the Republicans that even a great and historical party cantle! afford to subordinate its policy to the interests wealthy monopolists, monopolists, regardless of -those of 'the masses of the people.

div.head: TEMPERANCE CRUSADE -AT RUNOORN.
div.p: TEMPERANCE CRUSADE -AT RUNOORN.

Last night, Mr. Collins, of Manchester, commenced a three days crusade in connection with St. Edward's League at the Cross. Meetings will be held to-day (Saturday) and to-morrow in St. John the Baptist Schoolroom, and there will also be gatherings in the open air. Mr. Collins was one of the first disciples of that great temperance reformer, Father Mathew, and although 80 Years of age, he is yet a vigorous and con- vincing speaaer.and much good is expected to result.

div.p: FOUND DEAD IN THE CANAL AT,WESTON.POINT:.

On Tuesday afternoon at tile Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, an inquest was held on the body of a man un- known, which was found in the Salt Works dock in he Runcorn and Western canal on Sunday. The body had apparantly been in the water three weeks, and seemed to be that of a young Irishman from 25 to 30 years of age. There was nothing in the pockets to lead to identification, but they contained a florin, a shilling, and a halfpenny. A verdict of " Found dead" was returned. THE HEALTH OF RUNCORN.

From the returns of the Registrar-General for the past quarter, it appears that the births in Runcorn numbered 241, and deatos 126. Of the latter 43 were infants under one year, and 20 were those of persons over 60 years. The certified causes of death included one from small-pox,one from measles,one from scarlet lever,l4 from diarrcea,oue from cholera,and eight from violence (which includes accidents). A foot-Oote states that 13 deaths from fever occurred in the Runcorn Urban Sanitary District.

The prisoner protested that he was innocent.— 'Joseph Barker,of Bold, was also committed for trial on a charge of a similar character, the victim of the assault being Sarah Ann Batter, aged 11 years. div.head: – BURNING FATALITIES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: - BURNING FATALITIES AT RUNCORN.

Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, on Monday, held an inquiry at Widnes Accident Hospital, into the circum- stances of the death of Florrie Rankin, aged five years, whose parents reside at 13, Bank-street, Widnes. It appeared that during her mailer's absence from the house on Thursday, the deceased set her clothes on fire while poking the fire with the poker, and she received such injuries that she died nest day.—A verdict cf "Acci- dental death " was returned. —Mr. Brighouse also held an inquest at the Waterloo Hotel, on the body of Margaret Lawlor, nine years of age, of Duke-street, Ditton, On Friday, the 28th ult., the deceased was lying on the hearth, when some cinders fell from the fire, and set her clothes in flames. She lingered for a week, and then succumbed to her injuries. A verdict of " Ac- cidental death " was returned. •

Go to PRITCHARD'S for the best five guinea watch a work- ingman can have —Advt. , TRAINING A SON TO STEAL AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Polk.: Court, on Monday, before Messrs. F. H. Gossage and H. Wade-Deacon, Samuel Mainwar- ing was brought up under a warrant charged with receiving about 6-Cwt. of coal well knowing it to have been stolen from a waggon at West Bank siding, the property of the Hutchinson Trustees. Thomas Main- Waring, a son of the prisoner, twelve years of age, stated that during last week he brought coal about five times a day, and toelt it home ein each occasion. The prisoner saw him take the coal home and knew where he got it from. The Chairman said there was a considerable quantity of coal stolen from West Bank siding by chil- dren, who were sent out for the purpose by their parents. Prisoner would be committed to gaol for twenty-one days with hard labour, and he trusted that this would be a warning to other parents to cease such a regular system of coal stealing.

RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

At &meeting of this organization, held on Saturday evening, when there was a good attendance, the chair- man, Mr. Heesom, introduced the subject of "The Bishop of Chester's licensing scheme." He expressed himself unfavourable to the proposals, and stated that the Gothenburg project had proved a failure. He ac- knowledged that the present licensing system was a great evil, and contended that what was morally wrong - could not be politically right. He urged that they should not be content . with anything less than the granting of local option.—A discussion ensued, in which ' the following gentlemen took part: Messrs. Edward Key, S. M. Temperley, David Smith, Thomas J. Holt, Thomas Cook, and Daniel Bisbrown. The speakers ex- pressed a diversity of opinion. Some thought that the scheme, which was being prepared by Dr. Jayne, would be a step in the right direction, whilst others gave it as their belief that the public conscience would be drugged by money from the trade. JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- , at., and 4, Bridge-st., Runcorn.—Advt. ST. DWARD'S ROMAN' CATHOLIC CHURCH, Rugeoßv. T rmons at this church on Sunday were preached ie by t ev. Father Wiedenmann, S.J., of Ditton College. At nine o'clock over a hundred persons belonging to the Sacred Heart approached the Holy Communion. In the evening the rev, gentleman dealt with the subject of holiness that should exist in all Christian families. After the sermon was read the pontifical decree issued by the Pope in June last, with reference to "The Pious Asso- ciation of the Holy Family," in which his Holiness pointed out that the well-being, whether of individuals or of the community, depended chiefly on the family and the home. The more deeply virtue was rooted in the household, the more effectually religion was impressed upon the Children by the words and example of the fattier and mother, the more did the commonwealth pro- fit. Hence it was of the utmost importance that the society, which was called domestic—that was the family —should not only be holy in its constitution, but should also be governed by holy laws, and that true religion and general Christian life should be carefully and constantly ' cultivated therein. For fear of the true spirit of devo- tion being lost sight of, they had directed the Congre- gation or Rites to draw up statutes, by which Piaus Associations of the Holy Family througheut the Catholic world might be united under one president, who should rule and govern them. In accordance with this decree an association was formed on Sunday evening, when the parish priest, the Rev. Dr. Gaataldi, conferred his autho- rity on Father Wiedenmann, *ho received into fellow- ship 19 families. Rules were adopted for the guidance of the members.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.

A labourer named Daniel Crawley, lodging at 49, Nelson-street, died on Wednesday morning under peculiar circumstances. The deceased left work about nine o'clock on Saturday night, awl on his way home called at a public-house and had three glasses of beer, but was perfectly sober whenbe arrived at his lodgings. He was in the act of unfastening his clogs when he fell forward on the floor, striking his head rather violently. on the tiles. Dr. Allen is of opinion that the deceased had died from inflammation of the brain which might have been hastened by the fall. The inquest was held yesterday before Mr. Brighouse, and a verdict of " Natural causes" was returned. Josces Parrenann keeps spectacles to snit all sights from a shilling a pair.—Adrt. Pierpoint. Euphonium : T. Outhwaite. SALVATION ARMY FUNERAL AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday afternoon the remains of Mr. Joseph Hillidge, Cavvdor-st., were interred in the Runcorn Cemetery. The deceased, who died on Sunday, after a few days' illness,had for some time been associated with the Salvation Army.' The officers, corps, and band met at the barracks, and thence proceeded to the late resi- dence of their departed brother. Here a short service was held, in the open air. The cortege afterwards formed was in the following order :--The banner, the officers, the band, the coffin, borne by four soldiers, the mourners, and a number of the corps. There was a large concourse of people at the cemetery to witness the nerformanco of the obsequies. ThO service was con- ducted by Captain Joseph, and SilOrt addresses were delivered by Mr. Tones and Mr. Hillidge (son of the deceased). Mrs. Bellamy sang ah appropriate solo. If you want &lucky wedding ring go to 51, Ifron-sT.,whera yea will get a present with it.—Advt. SHOCEING FATALITY TO A SAILOR AT WESTON POINT.

On Thursday evening, a sailor named Nathan McLoughlin, oftthe schooner John Wignall, of Fleet- wood, died at the Sailors' Home Inn, Regent-st., Run- corn, from injuries received on Monday night last week, by falling into an empty lock at Weston Point. Another sailor named Charles Weeks, of the schooner Tullock- groun' of Peterhead, was proceeding to his vessel when be fell into the lock, and on recovering from the shock,. he found the deceased lying beside him embedded, in

the mud and unconscious. The raised an alarm, and a watchman brought a rope,and both men *ere drawn to the surface. McLoughlin was unconscious for over a week suffering from concussion of the brain, and death took place as stated. Weeks was fortunate in escaping without Serious injury. The lock is 23 feet deep.—Mr Warsley, coroner, held an inquest on the body yester- day, and a verdict of " Accidental death was returned.

WESLETIN FOREIGN MISSION MEETING AT Rtrttcomq. The annual sermons in connection with Efalton-road Chapel, for the benefit of the Wesleyan Foreign Mission- ary Society, were preached on Sunday,, in the morning by the Rev. P. Pizey of Frodsharn, and in the evening by the Rev. James Hanby. There was a good attend- ance at each service. On Thursday evening the annual meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. J. Simp- son, and on the platform were the Revs, E. R. Eslick, (deputation from Bangalore) ,T. Wilkes,W. Arrowsmith, and J. Flanbey, Messrs. J. R. Frith, Wm. Sbwerby, S. Pope, and E. Taylor. The Rev. W. Arrowsmith submit- ted the report, which showed that the total Income for 1891, from all sources, at home and abroad, was £125,128, being an increase of 0,057 on the previous year. The total expenditure for the same period was £129,197; or £3,658 less than the year before.—The Chairman expressed his pleasure at again visiting Halton-road, and said his lifelong interest In mission work had not abated.—The Rev. E. R. E.slick then gave an interesting account ot his labours in India, and the difficulties that had to be overcome by the missionaries. The usual votes of thanks were passed. JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- et.. and 4, Bridge at.. Runeorn.—Advt. FUNERAL OF THE Rev. W..PRITCHARD, OP WIDNES.

The mortal remains ef the Rev. Wm. Pritchard, superintendent of the Widnes Wesleyan Circuit, was committed to the grave in Farnworth churchyard on Wednesday afternoon. The rev, gentleman had died from pleurisy, after a brief illness, en Saturday last, at the age of 58 years, leaving a widow,three sons, and one daughter to mourn his loss. At two o'clock the body was conveyed from the residence at Mill Brow to Victoria-road chapel, where an impressive service was conducted by the following ministers: Rev. A. Bishop, Liverpool, (district secretary) ; Rev: .1. W. Craik, Liver- pool ; Rev. T. J. Kent, Widnes; Rev. J. Holmes, Not- tingham; and Rev. T. Wilkes, Runcorn. Addresses , were delivered by the Revs. Craik and Holmes. The service concluded with a pathetic rendering of Tennyson's "Crossing the Bar," and as the mourners filed out of the sacred edifice' the "Dead March" was played on the organ bi Mr. Skelton. The processionists, who numbered several hun- dreds, followed the hearse and mourning coaches in the fallowing order:—Circuit stewards,local preachers class leaders, society and poor stewards, Sunday school teachers, and members of society. Numerous windows were darkened as a toke n of respect to the deceased gentleman, and thousands lined the road as the mourn- ful cortege wended its way to Farnworth. The service at the graveside was con ducted by the Rev. A. Bishop, and in addition to the ministers previously mentioned there were present the Revs. A. Freeman ( Warrington), J. Hanbev and W. Arrowsmith (Runcorn), Owen Hughes (Welsh Wesleyan), R. G. Hughes, P. Pizey (Frodsham), J. Wright Williams (Vicar of Parnworth), G. A. Leßert (vicar of St. Ambrose), and J. R. Glover (curate).

div.head: GLASS BOTTLE TRADE.
div.p: THE GLASS BOTTLE TRADE.

The Labour Commission took evidence at Westminster on Tuesday, regardiog the glass bottle trade. The Secretary to the Glass Bottle Makers' Trade Protection Society of Yorkshire complained that in many cases the construction of the workshops was defective, and the heat was excessive, owing to the want of proper venti- lation. The President of the Yorkshire Glass Bottle Manufacturers' Association diSputed the correctness of this description of the workshops. A Barnsley manu- facturer said that through the M'Kinley tariff and toreign competition the glass trade was going to the dogs , as fast as it could.

div.p: THE EXAMINE, SATURDAY,, NOVEMB-R, 12. 1892.
WIWNES TOWN COUNCIL.
THE FIRST MEETtgG,

- Wednesday saw the dawn of a new era in the government of Widnes. The old Local Board, alter an existence of 37 years, had fulfilled its mission and had passed away. and in its place had arisen a Municipal Cotincil to carry oh the work. From the plane of a Local Board district, controlled in no small degree by a central Board in London, Abe town that day reached the altitude of a Cor- porate Borotigh, by virtue of a Charter quoted by her Majesty the Queen,and containing within itself all the powers necesiary for the good government of the people in everything that concerns their purely home affairs. On November let, the rate- payers had elected 18 council men to represent them, and these gentlemen were to meet in the Town Hall, at 12 noon, to conduct the business of Widnes according to new forms and formutre. On arare occasion such as this trivial debates interest, and it may be stated that to meet the altered conditions, the Board room had, under the guiding hand of the borough surveyor, Mr. J. S. Sinclair, been admirably arranged for the purposes of a Council Chamber. Two long tables, covered with red plush, were placed along the room from and to end, and in the centre, on a raised platform, was placed the civic chair, the seat of his Worship, the Mayor. Not far away, suitable provision had been made for those now-a-days indispensable servants of the public, the gentlemen of the Press ; but the exigencies of space prevented any accommodation being provided for the public themselves. On the opening of a new Parliament, the race amongA the members to be first at Westminster, is very keen ; and whether some such spirit of emulation animated Mr. Councillor Sadler or not, to him belongs' the honour of being the first mem`e'r to enter the Coun- cil Chamber of the BeroMeh on the eventful morning of Wednesday last. Ile sauntered into the roeni at 11.15, and entered i conversation with the acting Town Clerk, Mr. ti i ilieim . Shortly terwards Councillor" 'Longton, ci of the etre% of Fain weeth, glanced into the room and disa!,p,i,, reit, and at 1125, Mr. T. H. Gossage. soon to be Aklerine Mid Mayor, walked in and joined Councillor Sadler and the Town Clerk at the end of the room. A reiart r of an hour let e, Councillors Timmis and Smi Ito had successfully run in harness in West Bank NI entered that room together, and appeared to " nod " approval of the Surveyor's arrangement of the place. Next appeared the gentleman who enjoyed' the dist:l,mi -fl of le a. lying the largest-number of votes at the el, ~; :en, Councillor Ur I. Neil, and following on his heels were Councillors Shores -and Singleton. By this time most of the new Councillors had assembled in the are t-room, ' and a kind of subdued excitement seemed to pervade the whole. The picture would not be complete without mention of Mr.Whittle,the hail-keeper, who, attired in appropriate uniform, kept guard at the entrance to the chamber, and ushered in ftlie mem- bers with such dignity as became a Corporate official. ' The Councillors had taken their seats before twelve noon, and promptly at that hour, Mr. Gossage, by virtue of his appointment as provisional Mayor, took the chair, and Widnes Corporation was fairly launched up- on its way. In appropriate speeches, Councillors Sadler and Wareing proposed and seconded, and Councillor Shores supported the election of Mr. Gossage to the position of Mayor,,and popular opinion was ratified bY a unanimous vote, followed. by hearty applause. According to the formula provided, His Worship then took the oath if allegiance to the Queen—" I swear I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Her Msjesty, Queen Victoria, her heirs and successors according to the law, So help me God." He also took what is per- haps the more solemn judicial oath, which runs "I swear I will well and truly serve our Sovereign Lady, Queen Victoria, in the office of Mayor, and I will do right to all manner of peoPle after the laws and usages of this realm without fear or favour, affection, or ill- will. So help me God.' The proposer and seconder then took the oath of allegiance to the Mayor. The election of Aldermen, in which much interest was cen- tred, and which it was generally expected would pro- voke some discussion, was. a very quiet,not to say, tame business. Each Councillor was handed a form to fill up with the !Wiles of the gent lenien he wished to elevate to the Aldermanic Burl,, and, this done, he returned the form to the Mayor, the Clerk cast tip the vOtee, and the result was declared. The six erntlemen elected formed the fist' of the L'heral and Nationalist party, while the Isidepend nrs and Cnservatives voted for those gem 'yawn who had headed the poll in their par- ticular wards, an excepti in, of course, being made jai the case 01 the Mayor.; arid this will explain the fact that Alderman Timrnis and Alderman Tilley each re- ceived 18 votes. A long discussion took place upon the appointment of Town Clerk. The epeeches made showed that there was a string feeling that the appointment ought to have been advertised, and thus offered for greater competition, but the Mayor stated that the Act of Parlia merit had been complied with to the letter,and further pointed out that the appointment was not for life, but was held at the "pleasure of the Council." Point after point, and question after question, kept arising, and as the Mayor confessed he was no lawyer, the borough accountant, Mr. Hoyle, made numerous journeys between His Worship and the Clerk's office seek- ing advice and explanation from Mr.Oppenheim,who had retired thither immediately the subject arose. Eventu- ally Mr. Oppenheim was appointed by seven votes, the remainder of the Council abstaining from voting. The assignment of the Aldermen to the several wards, and the fixing of the times and dates of meetings, concluded the.' business which had occupied upwards of :three hours. At the invitation of the Mayor, the Council ad- journed into his parlour and partook of a lunch there provided.

div.head: BUSINESS.
div.p: THE BUSINESS.

The first quarterly meeting of the Widnes Town Council, took place on Wednesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage took the chair as provisional Mayor, and there were present CQuncillors Wareing., T. A.Bullough, W. Christie, C. P. Barlow' P. Longton,.T..Shuttleworth, S. Sadler, S. Owen, H. B. Shores, J. Tilley, S—Quinn, H. Singleton, J. Williamson, T. Carney, W. Hodgkinson, T. Smith, G. 1. Neil, and H. S. Timmis, with Mr.H.S.Oppenheim (acting town clerk), and Mr. T. Craik (assistant clerk).

div.head: ELECT/ ON OF MAYOR.
div.p: ELECT/ ON OF MAYOR.

Councillor Sadler said he had a proposal to lay before the Council, which he thought would meet with universal acceptance. They all knew the services Mr. Gossage had rendered to the late Board, and he was sure there were none of them but would be proud to see him in the position of Mayor of this Borough. He moved that Mr. Gossage be appointed Mayor of the Borough. Councillor Wareing said if he might be permitted as one who had a long connection ' with the gentleman whose name had been mentioned, he should like to second the proposition ; and his duty would be lightened by the fact that they all knew Mr. Gossage as well as he did. He was certain that )Ir. Gossage at the expiration of his year of office, would be found to have conducted the business of the Council in a satisfactory manner, and in such a manner as the most exacting could desire.

, Councillor Shores, as one of the new members, sup- ported the motion. Public opinion, undoubtedly pointed to Mr. Gossage, as the gentleman whom they should honour with the first mayoralty of the Borough, and in passing the proposition, they would be only voicing public opinion. Why was this ? It was because the name of Gossage had been invariable, it I was because the name of Gossage had been inseparably- connected with the life and growth of Widnes. Mr. William Gossage was one of the earliest settlers in the place, and it was due to his sagacity and foresight that they held the magnificent possessions they now enjoyed. With regard to Mr. F. H. Gossage, there could be no doubt whatry,,- ~f his services : they were within their own time and .:, llection. They all knew that when the Local Board had come into cllision with important and powerful interests,Mr. GOSSIL4e had most loyally and courageously supported the interests of the town, and in nut a few cases had come off victorious. In every work of charity, in every good enterprise, Mr. Gossage had been a foremost worker and a liberal giver, and it would be the wish of that Council, as it was the wish of the public, to confer upon Mr. Gossage, the first mayoralty, and he felt convinced they could not do better than trust the guidance of the early steps of this infant borough, to the wise and able man who had brought to a dignified demise the present Local Board. (Hear, hear.)

The acting Town Clerk put the proposition, which was carried unanimously, 'and there was loud applause when The Mayor rose to reply. He said he hardly knew how to begin. Ha thought they had conferred upon him, by electing him first Mayor of the Borough, the greatest honour that could be conferred upon a citizen in the Position in which he was. He, therefore, thanked them the more sincerely for it. As had been said, they knew him very well, and hence he trusted that every member would do his duty on every occasion that he was called upon. The business of any Corporation required the indulgence and support of the members of the Corpora- tion, and if at any time the ruling of the Mayor 'ap- peared to be a little harsh or hard they must take his ruling with a grain of salt. It would not be flippantly delivered, or lightly given, ha could assure them. He had in the past received the greatest possible courtesy from the representatives of that great body which ruled the place—the ratepayers—and he trusted in future he should be able to steer the ship as well as he had done in the past if he had health and strength to do so. iflear, hear.) He thanked them again most sincerely for the honour they had done him.

APPOINTMENT OF CLIIIIIILAN.
Dk.an. Finegan said tie would propose a gentleman for

They had lost the 'services of their late Chair- man, and he was sore they all regretted that Mr.Timmis was no longer with them. (Hear, hear.) div.head: WIDNES MURDER REVIVED.
div.p: A WIDNES MURDER REVIVED.
SENSATIONAL RUMOUR.

Mr. S. Brighouse the county coroner, on Monday afternoon held an inquest at the Waterloo Hotel, touching the death of a furnaceman named John Dillon, who had resided at 5 Cromwell-st. The evidence showed that on the 14th October, the d,eceased who was employed at the Widnes Alkali Works, complained to a fellow workman a haying burnt his hand by knocking it against the end of a Salt cake pot. There was a slight Wound on the hand, but he neglected it until he was unable to work in consequence, and he had to engage the services of Dr. Hutchinson. The man died on Sunday and Dr. Hut- chinson certified that death was caused through blood poisoning. A sensational rumour was current in Wid- nes on Monday night and spread as far as Runcorn. It was to the effect that Dillon on his death bed had confessed that he was the murderer of a young man named Delaney, 13 or 14 years ago. At that tirae. it appears a labour dispute on a small scale was proceed- ing at the works of Mr. T. Snape, M.P., on West Bank, and Delaney acted the part of a " knobstick " by returning to work. Early one morning his dead body was found in the yard, with the skull terribly smashed, and at his side was a crowbar smeared with blood and with human hair attached. Dillon who was at that time employed at Mr. Snapes, was arrested on the charge of committing the murder, but the evidence did not .ustain the accusation, and the man was discharged. Immediately on hearing the rumour of the alleged con- fession, Saperintendent Keighley instituted inquiries, with the result that he came to the conclusion that the story had not the slightest foundation in fact.

div.head: ItUNCORN.
div.p: ItUNCORN.
By AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

After a. discussion of two hours in private, the Runcorn Board of Commissiohers have decided to contribute the sum of £30,000 towards the cost cf constructing a vehicular bridge across the Mersey, connecting Lancashire an CLeshire at Runcorn and Widnes. A month ago Widnes .Local Board agreea to contribute a similar amount towards the project; and it .now remains for the respective councils of the two Committees ,to provide, the re- maining .£1.20,030 required. There is no reason to believe that /he County- uou ncil 'look unfavourably on the scheine, but rather otherwise, and judicious advocacy by OS County Councillors of the two towns may de much to secure acquiescence to the desires of the Commissioners of RancOrn and the new Town Council of Widnes:

To ssme ratepayers £30,000 may appear a very large sum, for a small district like litineorn to advance, but it may be asserted with confidence that it will be one of the best. investments ever made. In a matter of this kit.d it is itnpossible to state the advantages and benefits that will be de- rived with mathematical- precision—they cannot. be shown in figures, hut thoss. who by ability and far- sightedness are able to form a Found opinion, are confident that a vehicular bridge across the Mersey means the development of both Widnes an Run- c3rn in trade and population, and the subject must be viewed not in a carkiing spirit of criticism but in a broad-minded and whole-hearted way.

As Mr. Wiswall, the Chairman of the Runcorn Commissioners,has peinted out,there is a precedent for the Cheshire County Council to act upon in con- tributing £60,000. Some years ago the Westmin- ster Bridge at Chester was freed, that is, the pay- -inent of toll was abolished at a cost of many thousands of pounds—the exact figure is of no con- sequence—and to attam this end, the ratepiiyers of the whole of the county were called upon to pay their quota. Now, this bridge was practically a local one, and yet Runcorn, which was not inte- rested in the least, had to provide some hundreds 'of pounds. The proposed Mersey Bridge may he a more extensive and more expensive undertaking, but the principle is conceded that the County Connell can bear their proportion of the cost, and in this case a very large area of Cheshire will be directly benefited, and the•whole of the county indirectly by the progress that will result in the immediate district of Runcorn. Therefore, it is to be hoped that the County Council will see eye. to eye with the promoters of the scheme, and give them powerful .aid in carrying it out.

The old order of things gave place to the new at Widnes, on Wednesday. On the previoul4 day the Local Board had made a dignified exit. The mem- bers congratulated themselves, with a good rea- son: that they were handing over an inheritance which it, was the fortune of few new boroughs to receive, and with one accord they most cordially and sincerely thanked Mr..Glossage for his long services to the town and especially as Chairman of the Board. Nor were the officials forgotten. The services and abilities of these gentlemen, upon whom the practical work of the town devolves, were heartily acknowledged. .After a, few hand- shakes amongst the members, Widnes Local Board came to an end. The Town Council made a: successful etait,' , considering that all were new to their duties and somewhat in a fog, but the Mayor allowed an unusual latitude of debate, and every- thing went off smoothly, although there was not complete unanimity.

The selection of aldermen generally gives satisfac- tion, more especially from the fact that four mem- bers of the old Board have been honoured with the distinction, out of the five who were elected. As a consequence of the elevation of these gentlemen to the aldermanic Bench, there will be elections in the whole of the wards, except Farnworth, and the gentlemen lready mentioned as candidates are, Messrs. W. W. Gossage (L), D. Wright (I), J. Fitz- patrick (N), H. O'Donnell (N), G. Davies (I), F. Neil (I), J. W. Knowles (I), C. Hemingway (I), T. Handley (L) and J. Midwood (I). It is expected that the Liberals tad Nationalists will contest each ward. The cilia 'Mors elected for Victoria and West Bank lirbrds will serve for three years, those for Waterloo end Alums' Cross for two years, and the one for Halton Ward for one year.

SUCCESS OF THE NETHEULEY EXTENSION

The Engineer reported to the Gits and Water Com- mittee, that the new engine at Netherley commenced pumping for the first time on September 28th, and for several days previous to the 20th inst., the engine was run at the full speed of 11 strokes per minute. It was seen with the engine running up tb the specified rate of speed, that there would be no risk or difficulty in creasing the speed to say 13 strokes per minuto at which rate of pumping thetengine will deliver2imillion gallons per diem, or a quantity equal to the present total requirement of the town, thus placing Stock's Well practically on the reserve, the supply of water in the new boreholes so far appears to be most abundant..

div.head: FLOOD AT TRH DAS WORTS.
div.p: FLOOD AT TRH DAS WORTS.

_ The Engineer also reported that on the 3rd October Bower's Brook flooded the gas works through the heavy rainfall, and it was with difficulty an indifferent supply of gas was kept up to the town and had the water risen a few inches higher, the town would most assuredly hssnbeen,plunged into total darkness. So bad indeed Was the state in which the retorts were left, that it was no until the 7th October that sufficient gas was being made to ;Omit of full pressure to the town being re- sumed. The loss was put down at £275. Mr. Browa in moving the adoption of the minutes of- the Cemmittee, said the supply of water at Netherley seemed to be unlimited, and the works had exceeded their expectations. The new engine would save several hundred pounds per annum after paying the interest on sinking fund.—Mr. J. Taylor seconded the ination.—The Chairman remarked upon the expedition with which the extension had been carried out, the smallness of the cost, and the complete success achieved.—The motion was carried.

div.head: NIGHWAY 3f ATTERS._
div.p: NIGHWAY 3f ATTERS._

The minutes of the Highway Committee stated that a letter had been received from Messrs. Watts and Carr, solicitors, Liverpool. claiming in behalf of the Rev. James Clarke substantial compensation, for damage alleged to have been done to St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, in the course of certain drainage operations. and threatening proceedings in the matter.—The Clerk's reply thereto was approved.—Mr. Sadler moved the adoption of the minutes, and announced that the County Council had granted £B9O a year to the Board, towards the maintainance of the main roads in the dis- trict, and this would mean a difference of 2d. in the rates.—Mr. Owen asked if the lamps could be kept lighted for a more extended time than at present. In the early morning morning working-men could not see their way, and went stumbling into each other, and the matter ought to have attention in their interests.—Mr. Brown asked if fuller information could be given with regard to St. Mary's Church.—Mr. Sadler said to restore the Church to its original state would necessitate an ex- penditure of £1,500 to £2,000. The Law Clerk had decided that the Board were not responsible in any degree. As to the lamps, this su.bjeet would no doubt receive the attention of Commissioners formed under the Corporation.—ln reply to Mr. Tilley, the Law Clerk said Mr. Balmer, the contractor,.was a substantial mean, and there was no fe,ar that loss would be sustainsd in the matter of St. Mary's Church.—The minutea were approved.

div.head: HEALTH Or THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH Or THE TOWN.

The Medical Officer of Health reported that during October there were 95 births, and 41 deaths, being at the respective rates of 38.0 and 16.4- per 1,000. Coarasting Widnes with other townsin the kingdom,said the Medical Officer, " Weft(' that the death rate is vary favourable to us. The cases of scarlet fever notified are rather numerous, but they are scattered all over tbe town, and not confined to any particular district. Notwithstand- ing the prevalence of smallpox in Warrington and Liver- pool, it is satisfactory to find that a complete immunity from that disease prevails in this town, and we are tab- jog every precaution to avert it, as well as to be prepared for it."

amended that upon the trustees enterinA' into an under- taking to be prepare" by the clerk, „ot t use the land in question, otherwise than for religious Purposes, the Local Board do not press for payment of .the amount. div.head: RE-APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS.
div.p: RE-APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS.

Mr. Wright moved the re-appointment of Dr. O'Keeffe as medical officer and Mr. W. Lowe as nuisance inspec- tor, explaining that:this was a purely formal resolutipn passed in order to obtain half the salaries of the officers leom the County Council.—Mr.Tilley seconded. Carried.
FAREWELL SPEECHES. THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN.

Mr. Brown said before they had the last " dying speech and confession " of the Board, it became them as members who Had been associated together for so many years under the presidency of Mr. Gossage, that they should thank the Chairman for the services he had ren- dered to the town through that Board. It had been his (Mr. Brown's) privilege to be on the Committee of which Mr. Gossage was chairman for several years, when some important works were carried out, and he could bear testimony to the breadth of view Mr. Gossage took up then as to the requirements of Widnes. looking further ahead than the majority of those with whom he worked, and having to meet with considerable opposition. The largeness of Mr. Gossage's ideas and the breadth of his designs had proved to be right, and being carried out had conferred permanent benefit upon the town. (Applause.) They could all bear testimony to the im- partial, fair, and considerate and kind manner in which Mr. Gossage as Chairman of the Board had dealt with them, and dealt with the subjects that had been brought before them. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Sadler seconded the motion with.great pleasure, and bore testimony to the invariable kindness and courtesy the Chairman had displayed to every member. There had been occasions when he (Mr. Sadler) had had to be 'pulled up, and on mature consideration he had always concluded that the Chairman had acted wisely in every case. He endorged everything Mr. Brown had said. _ . .

Mr. Wright supported the proposition and said no words of his could portray the extreme kindness and cordiality the Chairman had shown to individual mem- ' , hers and under his rule everything had worked smoothly and harmoniously. Mr. Taylor and Mr. Houghton also supportel. Mr. Mid wood also spoke to the resolutions, and after a complimentary reference to the Chairman's rule, said Mr. Gossage's action in regard to the Water works some years ago in insisting upon securing Netherley and Bell Vale site had been the means of saving Widnes several thousand pounds. He hoped Mr. Gossage would live long to serve the town in the capacity of Mayor. Mr. TiMmis added his tribute to Mr. Gossage's kind and courteous ruling. Mr. S. Owen alluded to the help and encouragement Mr. Gossage accorded to new members, and as a new member, he (Mr. Owen) looked forward with hope and with confidence to the work that lay • before them under the guidance of one who had been so long at the head of affairs and who had indeed the esteem and affection of all those that had been about him. Mr. Neil said he felt proud to endorse all that had been said, and expressed the hope that Mr. Gossage would long ru'e and guide them on the Town Council. Mr. Beech and Mr. Tilley also bore their testimony.

The members passed the resolution by standing up and loudly applauding. Mr. Brown (addressing the chair) said :It is my duty to present to you not a formal vote of thanks, it is no simple lip expression ; but I can assure you, and I judge my brethren round the board as myself, thOt it is our heartfelt expression of deep gratitude, somewhat of affection that we present to you our thanks, and as we are come to a point where the two ways meet, and we trust y m will find as honest and as genuine support and submission to your ruling, and that you will prove a successful and efficient In yaur guidance, and that you will steer Widnes to a far greater pitch of prosperity, than it has been hitherto your privilege to do. (Applause.) Tne Chairman in reply said he felt overcome with the kindness with which what he had ever done for Widnes had been received. He was particularly thank- ful to those younger members who had expressed their opinion of his handling the position of chairman, because whenever any gentlemen came into a new as- sembly they were not acquainted with its duties, and he tlibughtlc3vasthe duty of the chairman to take care in

considering the propositions and speeches such members made. He thanked them more sincerely almost than the old members for their thanks because he felt they had been satisfied with his rulings and had been given fair play, Ond that no attempt had been made to sup- press anything they wished to express. (Hear, hear.) As to the old members they were a class together; they had worked together, and worked successfully. The discussions had been most temperate and not only that, but intelligent and it had made him as chairman feel that everybody was trying to do their duty honestly and straightforwardly for their masters, the ratepayers. Whenever they had spent the ratepayers money, they had spent it, as they believed invested it for the future benefit of the town, and working with those gentlemen had been an extreme pleasure, because he never asked for advice but he got it from the Board, and any surges- tion he had made had been received with the kind at- tention of `the Board. Therefore his duty had been simplified and he cculd only feel grateful fnr the kind services of the Board and their obedience to the ruling of the chair that bad been given ever since he had been chairman. He hoped the future of the town would be as prosperous as it hid been in the past.

div.head: THANES TO THE OFFICIALS.
div.p: THANES TO THE OFFICIALS.

31r. Midwood moved a vote ot thanks to the officials of the Board, remarking that he never met with a staff which worked better and more harmoniously together than the officials of that Board.—The Chairman se- conded the motion and said he should feel grateful to the Town Council if the present officials are allowed to continue to fill their offices under the Corporation. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Wright supported the motion, which was carried unanimously.— The Clerk, in acknowledg- ment. Mid the whole of the officials were animated with a desire to perform their duty, and he thought they had been fairly successful. He should like to add that it had been a proud privilege to have been enabled to serve the Board as Clerk for the last year and eight months.—Dr. Ci4KeelTe also replied, remarking that he hoped he had given satisfaction in the past, as he would continue to do his utmost to.fulfil the duties and obliga- tions of his office for the benefit of the town.—Mr. Hoyle was called upon also to respond, and he remarked that although the youngest official at the head of a depart- ment, still in another sense he was the oldest official. It was nearly sixteen years since he came under the Board, and he personalty thanked the members for the consideration andkindness which had been shown to him. .He only hoped that they would all get on as wen with the new Council as they had with the Local Board. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: BRAVE BOYS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: BRAVE BOYS AT RUNCORN.

An interesting presentation took place in the Seamans' Institute at Runcorn on Saturday by Mr. R. Dobson. the deputy coroner, in the presence of a number of ladies and gentlemen. The remarks ot the deputy coroner fully describe the circumstances. Mr. Dobson said his duty that afternoon was an exceed- ingly pleasant one. The occasions which brought him to Runcorn from time to time, usually had associated with their circumstances of a very sad nature, in which .loss of life was involved. The history of the case which had brought them together was that on Sunday the 21st August, an exceedingly hot day, three boys named Alfred Cox,JOhn Wilson, and Charles Jones, went to bathe in that part of the Old Quay Canal which was , now blocked up and formed a lake. After splashing about in the water about 20 minutes, Cox got beyond his depth,, sank, and did not rise again, because, it was thought,. his feet had stuck in the mud. Wilson, who could swim a little, attempted to rescue Cox, who,how- ever, caught hold of Wilson and dragged him under the water. After a struggle Wilson got clear, and on reach- ing the-bank fell down exhausted.Jrnots nes: n made pulled,and an attempt. He caught hold of Cox.s a hot cctild not move him, and then he himself began to drown for he could rot swim. Then Robert Rowland Harrison aged 13, who had previously been bathing, slipped off his trousers, and Jumped into the water to Jones's assistance. While in the water he divested him- self of his shirt, and, with great presence of mind, retained one portion in his hand and extended the other portion to /ones, who caught bold of it, was drawn to the bank, and saved. Had it not been for Harrison's courage Jones would certainly have shared the fate of Ctta. These facts having been put before the Royal Humans Society, that Society had awarded Harrison a bronze medal, and an honorary certificate, and to Jcmes and Wilson a testimonial on parchment. He (Mr. Dobson) thought the audience would agree with hlm that the conduct of those boys was beyond all praise, but at the same time, no gift or reward, in his opinion, could add to the value of a brave deed, though it was well that brave deeds should be recognised Mr. Dobson then attached the medal to Harrison's coat, and handed him the certificate. Jones and Wilson were at work and unable to be present. and Mr. Shaw undertook to deliver , them into their hands. Harrison said be did not rescue

Jones for a reward, but because it was his duty. After a few remarks from Mr. Shaw, the Coroner_ thanked that youth for his kindness in making a rrangeThen ts for the presentation, and to the Committee of the Institute for allowing him the use of the room. He thought the Institute a most convenient and useful placr, an I hav- ing such a building in the town, it struck brae AB strange, that these should not be public baths. He had heard, however, that a Committee of tile Commi— ion .rs had set about making arrangements for the erect,oyi O baths, and he hoped they would act with promitatti le, and • Wilt before another summer came, there w ruld be suitable provision for the youths of the town uo bathe under cover. Of nearly all the cases of drowning while bathing, that came underlithe notice of the Coroner and himself, it could be said, they would riot have taken place if there had been baths in the town.—Mr. Shaw proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Dobson, for having taken this matter in hand, and for having made the pre- sentation.—Mr. R. Abel seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously, and Mr. Dobson having replied, the proceedings terminated.

div.head: TaINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: TaINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

. I have been inamensly pleased to see that one of the working men selected for the magistracy, Mr.S. Wright, has been appointed on the commission o the peace. I hope he will prove a credit to that body and work as well upon the magisterial bench as has worked at other benches. It will be incumbent upon him, more than upon other Magistrates to be careful, for his conduct as a mag- istrate will be subjected to closer examination, and keener criticism than that of others' for there are a large number of people who think that working men have no right to fill any public office. To all those who may meet him in this spirit it is to be hoped Mr. Wright, as a filesmith by trade, will 13,1 pre- pared to apply the old Latin saying—Cease vipers; ye bite a file.-

The mirarrington Trades Council may have other work than they have already attempted, in the direction of democratising our institutions, to do before long. There is a probability, it is reported, of the present Government by an order in Council in the coal-4.e of next year, abolishing the property qualification for membership of the Boards Of Ouardians. They will thus be thrown open to that class who are most concerned in the administra- tion of the poor law, and who therefore ought to bace a due amount of direct representation in the bodies that administer it. I hope that Warrington Trades Council will have an opportunity in time for the next election of our local Board of Guar- dians, to make selections of working men for that authority.

It was a great pity that lifeboat Saturday in Warrington, and the Cricket and Bowling Club's pyrotechnic exhibition ahould both have been fixed for the same day. Is this unfortunate clashing did occur—and it is a sort of thing which happens too frequently in Warrington—the result was un- doubtedly a much smaller collection for the life- boat movement than tkere otherwise would have been. The fireworks exhibited by the Cricket and Bowling Club must have-exercised the minds of a, great many much more than the water works—if I might put the matter in this antithetical form— performed by our heroic lifeboat men, even though these involved the preservation of human life. The consequence, therefore, was undoubtedly much less support for the latter cause.

But it seems to me that the firework exhibition might" have even been made an auxiliary to the Lifeboat movement with a little management. There were elaborate representations of a palace, of Blondin crossing the tight rope, and so on. Now, what could have been produced with happier effect than the sudden apparition, in fiery relief, against the heavens, of a well-manned lifeboat ? And the effect would have been enhanced could the image of a ship in distress have been made to loom in the distance. The band could at the same instant have struck up the air "Man the lifeboat." The enthusiasm which would have thus been created, would have been such that a few collectors going among the crowd immediately after, would have collected a handsome sum for the Lifeboat Saturday Fund.

The fireworks exhibition was good in quality but by no means in quantity. Only a few items of "an extensive programme were given, and when the spectators wera anticipating an hour or two more of a diversion which they were highly appreciat- ing suddenly the words "Good night" flashed out upon them in fiery characters, and they understood that all was over; and very large numbers of the people, if not the majority, made their exit from the field, considerably disappointed. There were, however, one or two more star-showers, but with the" Good night," the exhibition had practically ended. It was reported that this device accidentally and prematurely caught fire ; and that, this being the case, they did not like to proceed with the entertainment.

Mr. Henry Welsby, one of the jury at the inquest at the Cemetery Inn, on Saturday, on the child Moody that died of smallpox, seemed determined to distinguish himself on that occasion, by a display of reckless bravado, which is happily uncommon amongst jurymen. The Coroner expressly provided against the jury incurring any danger through their having to observe the absurd old ceremony of viewing the body, he having arranged for them merely to take a sight of it through the window of the mortuary, in which the remains were. Mr Welsby, it seems, neither appreciated the considera- of the Coroner, nor the safety of himself and others, but demanded the key of the mortuary from Police Sergeant Smith, who was in attendance, and des- pite the advice of the Coroner and Dr. Gornall, who was present, insisted on entering the building, and having a :private view of the body of his. own. He did make this much, concession to the feeling of those who remained without that he closed the door, thus reducing the peril to which lie exposed them. But as the door concealed his proceedings from view. there is no knowing what his curiosity prompted , him to do when he got inside: When he came out he returned to the Cemetery Inn,but was prevented,. on the protest of Mr. Critchley, one of the jury, from taking further part in the inquest or even entering the room. He had, however, re-entered the inn, and he also had to withdraw from thence.

Mr. Welsby, probably is one of those who.hold that fear is one great cause of the extension of an epidemic, and wanted to give a practical expression .of this belief and a proof of his courage for the of his brother jurymen. But be surely must know that there is a very great difference between not giving way to unmanly and panic fear and deliberately thrusting oneself into daager. Besides there is not the slightest doubt that a large number of the cases of smallpox in the town have been caused by just such reckless conduct.

An instance of the 'shameful neglect to which, some of our poorer children are subjected came out in a case before the Borough Bench. on Thursday, Two boys, Percy Quinn and Carey, both still of the tender age of 12,were charged with frequenting the Market Place for an unlawful pvrpose at a. late • honr; the previous night. Quinn has been before the Bench seven or eight times for theft and vag- rancy. On one occasion,when he was charged with theft, theß'ench refrained from punishing him, be- cause his father had the same 6iy kicked and beat him so that they were moved to compassion for the child,. It was then stated that the boy had, absented himself from home, c..n many occasions.for weeks at a time, out of sheer fear. Os other occa- sions,, when the child was brought before the Bench, the police proved that h.* had been living hi the streets for a considerable time sleep;ng during the cold nights of-winter in. an open shec4 and stealing 0/ begging fragments of food when hungry. The parents Were warned to appear ia court,,but on each occasion they treated the in- stractiou with contempt. They have been lined innumerable times for neglecting to send the boy •to school. One,of their children has been sent toe. reformatory school, and they refuse to pap 9d. per week for his maintenance. The Chief Constable • alleged that their inteution was to get Percy off- their hands in a similar manner. It is to be hoped this will not be so, and that if no one else, can im-. press the parents with their responsibility, the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, will take the matter up. It is certainly a suffici... ently serious case for their treatment.
