div.head: TIIIIFT OF A FOOTBALLER'S _CLOTHES,
div.p: TIIIIFT OF A FOOTBALLER'S _CLOTHES,

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, James Taylor, a discharged soldier, who was remanded yesterday week, was charged with stealing a handbag and articles of clothing valued at 203. belonging to Jas. Hamblett, a footballer, of 143, Knutsford-road, from a clubroom at the Old Crow Inn, on the afternoon of the 22nd ult. The club members met at the inn to change their clothing, and during their absence on the football field, the prisoner stole the articles, which had been left at the inn. He offered them for sale to Mrs. Leslie, Mersey-et., and betrayed himself by telling her he had bought them at her shop. The articles were detained, and he hastened away while she informed the police. Prisoner subsequently surrendered himself to them.— H.S. Monaghan in giving evidence against the prisoner said he had been going about the town pretending to have fits. He took him to the Infirmary some time since, and the doctor said he was drunk and had had no fits.—Alderman Francomb remarked to Mrs. Leslie that she was as good as a detective.—The Chief Constable : One of the best we have.—The prisoner was sent to jail for two months with hard labour.

div.head: MINOR GASES.
div.p: MINOR GASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Mosnev.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall), and Aldermen Francomb and Harrison. DRUNE.—Catherine Brown, drunk in Bridge-at-, on Saturday, &L—James Murphy, on Town Hill,that morn- ing, dismissed. Elizabeth Ann Taylor, drunk and indecent on Sunday morning soon after midnight, in Wilderepool-road, seven days with hard labour.—Julia Barrett, drunk in Cairo-st., on Sunday morning, seven days with hard labmr. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. —George Barker, drunk and disorderly on Saturday night at Market Gate, fined 4s.— Wm. Jones and Arthur Heaton, in the Market Place, on Saturday night, 55. and costs.—Thomas Llewellyn, in Buttermarket-it., on Saturday night, Bs., including costs.—Michael and Catherine Hawkins, father and daughter, and Mary Ann Mannien, in Rose and Crown- at., the same night. Both the women had black eyes, which it appeared they had got in tumbling about the streets. 'they had got drunk at a private house.-ss. each .—Mary Ann Mannion,a married woman,in Turner- street, that (Monday) morning, 7s. and costs.—Sabina Mc Loughlin, widow, in Robinson's Yard, off Fennell-st. ' She had been locked out by her son because she was drunk, and the neighbours were calling out to P.S. Longbothass, who proved the case,to lock her up.—The case was dismiased.—James O'Brien and George Archer in Tanner's-lane the previous Tueeday night, 10s. and costs each. FIGIITING.—MichaeI Broderick, labourer, 5, Old-road, Wm. Scott, 1, Jackson's Row, Church-st., Winifred Jennings, Silver-st., and Alice Thomas, 3, Naylor-st., were charged with fighting in MoUnt-st., at 10.30 p.m., on the night of the 27th ult. P.C's Corcoran and Bell deposed that the defendants were fighting with three soldiers. Warrants were iesued for the apprehension of Broderick and Thomas, who did not appear, and the other defendants were bound over to keep the peace for six months. OBSTRUCTING PHI TROROUGRFARE.—MichaeI New- comb, boot dealer, 90, Sonkey-stroet, for obstructing the thoroughfare, by placing goods on the footpath, had to pay 3s. 6d. costs. ALLOWING A HORSE TO STRAP—John Hamblett,

marine store dealer, Winwick-street, for allowing a horse to stray in Church-street, on the 29th ult., had to pay 3s. ed. costs. STREET GAMBLE as.—John Watson, 65, Watkin-street, Daniel Crooks, 63, Watkin-street, John Fligham, 9, Silver-street, and Michael Carter, 20, Phillip-street, for playing at pitch and toss for money, on the 30th ult., had to pay 3s. (id. costs each. FILLUDITLICTT ENLISTIMIT.-41 illiam DaTiee,was charged with making a wilfully false answer, on attestation on enlistment. A month's hard labour. CHIMNEYS ON Fins—Ellen Hunter, widow, 18, Napier. street, and Thomas Woodfine, 19, Heath Side, for having their chimneys on fire, were fined Is. each. TUBSDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (in the chair), and Mr. E. J. Guest.

_ AN UNGENEROUS LODGER.—James Lynch was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank-st„ on Mon- day night, and also with assaulting Margaret Wheeler. —P.O Bell stated that on Monday evening he received information that a man was assaulting a woman in Bank-st. He went there, but saw no one. Later on he received a similar complaint,so he went down again,and ' saw prisoner running away from a house. He detained him and took him back to the house. Here he found Mrs. Wheeler with her head bruised. She complained of being assaulted by the prisoner. She said he had been a lodger of hers, but came that day and burst in the door, and , -then knocked her down. The man was drunk.—Mrs. ' Wheeler was unable to attend, but she sent word that I she did not want to prosecute.—Prisoner was fined 105.1 and costs, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. WANTED TO CUT HIS MOTHER'S TIERGAT.—A young man named Albert Allcock, of Winwick-at., was charged with being drunk and using threats to his mother, on Monday night. It seemed that prisoner, who lived with his parents, was in the habit of misbehaving himself. On the night in question he went home drunk, and after amusing himself by kicking the doer and swearing, his mother tried to send him away. At this time P.C. Berry came along, just in time to hear the youth threaten in a savage manner to cut his mother's throat.—The mother said her son was incorrigible, and she merely wanted to be protected from him.—Upon the under- standing that prisoner would sign the pledge with the court missionary, he was discharged with a conviction recorded against him. " Hs WAS A BIGGER MAN THAN Mg.—A' ticket-or- leave " man named George Connoley, of King-st., was charged with being on the premises of Edward Connor, cab proprietor, the previous night, for a felonious par- pose.—P.C. flollingworth described how he and another constable went into Mr. Connor's yard late at night, and commenced to investigate. They reached a 'bus, and witness upon throwing his light into it saw the prisoner lying beneath a ruf,.—Prisoner, who had a black eye, said he went to the 'bus for shelter, in consequence of having to leave his lodgings because another lodger was thrashing him.—The Bench gave prisoner the benefit of the doubt, ard discharged him. INSPECTOR RILEY'S PATIENTS.—The following persons . were charged at the instance of Inspector Riley, school attendance officer, with neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—John Heaton, Back Howard-st. ; Noah Whitehead, 36. Bostock-street ; John Swanton, 21. Eldon-street ; James Hill, 10, Litton's Row ; Henry Taylor, Delooze's Yard ; William Howell, Albert-street ; James raylor, 113, School Brow. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Wright (in the chair), and Mr, J. Fairclough. FATHER AND SON IN TROUELE.—Mark Worker, and his son Frank Worker, were charged with stealing a pair of

boots valued at Bs. 9d. from the shop of Mr. Hankins, Bridge-street, (,n the previous Thursday night.—Detec- tive Monaghan said he had received information from Mr. Rankin, respecting the theft of the boots. On Tuesday night he ma Mark Worker, at Market Gate, wearing the boots in question. Upon learning from him that he had obtained the boots from home he took him into custody in company with his son .—Mark Worker said he found the boots lying in his house, and without enquiring where they came from ke put them on.— Frank Worker said he bought the boots from a man that he met on the iron bridge. He only gave 2s. Bd. for them.—The father, who had been previously convicted, was sent to jail for one month, and the son for 14 days. THURSDAT.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Sutton, Mr. J. Fairclough, Captain Ridgway, Dr. Starkey Smith, and Messrs. T. Birchall, William Pier- point, J. W. Hayward, J. H. Fleming, and S. Wright. THEFT OP BOOTS.—Thomas Morris,of no settled abode, was sent to jail for one month, for stealing a pair of second hand boots, value 25.9 d., from the shop of Mary Leslie, pawnbroker, Mersey-et. The case was proved by Detective Monaghan, who found prisoner walking about with the boots under his coat, on Wednesday. ALLEGED NEGLECT OP CHILDHEIN.—Percy Quinn and Thomas Carey, two boys, were charged with frequenting the Market Place the previous night, for unlawful pur- poses. Both boys have been before the Bench several times for similar offences.—The Mayor said he knew that in the case o: Quinn the parents were amenable for the boy's condition because of their neglect. On one occasion when the boy was before them they refrained from punishiro, him because of ill-usage which he had been subjected to by his father. One of the Quinn's brothers had been sent to a reformatory, and his parents would not pay the 9d. per week asked of them. They evidently thought to rid themselves of Percy in the same way. But he would try and have them dealt with by the R.S.P.C.A.—The boys were discharged.
FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (in the ohair), and

Alderman Wright. DRUNEENNESS.—Edward Alcock, Winwick-road, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disoraerly in Winwick-road, the previous night. FOND OF CHEESE.—A disreputable looking man named Thomas McNally, of Blackburn, was charged with stealing a cheese value 7s. from the shop of Frederick Hallwood, Buttermarket-st. —The Chief Constable said shcrtly after six o'clock on Thursday evening, prisoner strolled into Mr. Hallwood's shop. Mr. Bellwood was engaged just at the time, and after standing about for a few moments prisoner took up the cheese and walked out, without even speaking. Mr. Hallwood followed him. Prisoner commenced to go along hurriedly—in fact he ran. Mr. Hallwood ran after him. Just as they approached Market Gate, prisoner ran into the arms of P.C. Cochrane. "Wait just a moment please" said the officer, and then he pulled the cheese from untie' prisoner's coat. Prisoner could not account for the cheese just then,so the officer took him to the police station, where he remained all night. He refused to say anything about the cheese to the Bench, and was committed for 14 day's imprison- ment.

CRUELTY TO Ammer.s.—John Drinkwater, Great Bud- worth, was charged with illtreating a horse on the 23rd of last month.—Sergeant Taylor said that on the day in question he saw the defendant driving a mare, which was attached to a spring cart. It was extremely lame. He stopped the horse and examined it, and found it was swollen about the knees, and in a generally bad condi- tion. Defendant said the animal had never been at- tended by a veterinary surgeon.—lnspector Dowty, who examined the animal, proved it to be suffering from ex- treme lameness.—Fined 10s. and costs.

NON-COMPLIANCH WITH MAINTHNANCH ORDMRS.-Wm. Nicholson, Aikin-st., was committed for 14 days' im- prisonment, for non-compliance with a maintenance order made upon him in favour of his mother. Benja- men Taylor was committed to a month's imprisonment, fora similar offence.

DIDN'T COMPLETE THE CONTEACT.—James Mather, a toolmaker, was summoned by Councillor G. Plumpton, for the sum of £1 35., for non-fulfilment of contract.— Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant. It ap- pears that defendant left work on the 11th October, without giving notice and finishing the work which he had uudertaken on pieca rate. When leaving his work, defendant obtained a "sub," or fis. upon the work which he had not completed.—Defendant said he bad intended to go back and finish the work, but was at present a little too busy.—Ordered to pay £1 damages, by weekly instalments. ILLTREATING ANIMALS—Thomas Lawless, Heath Side, was fined 103. and costs for illtreating a horse, and Frederick Roberts, of Mill-lane, was fined 10s. or 14 days days' imprisonment for ill-treating a goat.—Charles Purslow, Appleton, was fined 10s, for illtreating a horse. The latter upon leaving the court said that if Inspector Dowty came to his house again he would be " lamer" than the horse.—Alderman Harrison had defendant brought back, and made him apologise both to the Bench and to the inspector.
A WEAR C.—James Rowson, Bark Stamford-street, was summoned for assaulting his uncle, James Howson, Jones-buildings.—The evidence of the uncle was weak, and the case was dismissed. _ . -

..... A NEIGHBOURS. Quaneat.--Susannah Colman, 8, Dut- ton-at., and Ellen Green, 8, Dutton-at., appeared on each other's cross-summons, on charges of assault. The evidence showed that they had been mixed up in a "neighbours' quarrel." Both were bound over to keep the peace for six months.

MORE COAL STRALERS.—Catherine Lewis (9), 56, Dock-st., and Margaret Dodd (9), 54, Dock-st., were charged with stealing a quantity of coal, valued at 2d., the property of Hutchinson's Trustees.—Mr. Gossage said the girls would be dismissed, but it was a great pity the parents could not be dealt with, as the Bench were convinced that in many cases the parents sent their children for coal.—Wm. Roach (11), Nelson-st., and James Bell (11), Nelsomst., were also charged with stealing lowt. of eoal, the property of Hutchinson's Trustees. FacoNtes.—George Fairclough, a boatman, pleaded guilty to having on the 29th October at Burston Bridge, .near Stone Staffordshire, stolen a gold wedding ring be- longing to Elizabeth Seymour, a boatwoman.—The pri- soner who had been previously convicted Wd3 sentenced to a month's hard labour.—For stealing a shirt and handkerchief the property of John Baines, a boatman ,employed by Mr. Joseph Horsefield, John Wilson, was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.—Joseph Gynor and Thomas McCurley, navvies, were charged on suspicion .of stealing an ulster value £l, from the house of Emma Ford, of Mersey Square.—The men were discharged. A REFRESHMENT Room- SCENI3.—Ann Smith, wife of Wm. Smith, 19 Waterloo-road, was summoned for as- saulting Jane Sole, a married woman, keeper of a refreshment house in Church-at. There was a cross- summons charging Mrs. Sole with assaulting Mrs. Smith. —Mrs. Sole had served a woman with a bottle of soda water on the 25th October, when Mrs. Smith entered the shop, told the woman not to pay, made use of filthy language, and struck Mrs. Sole on the head with an umbrella, raising a lump the size of a hen's egg.—lt was alleged on behalf of Mrs. Smith that Mrs. Sole threw the soda water upon Mrs. Smith and made use of violent language, and that the umbrella was used to protect the women from the soda water, and Mrs. Sole broke the handle off. It was denied that a blow was struck. After hearing a number of witnesses, the Bench fined Mrs. Smith 10s. and costs 17s. 6d., or in default 14 days hard labour. The summons against Mrs. Sole was dis- missed.—Mr. Burton appeared for Mrs. Sole, and Mr. Humphreys for Mrs. Smith. CRUELTY TO A HORSE—John Owen, a youth, was Sum- moned for having on the 21st October, cruelly illtreated a horse by working the animal in an unfit state. Wm. Rustage, horse keeper, at the Canal Warehouse, Preston Brook, was summoned for causing the horse to be worked.—P.C. Proctor found that the horse, which was drawing a flat from Preston Brook to Runcorn, had three raw wounds on its shoulders, and Owen stated that the horse keeper at Preston Brook had ordered him to use the horse.—Rustage denied that he ordered Owen to take the horse out.—Owen was fined 103. and costs and Rustage was fined 20s. and costs. STREET OBSTRUCTION.—Charles Hunt and Edward Jones, boys, were summoned for obstructing the foot- path in Church-st. on Sunday afternoon, the 30th ult. They were ordered to pay the costs 4s. 6d.—Ernest Parker and Thomas Ockleston, boys, were charged with obstructing the footpath in Church-st. on the same day, and were dealt with in_a like manner.

div.head: EVICTED TENANTS COSIAIISSION.
div.p: THE EVICTED TENANTS COSIAIISSION.

The Evicted Tenants Commission held its first sitting in Dublin on Monday, under the presidency of Mr. Jus- tice Mathew. In opening the proceedings the President explained the object and scope of the inquiry, as well as the course which the Commissioners intended to pursue. He hoped this inquiry would lead to peace and reconcilia- tion between landlords and tenants. The proceedings would be opened to the press so long as the newspapea refrained from commenting on the evidence or the course of procedure, but if any infringement of this rule took place the reporters would be evicted, without any hope of reinstatement. Referring to Lord Clanricarde, the President said he stood alone almost among Irish land- lords in refusing to come to terms with his tenants, but it was to be hoped that now, late as it was, he would ' allow the Commissioners to help him out of a position which nobody could envy. They would be very glad to hear what Lord Clanricarde had to say, and a courteous letter had been sent to him asking for information about his estate, but he had written refusing to have anything to do with the proceedings. Mr. John Roche, M.P., who has suffered heavily for his exertions in behalf of Lord Clanricarde's tenants at Woodford and Loughrea, gave evidence as to the evictions at Woodford, and Mr. Car- son, Q.C., M.P., claimed the right to cross-examine on behalf of Lord Clanricarde. The President pointed out that, according to the course of procedure which he had explained, the cross-examination could not be allowed, whereupon Mr. Carson said the inquiry was a farce and a sham, and used other expressions which were charac- terised by Mr. Justice Mathew as impertinent and dis- graceful.

div.head: ANOTHER FEAT BY TOMMY BURNS.
div.p: ANOTHER FEAT BY TOMMY BURNS.
DIVING FRONI A TRAMCAR INTO A DOCK.

with about as much regularity as each season's sea- serpent stories make their appearance does Tommy Burns turn up in his native city to provide the many admirers of his aquatic abilities with some fresh food for reflection. His latest feat was accomplished on Thursday morning, and it consisted of diving from a tramcar, as it was crossing the bridge at the bottom of James-at. to Mann Island, into the entrance to the George's Dock Tommy donned his bathing costume in a Mann Island public-house, and then by devious ways in order to escape the vigilance of the police dressed in an old coat,a pair of trousers, and a cap, and accom- panied by a couple of friends,he walked int, the town to board a tram. At about a quarter to eleven o'clock the three were seen coming down James-st., on the top of a Walton car, and as it gained the centre of the bridge, Tommy, by the aid of his two friends, balanced himself on the rail and dived into the water. There were hardly a score of persons about when he actually performed the feat, but an immense crowd quickly assembled on the bridge and along the dock wall, eager to ascertain what had taken place When it became generally known that nothing more serious had happened than a dive by Tommy Burns, many of the expressions that were heard were anything but complimentary tcwards the hero of the hour. Having, divested himself, while in the water, of Ms coat and trousers, Burns proceeded to give an exhibition of his swimming powers, and remained in the water for about ten minutes. Although the police on duty near the bridge were cognisant of the dive being likely to take place, no endeavour was made to prevent it ; but it is stated it is their intention to pro- ceed against Burns by summons.

div.head: " LOOKIN' BACK A BIT !
div.p: " LOOKIN' BACK A BIT !

Sumtimes, lads, wen aw'm deawn meauth, An' feelin' sad an' dull, Aw think abeawt thoose sprees we lied, I' that owd snug at th'" Wen argyments flew thick an' fait, That mebbe wur sublime, If th' speykers hodn't kept agate, Ten on ries at a time! Aw dream o' Bashaw an' Ids bride, His quare Shim Rappits too; An' wish that aw cud just see neaw, His amraichoor " Zoo." Aw'm puzzlet siot he'll bring eawt next, I' blacks, or blues, er reds ; Aw shudn't wonder if he breeds Suns checky-micks beawt yeds Will he be able t' teych his brids To sing or play a tune ; Or raise sum wommers that 'll go Reet timer an' back to th' moon? Nowt 'nil surptize me what he du; I' th' pigeon breedin' trade ; For, tak' my tip, a cuter chap Then him wur never made ! Hez Uncle George done grumblin' yet, An' g'en o'er takkin Cl' pet? Or is he like that horse-ball't corpse, An' workin' at it yet? So wot he'a (loin' aw don't care— Aw'd like to shake his flat ; Tiler's not a mon amung um aw, That aw've moor badly miss'd. Ile¢ Ramsay's bloomin' widow an' Th' owd skoller made a match? An' did boo sing " Oh, Tegallie," To bring him up to th' scratch? "Lobelia's George 1" duz he prescribe His " Benbow Mixcher "doze, To noose i'tle snug, an' thoose by th' church, " Down where the Blue Bell grows ?" Dust Cocker still in rapture sing His Bontinental Hymns? An' when he's interrupted, bless His nayburs' een an' limbs? Owd Birley Bill's lung worded quips Keep rowlin' throo my nob; Wile Randle, oft aw think o' thee, An' last, not least, Baur Bob But aw mun cut it short, just neaw, My rhyme's reet deawn to tie dregs; Sum other time all write agen— Yore's truly, Rose Bonk, 9, 11, 92.
TUDI 0' F.'EGS.

div.p: RUGBY.

RTINCORN lIORNIITS T. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH 2ND.—Played at Runcorn. After a well-fought game the Hornets won by one zoal and one try to their op- ponent? one try. It may be stated that the Runcorn team have lost one of their forwards, namely, William Stubbs, of Bootle, who succumbed to injuries sustained whilst following his employment on the Manchester Ship Canal. As a mark of respect to his memory, the Hornets will wear a badge of mourning during the re- mainder of the season.

WIDNES T. BARROW.—Played at Widnes before 2,009 spectators. The ground was in wretched condition, hut the game was fast nevertheless. Alford dropped a flue goal for Widnes. Then Girdwood scored for the visitors, and kicked a goal. Widnes attacked again, and Wright scored. In the second half play was lively and even, but about a quarter of an hour from the finish Haney, of Barrow, had to retire through an injury. Widnes pressed hard, but could not score. Final score:— Widnes, one goal and tone try; Barrow, one goal.

SALE V. RUNCORN.-At Sale. Both sides were very weak, owing to the county match and other causes. Sale kicked off, a poor return being made. From a scrimmage 'rkorpe passed to Smith, who ran through all opposition, but unfortunately stumbled when close to the line. several free kicks were given against the visitors for off-side play. Davies was very conspicuous at half-back. The ball travelled to and fro, but nothing was scored up to half-time. In the second half both sides made strenuJos efforts to score, Sawers and Smith for Sale and Pendlebury for Runcorn being very prom is- est. Sowers obtained a try for Sale in brilliant style, S. Harvey kicking a goal. Pendlebury them scored for Runcorn, after a good run, the kick at goal failisg. Runcorn had hard lines on several occasions. Final score : Sale, one goal; Rundorn, one try. STOCKTON HEATIr V. WALALIRS' BRRWERT.-With the Warrington and St.Helens Recreation fixture abandoned, these teams played their tie on the enclosure at Wilders- pool, on Saturday. There would be nearly 400 present when Stockton Heath kicked off against the slight breeze towards the pavilion goal. In point of physique the Brewery representatives had the advantage, but they lacked that science which is so conducive to success. As a result, Stockton Heath quickly assailed their op- ponents' goal and a neat piece of passing saw Cross throwing to Broady, a clever try being the result. Still aggressive, Stockton Heath again scored, this time Cross doing the needful, after a really brilliant run. Fine fielding of the oval gave Broady a second chance of showing his capabilities, and Cross this time augmented the score by live points, the interval arriving with the Brewery in a minority by a goal and two tries. During the early portion of the second half the Brewery men presented a bold front, and were decidedly unfortunate. Their efforts were but a mere flash-in-the-pan, for Stockton Heath gradually forced the oval back to the railway goal, but beyond minors, nothing was credited to the leaders,and the final score read :—Stockton Heath, a goal and two tries ; Brewery, nil.

WARRINGTON RANGRRS T. LRIOR " A."—These teams met for the Resit time on Saturday, on the ground of the former. The visitors who arrived short, had the assis- tance of Ashurst and Eden, of the Warrington F.C. The Rangers losing ths toss, kicked off against a strong sun, and no return being made,the homesters at once pressed. The visitor. however, warming to their work, laurst away with a strong rush, hut fine kicking by Harnblett sant them back. The Rangers' forwards, who were now playing a splendid combined game, took the ball in the Leigh quarters,where the oval was sent across to Massey, who, after a short run, was pulled up on the line, and from the eacoseding scrimmage Savage scored a good try, Clarke failing at goal. From the drop out the home team still kept up the pressure, and Broadhurst breaking away from the pack dribbled over in fine style. Clarke this time landed a goal from the place. This reverse roused the Leighites, and Hilton was instrumen- tal in taking play inte the Warrington half, where the home backs were at fault, and the visitors, profitiNg by the mistake, carried the ball over the line, Pilkington claiming a try, but no success marked the kick at goal. Leigh again attacked from the drop-out, but Clara relieved by taking an opponents' pass, and punting well down the field, followed up quickly, and prevented Askurst from returning. The Rangers continued to have the best ofit,and Thompson securing from a scrim- mage smartly tricked the Leigh backs, and grounded the oval between the posts, Clarke again placing a goal. Half-time being ca!led,the score read—Rangers, 2 goals, 1 try, Leigh, one try. After the interval the visitors played up in surprising manner, and clever passing between Hilton and Pendlebury resulted in Poole secur- ing an unimproved try. The Leighites, who were show- ing better staving powers, now evidently had the measure of the home team, whose play had fallen off considerably, and the visitors again, after several repeated attacks, scored their third try, the kick at goal again being at fault. The game finally ended in a wia ter the Rangers by two goals, ,one try, to Leigh three tries.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

rADeLTE V. ST. ELPHIE'S (RESERVE.) The newly. formed Padgate team played their first match on Satur- day, haviNg as their opponents the reserve team of the St. Elphin's club. The match was played at Padgate and resulted in a win for St. Elphia's by 4 goals to nil. Parreerrff V. Runcons.—Played at Penketh on Satur- day. Dumbell kicked off for the home team, and the visitors pressed for the first quarter of an hour. At last the home forwards broke away, and Dumbell scored the first goal, but the visitors equalised before half time. On restarting the home team pressed and Eligham scored a second goal. A nice bit of passing between the Brothers Bowyer and Duml_yell ended in J. Bowyer scor- ing a good goal. The game ended in a win for Panketh by 3 goals to 1. FRIHNDS' SCHOOL, PENKIITH V. FARNWORTH C.E.T.S. A.F.C.—Played at Penketh. The home team at once pressed. Smith scored with a good shot, and Theobald put the finishing touch to a grnd centre from Reynolds. Smith scored two more before half-time. On changing ends the visitors defended stubbornly, and a good rush by their forwards nearly resulted in a goal. Then Lb. nay scored for Penketh School with a long shot from back, and Reynolds scored two more. Theobald and Reynolds added further points, when Farnworth woke up and getting into the hame quarters scored about ten minutes, before time. Penketh Friends' School nine ; Far nworth one. _ _ _

WARRINGTON CRICKET A.F.C. V. OI,D AMPLEFORDIANS. —These clubs met at Warrington, on Saturday. The visitors kicked off, and began to press, but the home backs managed to relieve, and some very fast work was put in by both sides. After a short time Connor scored the first goal for the visitors. After restarting the home left wing made a good run, and Reid soon afterwards scored with a very well placed shot. Very even play followed, both sides pressing in turns. The visitors got the ball through. but the point was disallowed for off- side. Before half time the home team again scored, mak- ing the score 2-1 in their favour. Hoare scored a third goal for them. The light towards the end of the game got very had, but the visitors getting hold of the ball took it down, and managed to get a second goal. This proved to be the last point scored, leaving the Cricket Club winners of a very pleasant game by three goals to the visitors' two. WARRINGTON RESERVE V. MOORE ROVERS.—The above teams met at Arpley on Saturday. The home team hav- ing the advantage of the wind, the visitors kicked off rather late. They had the best of the opening exchanges but were quickly repulsed, and the home forwards gain- ing possession, Radford passed to Hayes, who placed a well-directed shot, J. Mather improving. The visitors next made a strong attack on Fagan, hut Bannon re- lieved, Radford racing towards the visitors end, his final effort proving futile. The visitors' next equalised with an easy shot, and keeping up the pressure the home backs displayed good defensive powers. Moor,however, had a goal disallowed for off-side play,half-time arriving with Warrington one goal, Moore one. Restarting, the visitors made for Fagan,scoring in the first five minutes. The play was now of an even character, each end being visited in turn. Warrington secured a free kick close in goal, which resulted in J. Mather scoring, the goal- keeper touching as it was going through. The visitors playing up were the next to score, and after some very rough play was witnessed, the referee having to severly caution the players on several occasions. Result :—War- rington Reserve, three goals ; Moore Rovers, three goals

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

As things were after the deluge, so Warrington ap- peared to be on Saturday. Evervthing was desolate and dreary, and if there had only been a little more rain, a modern ark might have been requisitioned. The heart of the football lover was low, and his socks were damp. He wandered ahnlessly around,not like ”Japhet, in search of a father," but in search of sonic delectation. The match between the home team and St. Helens Recs. had been postponed !

At first no one knew the cause of this, but presently rumour, with her tinkling tongue, came along, and said, "The Recs. are squeatny. They ain't got no more pluck nor plicemen. Their secretary carn't get them toge- ther to fight Warrington. Yah ! They skoot before their enemy." People corsequently began to brand the Recs. as cowardly and ignoble, *and it is said that the Parish Church club became so scornful, that they were negotiating on the advisability of challenging the Recs. and laying into them. H weever, before they could do this, another version of the story came. A message came from St. Helens stating that the Recs. had been quite agreeable to take their luck with Warrington, but the Corporation had prohibited them I They had been told by the municipal powers that it was too dangerous to allow a throng of people to come from smallpox stricken Warrington to their town. The Cor- poration are also said to have gone to the officials of the . London and North-Western Railway and induced them to cancel an advertised football trip from Warrington to St. Helens.

If this is so we can scarcely blame the St. Helens Cor- poration, for the risk was iict imaginary. But, although there is a certain amount of public danger occasioned by the prevalence of the epidemic in town, there is no reason for our neighbours for a few miles around, to tremble and fear in the absurd way they do. The greater portion of them are the dupes of gigantic ex- aggeration. In St. Helens last Saturday, the most terrifying rumours were being handed round respecting our condition. It was aaid that the black flag was flying from the Town Hall, and that one half the shops were closed, and it was further rumoured that the victims to the epidemic were being buried a dozen at a time, at the dead of night, and without religious rites being per- formed. The supreme and preponderous proportions of this elongation of the truth does credit to the author. lilut the style is out of date now, and he ought to have lived, and died, in time to have described the plague of London.

However, whether the St. Helens Corporation did, or did not suffer from this exaggeration, the fact remains that the match was postponed. The Warrington players ' were naturally both annoyed and disgusted, especially during the evening, when the latest results of the com- petition showed them that they no longer took the lead in the district. Swinton, their most formidable enemy, Is before them in consequence of having beaten Brough- ton. liespecting the competition the following are the RPRITLTS UP TO SATURDAY.
For. Aget. Won. Lost. Drn. G.T. G.T. Pte. Swinton

When people heard that the match tietween Warring- ton and St. Helena Recs. would not take place, some directed their attention to the Warrington junior cup competition, whilst others travelled to Birkenhead to witness the match between Lancashire and Cheshire. About 400 persons visited Wilderspool to witness Walkers' Brewery and Stockton Heath engage in the former con- test, whilst at least a hundred people went to Birken- head. The event at the latter place was certainly an ex- citing one. It was seen from the commencement that the Cheshire team was in an improved condition, and was Firely to wrench itself from the thraldom of its sub- jugators, for subjugated they have been to the Lanca- shire team, and that cannot be denied in the face of the fact that out of 17 matches, Lancashire have only lost two. But anyone who saw the game on Saturday, knew that this did not provide much consolation to Lan- cashire. They were beaten by sheer merit, and the victors cannot but admit that this result was chiefly owing to their possession of six capable Runcorn men. The result of the match was Cheshire 0-3-0, Lancashire 1-1-0.

" Turn we now " (vide ancient monarch) to the War- rington Junior Cup Competition. A distinct feature of the match on Saturday was that if mere physical strength would win the game, the knights of the Vat would certainly the laurel wreath wear without weary waiting, or in other words they would confiscate that popular token of triumph, the plumleas " bun." But they didn't. Chiefly owing to the efforts of Cross and Broady,"Stockton Heath won by a goal and a try to nothing. This now leaves Stockton Heath no one to fear but St. Mary's, as the following results show :

For Agst. Plyd. Won. Lost. Drs. G.T. O.T. Pts. St. Mary's 1 1 0 0 Stockton Heath ... 2 ... 1 ... 1 ... 0 Walkers Brewery 1 '1 1 . 0 Ranier s 0 . 0 . 0 . 0 ParlshChnrch 0 . 0 . 0 . 0 Juniors 0 0 . 0 . 0 Latchford ..........0 0 . 0 . 0 Latchford Rec.. 0 0 . 0 . 0

Connected with this match, however, there is an in- stance of the Spartan-like zeal entertained by some people for football. There are two young men, living so more than a mile from the " Examiner" Office, who were very much reduced in pecuniary matters. They lodge together, and were last week compelled to send to their" uncle," all their clothes except one suit,tvro pair of shoes and an overcoat. But each had a conflicting desire to witness the game at Wilderspool. A protracted dis- pute ensued It culminated with the parties "tossing up" to decide who should have the prior claim to the complete suit. The gentleman who surname initial is T-- won. He wore the suit, and went to the match. His friend accompanied him in the quasi-Highland costume of one sat, one shirt, one long overcoat, two hoots, two socks, one pipe.

Most of our readers will be glad to hear that Frank Turner is quickly recovering, arid has been able o get out of .16ors during the past few days. We hope he will soon be in full possession of his health and strength, and making himself familiar with the leather again. Frank has been rather unfortunate. If he permits accidents and illnesses to fraternize with him too much he will become like the unfortunate young man, and part from himself in sections. He ought to be careful !

The Warrington Association Club are rather unfortui • ate in their engagements. During the past few weeks they were to have met both the renkez-h Friends School Club and a St. Helens Club, but the secretaries of both combinations cancelled the matches on account of the prevailing epidemic in town. To-day (Saturday) they were to have met the Liverpool National Telephone Co. Club, but the secretary of that combination cancelled the engagement for the same reason.

div.head: MrscßLLAruious .
div.p: MrscßLLAruious .

The "Gym." Committee held a meeting on Saturday night and decided to enter the Challenge Shield compe- tition. Considering the performance they gave last year, they would be foolish not to make another attempt to gain the shield, when they are in possession of the bene- fits of more practice and experience. At first it was thought that the new exercises which the new conductor has introduced would cause some dissatiefactien. But this is not so. The whole of the members, leaders in- cluded, are showing the greatest interest in their new work, and believe that the principle which the whole of the exercises aim at, is a good one. h is to make the members good all round athletes instead of specialists.

A feature, which in almost all matters, is essential to success, is lacking at the " Gym." It is tha presence of the fairra sex. The ladies' classes, which were well attended last year, are now almost falling through, from want of members. The cause, it is said, lies in the fair ones' modesty, for most of the young ladies who have been asked to join,pout their pretty lips,and say," I don't like to join first. I'll wait till I know who are mem- bers." Now, this is a dreadful confession of the witnt of courage, in an age when woman is aiming at her eman- cipation—when Mrs. Grundy stalks around with her umbrella declaring her equality with man. She must have a fund of physical strength to support her claim in emergencies ! And how can she obtain that strength better than by gymnastic training P It is rather interesting to notice, now the cycling season is closed, that Mr. Pickavance, the genial secre- tary of the W.C.C., is still lift in undisturtsed possession of the 100 miles record medal, which he won some weeks ago. Mr. Pickavance did the distance in seven hours and four minutes. Since then Mr. J. Waddington en- dt avoured to break the record, but was only able to get through the run in seven hours ten minutes. Whilst expressing great admiration, and praise for Mr. Wad- dington's performances, we are not altogether sorry that he did not break that record. Mr. Pickavance deserves some kind of a reward, for the enterprise and labour which he has expended for the benefit of the club. And when he won a laurel by proving himself a clever rider, those who know him felt that they would almost have preferred to have allowed merit to go unrecognized rather than deprive him of his hard. earned prize.

Speaking of the Warrington Cycling Club we might mention that some of the present members intend next year to raise the subscriptions from 2s. to be. and restrict the number of membership to 50 or thereabouts. The object of this is to make the club a more congenial in- stitution. Well, the W.C.C. men are sufficiently con- genial as it is, but if they can make themselves more so, why, let them do it.

THE -FEVER 'HOSPITAL. -AN APPEAL.

Sir.-1I shall be much obliged if you will allow me, 'through the medium of your paper, to make an appeal for gifts of old linen and calico, which are greatly need- ed for the use of the patients.—Yours truly, M. WALKER, Matron.
Fever Hospital, Warrington.
THE EPIDEMIC.

Sir,—l am rarprised at the apathy -shown by our town -authorities in regard to the prevailing epidemic, seeing that it is spreading now, more than ever. There has been little or nothing done to prevent it, as 'I cannot acknowledge that the Hope Hospital, from the fact of it being situate so closely to a densely populated neigh- bourhood, was a step in the right direction. The number of cases reported from the districts surrounding it goes to proVe, that our authorities have blundered in the matter. What has been done in the town to check the disease? Absolutely nothing. Instead of seeing that our courts and alleys are limewashed, and disinfectants laid and scattered about the streets, the sewers flushed with dilute carbolic, we have bad to read of squabbles and discussions arising out -of petty .jealousies in the Council chamber, when efforts ought to have been made ' to endeavour to find out the cause of our town being a veritable plague spot; and after discovering the cause, devising a remedy. Seeing that the authorities are either incapable or reluctant to grasp the situation, I think it is time a government inquiry was asked for, when I am sure sufficient evidence could easily be pro- duced to prove that with the existing sanitary arrange- •-ments in the borough we shall have to put up with these • epidemic visitations.—Yours, &c.,
SANITAS.
CHESTER DIOCESAN CONFERENCE.

Sir.—Bishop Jayne approves of the-Lincoln judgment, and "considers the nation under a deep debt of gratitude to the Archbishop and his assessors for their ' right judgment' in a cause which • was pregnant with such vital issues." The Act of Uniformity says the service of the Church of England shall he conducted entirely on the lines laid down in the prayer book. In vain do I look for processions, crosses,and banners, altars, candles, eastward-priestward, backward or sacrificing position, or burning of incense. I find the service is to commence with one or more passages of Scripture being read, not with a processional hymn in order to make the laity stand and pay homage to these would-be priests. This is stated in the Ritualistic plan of campaign. At the Nicene creed the Rubric clearly states that there is to be no turning round, "but standing as before." The com- mittee recommend that lessons be given from the pulpit on the prayer book.; this Bishop Jayne commended. Why not have them in a public room and invite discus- sion? Because they know it contains germs of Popery, viz., infant baptism end three orders of the ministry, both condemned by the late J. B. Lightfoot, the scholarly bishop of Durham. McNeile says "The W ord of God is silent with regard to the baptism of infants." A vicar told me, "If there had not been an infant in Lydia's household it would have said so." I advised him to read Prov. xxx, 6, and to supply me with proof that she was a married worneir, or widow, Led that she than had her -Want with her. Needless to say, I have not yet got the answer. Where in the New Testament do we find Christ telling the parents that they are to provide three spon- sors; and where does Re inculcate Sunday garden parties with bands? Will Bishop Jayne answer this? No, they shield themselves in the pulpit. Frodsham, Nov. 9, 1592.

div.head: ROBERT FOULKES.
div.p: ROBERT FOULKES.
THE ROYAL COMMISSIONERS ON VACCINA-
TION.

Sir,—As the Royal. Commission has just resumed its important investigations into the results of vaccination, "The rimes" intimated a few weeks ago that the duties of the Lord Chancellor, who is President of the Commission, would prevent his lordship's regular atten- dance, and that Sir James Paget would occupy Lord Herschell's place as chairman. Allow me to say that while no more appropriate-choice could be madeamonest the medical members of the Commission than Sir James Paget, yet it is undesirable on many grounds to appoint a partisan in the case as Chairman at all,nor is there any such necessity. The Commission contains two mem- bers entirely uncommitted to either one side or the other of this much vexed question. Mr. Samuel Whitehead, M.P., who for the conspicuous judicial impartiality of his character is always listened to with respect in the House, and Mr. Meadows White, Q.C., both eminently fitted for the position, and whose appointment would inspire public confidence in the fairness of the Commis- sioners' deliberations. _ .

The other matter is also personal. The Commission has now been in existence three and a half years, or six months longer than was expected when it was appointed in April, 1889, and, although its proceedings are draw- ing to a close there are no signs of the appearance as witnesses of the most notable exponents and advocates of enforced vaccination. These are Lord Playfair, Dr. Ernest Hart (the author of "The truth about vaccina- tion ") and the late chief Medical Officer of the Local Government Board, Sir George Buchanan. The Secre- tary of the Vaccination Commission informed we in answer to an inquiry two years ago that the last-named gentivman would certainly give evidence, These eminent pro-vaccinationists (with Sir John Simon,whose cross-examination has just been heard), have by their -speeches, pamphlets, and manifestoes, done more to 'perpetuate compulsory vaccination upon the land, than all other agencies combined, and, when giving evidence before the Commission, I ventured to call Lord Herschell's attention to the matter, and respectfully re- quested that they should be summoned. It has been said of Lord Playfaies remarkable speech in the Vaccination debate, June 19th, 1883, that it • changed more votes than any speech ever made in Par- •liament. The opponents of this form of state Medi- Me reasonably wish to see whether the alleged facts and extraordinary statistics, received with ringing cheers by an excited but uninformed Parliament, will stand the -test of cool cross-examination. The inquisition Will not .be complete without the presence of these distinguished witnesses.
WILLIAM TEBB. 'Devonshire Club, St. James's, London, Nov. sth, 1892.
TUE FAGE OF TENKETH IN A RAGE.

43/r.--Had the Sage of Penketh not lost his judgment in fury, he would have taken care not to have invoked the shade of ?Jr. John Stuart Mill. A knowledge of his great work on logic, and a still less acquaintance with the" female feline feeling " of fury, would have prevented him from falling into the mistake be com- mitted in a former letter, when he wrote of" logical deductions from observations of nature." Such a reck- less confusion of the methods of induction and deiluc- -tion, ought not to occur in the writings of a mere tyro in logic. Again, the Cage of Penketh does notnoncede to men the right to exterminate vermin, except when they "intrude," say,, into his garden or his night cap. Would the Sage of Penketh extend the same law to man ? Would he exterminate the roguish urchin who "intruded "into his garden for the purpose of pilfering his fruit? If not, he must produce a reason why the -urchin escapes extermination, much more so considering that he links man on to the lower animals by means of necessary and immutable laws. This is a difficulty which I produced on a former occasion, and which the Sage of Penketh has not yet answered, nor is his con- vulsive invocation of the shades of Waits, Mill, and Whately of much service. Indeed, a greater acquain- tance with their works, especially Mill's Logic, would teach him how to reason better, and to indulge less in spasmodic invocations of their shades. Notwithstanding the Sage's sturdy defence of the rights of the lower animals, he yet exhibits a remarkable antipathy to some of the most innocent and tiny of their tribe. This is evidenced by his conduct towards ,a cockroach when "down by the sea." His description of the in- cident is simply charming by reason of its simplicity. pungrY and eager for breakfast he entered a refresh-

THE TOWN COUNCIL AND THE SHIP CANAL. Sir,—lt appears that our Town Council, or at least, some of its members, were desirous of advancing the very modest sum of £150,000 to the Ship Canal Company with the object of expediting the making of docks at •Warrington. It would be instructive to know who were the concocters of this little job, and the motive which lay at the bottom of it. Perhaps the investment of some loose cash, and a seat or two in the Directorate of • the canal might have had something to do with the inception of the scheme, and the venerable and well .worn stock phrase, " for the good of the town" vigor- ously shouted from the house tops would have silenced the gainsayers. The cool impudence of a few wire pullers in initiating steps to saddle the town with a debt of £150,000 and interest thereon, without any reference whatever to the ratepayers was sublime in its audacity. I am glad to note that the scheme has been nipped in the bud, and the woulthbe investors and directors must wait a more favourable turn of the wheel of for- tune for filling their pockets, and setting them on high above their fellows. In the meantime, a few remarks on the present financial position of the Corporation may not be out of place as showing that retrenchment, and not extravagance, is what we sorely need. Business in all departments is greatly depressed, through short time and low wages. Many of our working people are in very poor circumstances; and tradesmen and shopkeepers with diminished receipts and oppressive local taxation find it very difficult to make ends meet. Then, unfortunately, the town is at present afflicted with fever and smallpox, to a disquiet- ing extent, and remedial measures for these will involve a considerable expenditure of the ratepayers money. But, in addition to these powerful reasons for economy, there is another most important one to which I ask the special attention of your readers. At the close of the financial year which ended m the 25th of March last, the bonded liabilities of Warrington stood at £548,343 17s. 2d.. a sum nearly equal to four times the present assessable value of the property in the borough, and equivalent to a debt of £II each upon every man., woman and child within the boundaries of Warrington. And what have we got to sho'w against this enormous debt P A private gentleman's cast off mansion turned into a Town Hall, with five acres of land attached ; gas and water works of very ordinary capacity; a market hall and sheds ; two miserable structures called inter- cepting depots, with their compliment of" Dolly Var- dens ;" a manure manufactory on a very small scale, with plant worth the price of old iron • badly paved streets, and streets not paved at all, and a few other items not worth mentioning. Of course the security of the bondholders does not lie in these, but in the con- tinned ability of the ratepayers to bear a strain of tax- ation to the extent of some 6s. in the £ on their rental. I trust this ability may continue, but if, through stress of circumstances, it should become greatly diminished, or cease altogether, the prospect of the smallest dividend for the creditors of the Corporation out of the realiza- tion of the " stock in trade" would be small indeed. Under these circumstances I consider the action of the Council clique in attempting to add £150,000 to our debt, and Bd. in thief to our present oppressive rates as deserving of the strongest possible condemnation. No doubt the projectors of the big ditch between Liverpool and Manchester would have been glad to receive help, even from Warrington, in their time of need. Like other foolish builders they set about cohstructing their house without having previously counted the cost, and the result is the present mess in which the undertaking is involved. But what on earth have the ratepayers of Warrington to do with that ! The prime motive in the Canal scheme was the benefit of Cottonopolis, and if docks are required at Ward n,gton let Cottonopolis see to their construction, as it would assuredly take care that War- rington traffic should bear its share of the Canal dues. Whoever heard of a Corporation being called upon to provide station accommodation for a railway cOmpany 'rho thing is absurd.
OBSERVER.
LEGAL EIGHT HOVRS FOR MINERS.

Sir,—Your bold correspondent " Cymro " cannot deny that he commenced his mewl attack on miners. He based his attack on his knowledge "of coal getting, its difficulties and dangers. Further, he says he witnessed "two explosions under ground, with six men killed each time." In your issue of the 22nd ult. he glories that he "Can assure me (R. 8.) that I ("Cymro") have as much sympathy—practical sympathy—with miners and other bard worked people as even., he (R. 8.) 'has. Where, then, is the pretence he talks of? Nowhere, but in the distorted imagination of a splenetic mind. Now, "Cymro." I have again copied your own words, and put in brackets my cowardly name, and your heroic phan- tom, so far as I know it. Illy relations, Sm., are still in the coal mines for whose sake—thrice—when I was sent as a delegate to see the employers, or managers, not concerning £ s. d., but dangers to life and limb, and the Employers' Liability Act, when forced to contract out of it, in the beginning of 1881. Yet,when a terrible explo- sion occurred,on one occasion,when I was down the shaft widening the return air road, the flames, Heaven be thanked, did not come where I was within about 200 yards. Escaping, I went home to comfort my wife, and despite her pleadings, went back to the pit bank, and volunteered to go down again, and did, to help to rescue my fellowmen. " Cymro" where were you when the two explosions occurred, to which you referred in your first letter ? You say that you witnessed two explosions underground If you saw them underground, then, surely you must have been under ground. Is your statement true ? If

so, you, like myself, owe much to Him who saved us at sucis an .awful time. Did you or did you not risk , your life as I did ? Tell me that? If not, let me give you your own taunt. " Where then is Cymro's pretence ot practical sympathy ?" He tells what a teacher he has been of political history, &c. Alas! fvr their im- provement, if he taught them no more history than be has taught your readers in his three letters against " legal -enactments "—not a word ! el). Let past his- toric facts of legal enactments, which have brought many blessings to English working-men, women, and children teach,—as experience ought to teach him—to be wise. But " Gyaro " says, to use his own words : " What I oppose if there is any force in words, is legal enactment , of any nutriber of hours as a day's work-for adult man- hood." " Cymro "is out of date,and cannot undo the,past. (2). Be thought to prove how much evil has arisen from past le.gal shortening of working hours, to the,em- ployers and employed, as the ground of his present condemnation of such acts. (3). He is unwise and wrong, in comparing legal 4tarting of working hours in any employment, to a mother's natural duty to suckle her " baby ," put it to bed, soothe it when crying. fcc. (4). This shows that ." Cymro needs to think deeper about the fundamental laws of human life—that' he is putting out his mental eve. While seeking to help women, &c., he runs blindly into the ditch of inhu Ban- , ity. Sweet woman, 4. Cymro;" is your foe. (5). Think deeper about principles than have hitherto blessed tilte human race, ,and ' less about politics, that have done so much to curse poor working men, and keep rich Barrahas full-handed with the hire of those that have reaped down his fields,lcc., whereby such have long opposed legal equality, representation, in St. Stephens Boards of Guardians, or Magisterial Beeches, &c. It is principles of justice, not blind party politics, that will reform and bless the human race. Even John Bright stumbled once, yea, twice, fearfully- (l), over the Ten Hours Bill; (2) over the Home Rule question. He repented of the fc rmer,and amend his mar, nem I doubt not, but that God forgave him for the

I have been thinking, Sir, that this useful but defence- less body of people require as much protection as any other class of workers. There is another class of people who have my sympathy. I have none to waste on men who can take care of themselves. I mean what are called needlewomen—women who make boys' shirts, ! ending their own thread for 6d. a dozen, and men's full ' size shirts for is. id. a dozen. A gross of buttons are sewed on shirts with the sewer's own thread for 2id. —and to do this work, two women hire a machine between them, paying lad. a week • one will work by day and the other by night,and by the time the machine is paid for it is worn out. Those splendid enera cloaks, costing from £5 to £lO each, are made for 2s. 61., tak- ing two long days to do, of superior needlework stitch- ing and quilting, the makers finding thread and sewing silk, and with aching eyes and sad hearts, earning Is. a day. I have written to you, Sir, on this subject before now. You have kindly granted me space in your valu- able paper, but where was R. Storey then ? He was a dumb dog who never barked on the subject Our national wealth has grown, R.S. asserts, in consequenal of shortened hours. I say that shortened hours were a boon, and so is factory inspection—but our national wealth has grown from other causes—the development of steam in ocean navigation, improved sailing ships, the electric telegraph, railways, improved machinery, the discoveries of science in the manufacture 9f iron and steel, and in every branch of manufacture, in chemistry

and electricity. 1 have been studying, Sir, at the com- mand of R. Storey—yes-4 have studied human nature, I have studied him, I have done with him, lie acknow- ledges himself beaten on his hobby " legal eight hours." I shall pursue the "even tenour o-f my way "undeterred by the mud thrown at me by R.Storey : it will not stick. —I am, sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, Oct. 31, 1892. P.S.—R. Storey is terribly put about as to my identity. He can have it by asking for it, if it will do him any any good.
CYMRO.

merit room, and" took it by assault." On sitting down to satisfy the cravings of hunger a cockroach appears on the rim of his saucer. Immediately the Sage of Penketh takes to his heels and" runs away." But what should be the cause of such a scamper? Had a hungry lion, prowling about for his prey, peered through the window and,on seeing a hungry sage sit down to breakfast,roared with terrible majesty one could understand how the Sage of Penketh should scamper off in such confusion. But the cause of this precipitate retreat was an innocent and tiny cockroach. I have known a child of tender years play with this creature, and, when wearied of the sport, paralyze and kill it with a single blow. I can scarcely conceive of the Sage of Penkethrellecting upon it afterwards without seeing, in rny mind's eye, a "smile on his lips and a tear in his eye "—a smile at so much - ado about nothing—a tear at the loss of a breakfast so suited for satisfying the clamorous cravings of hun- ger. Mr. Peers must not be offended when I tell him he cannot act similarly in the future. By doing so, ho may at some evening's entertainment, find his host place him a cockroach, for the amusement of his guests, to see a learned sage and modern agnostic ' run away" and scamper off, pell-mell, as fast as.legs and arms can carry him. Now, that Mr. Peers has pretty well exhausted his armoury of invective, he might turn for a while to his armoury of argument. Ile admits that there is a super- abundance of writers but a dearth of thinkers. Os these grounds he should hesitate less considering that he is one of the leading lights of evolution. In doing so, I must ask for one concession, and that is, his theory must be consistent With all the teachings of science. The conclusion he conies to in Blology must not conflict with the great law of the Conservation of Energy. How then, on this condition, can a lower species generate a higher, that is, how can an intelligent species such as man, originate from an unintelligent species ? If so, a certain amount of energy must be transformed into sensation and consciousness, and,on the other hand, sensation and consciousness must be capable of trans- formation into other forms hf energy, say heat, light, electricity, &c. This difficulty, admitted even by Pro- fessor Tyndall to be insurmountable and unanswerable, has not, so far as I am aware, been once referred to in the writings of the Sage of Penketh.—l am yours, &c., A LEARNER. Nov. 7th, 1892.

second blunder .41so. I can easily bear with " Cymro's " personal and *groundless hints, as to my love of £ s. d., and idleness.. What he first needs is to pull the beam ont of his own eye.—Yours faithfully, i. STOREY. 160, Orford•lane, Warrington.

Sir,—lL Storey asks you for one word, which he I extends to more than half a column, and in that one ' word he has quoted my patronymic sixteen times. I shall make, sir, but very few references to his distorted quotations from my letters, which ferm the bulk of his " one word" half column, interlarded with " Cymro " says this and" Cymro says that, and " Cymro " think, "Cymro," study deeper, and so on in the same cuckoo strain. I have thought,sir,and I have studied,but not at his bidding. I have nearly done with him,and given him his quietus. He admits all 1 want—this is what he says —" I as a miner must have been a very dull unthink- ing scholar."—l endorse that—to know nothing about miners in Lancashire &c., having during 40 years or a little more repeatedly tried to secure an eight hours working day, by Trades Union effort, but never having succeeded." fime you had it, Mr. Stores', but never mind—run out the half century.—lt is time that he began to "think" and"study deeper." He says "Cymro" scorned the Trades Union leaders ; this is a simply not true. I ask a simple question. He construes it into an assertion and raves about my inhumanity. I fling him back the inhumanity—he is wrong in his his- tory, as well as in his distorting quotations from my letters. He passes by the poor domestic servant and the toiling housewife by a side wino remark that" when men get eight hours toiling women will also."— Think "R. Storey. "Study deeper." You see lam an apt scholar—l appeal to the past ; men's working hours have been shortened in factories and workshops in many cases, to nine hours and under. Has the toil- ing housewife or the domestic servant benefitted in like manner? I say no.—What I write about domestic ser- vants sir, is not " cant " but sober, sad fact. As a body they are the most respectable and best conducted of the working classes,to say nothing of their usefulness, and yet they are very lightly esteemed, and how often are they the victims of tyranny, brutality, seduction, and lust ! Many of them are orphans and friendless,many of them scores, not to say hundreds, of miles from home and how many of them have no home but the wide world ! Some of them have had temporary shelter under my humble roof before now until they could be better suited. They are subject to great temptation, especially if they have the fatal gift of good looks. Servants are often the victims of the sensualist and the libertine. _

WAURINOTON TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of the above was held on Tuesday at the Horsemarket-st., Cocoa Rooms,there being a good attendance of delegates. A discussion atose upon the Municipal Elections. The Trades Council bid previous to lstr of November, appmached both political parties with a view to see- ing if they could see their way to concede a seat in the Town Council for a labour representative. It was found that neither party was willing to con- cede a seat, but the Council ultimately decided to let the matter stand over till a favourable oppor- tunity arrives for the Council to contest one or more of the wards. A resolution was unanimously passed,accord- ing the best thanks of the Trades Council to the Chancel- lor of the Duchy of Lancaster, for his placing working- men of the town oh the Commission of the Peace for the Borough. They also congratulated Mr. Wm. Matkin, of Liverpool, on his elevation to the Bench. Although Mr. S. Wright, the President of the Council for the year, was not a nominee ef the Council, his name not having beea submitted to the Chancellor of the Duchy with those names sent up, they still recognised the appoint- ment as a step towards labour representation on all public bodies, he, being a Trade Unionist and a mem- ber of the Council. The best wishes of the members were given to Mr. Wright in connection with the honour conferred upon him. Mr. Wright baying thanked the Council for their kindness towards him, the meeting terminated with a vote of thankalo the Chairman.

div.head: POSITION OF SHOP ASSISTANTS.
div.p: THE POSITION OF SHOP ASSISTANTS.

The evidence given on Wednesday before the Labour Commission chiefly related to the shop assistants of Manchester. Mr. W. Johnson and Mr. R. Davies, re- presenting the National Shop Assistants' Union, we examined, and spoke as to the working hours and con- ditions of life of the assistants. In some of the principal streets of the city, they said, the average number of hours at .the shops was 53 or 54 per week ; but at many others the average was from 80 to 84 hours per week. The early closing of shops, it was held, would never be brought about by voluntary arrangement. The only remedy was to pass an Act giving the local authority power to enforce any regulation for the closing of shops which received the support of two-thirds of the shop- keepers of any town or district. The witnesses COM- plained of the stifling atmosphere of some of the shops and upper rooms as detrimental to the health of the assistants. ' ;LECTURE ON VIVISECTION.

At a meeting of the Primitive Methodist Literary I and Debating Society, on Monday night. Dr. Mouncey gave a lecture entitled" Does Vivisection teach us anything." Mr. P. Thompson, jun.. pre- sided, And there was a large attendance. The lecture was of a most interesting character, and was ren- dered more lucid by the aid of charts and diagrams: Dr. Mouncey said that prior to 1861, the human' body to the medical men of that time was like a big dark continent. There were a few operations taken in connection with the brain, but unfortun- ately very frequently' they were fatal, and his hearerti could thus understand the great reluct- ance that medical and scientific men felt in deal- ing with the brain. After death many injuries and diseases were discovered, and they were found to be easily got at, if they could only be discovered during life. Numberless experiments were tried both here and on the Continent, but up to 1861 no idea of the uses of the brain was known. Then it was that a certain doc- tor had three cases, one after the other, and these, cases were associated with a curious accident. In one case the patient could breath but could not speak, ad after death a post-mortem examination was .made, when certain injuries to the brain were discovered, and the ' doctor made the assertion that that particular part of. the brain governed articulation, but he was ridiculed. , Scientific men, however, ultimately came to believe in his theory was the right one, and that was all that was known of the brain until 1870, when a professor of physiology developed the idea • of electrical stimulation, and wonderful things were found. He found' that electrical stimulation applied to particular parts of the brain governed the various organs and parts of the body ; the experiments also extended, to the nerves and such things, and information was gleamed, which had never been dreamt of until that time. Had all those experiments taught them anything by which they could relieve the suffering of our fellow beings? Per 9 years knowledge went on spreading, and the localising of the functions of the brave wereteing mapped out. In Glasgow a boy fell down, and bruised his face, and hurt his forehead. He was taken to the Glasgow Infirmary, and was put to bed, and in 48 hours he was all right, and his parents wanted to' take him home. The doctor who had charge of the case thought they had better leave him, as there might 'be an injury -to the brain. The buy seemed to be all right, but the doctor kept him in bid. On the sixth day a curious thing took place. He commenced to twitch on the left side of his face at intervals, then the twitching spread to his left arm, and then the leg, in fact, he had localised con- vulsions. This went on for 24 hours, and on the seventh day the lad became unconscious, and he had an ordi- nary epileptie fit. The doctor wanted to make an op- eration,but the other medical man pooh-poohed the idea. He proceeded with the operation, shaving the hair from the spot where thelad localiqed the injury to the brain. but there Was rso sign of a bruise. When the scalp was reflected back, however, a minute crack was found in the bone of the skull. They cut through the bone and opened the brain when two ounces of fluid blood spurted otrt, together with several clots. The bone was put bacir,it healed up, and the lad recovered and he was shown about three years ago before the British Medical Association; a healthy strong young man. (Applause.) The information derived from those experiments ,was in direct opposition to anything that had ever been believe,' or thought about: Since then namberless operations had been cal-ried oat, of a most wonderful description. That was what vivisection had taught them upon one particular subject. Another point was the disease called anthrat,wliich affected horn- cattle, horses, and humad beings who handled the flesh of animals which had died from the4decesse, or who had drank the taint of cows suffering from it. The disease was of two forms, external and internal. He then pro- ceeded to describe the nature of the disease, and the means by which it can be discovered. As a preventive he advocated inoculation with the bacellus, and stated that from expetiments it was found that atter inocula- tion, only one in 500 animals died from the disease, but without' inoculation 70 out of 500 would 'have tiW. Kidney disease was the next point dwelt upon, and he showed that by experiment it had been foundthat a man could live for a number of years with only one kidney. He Foncluded by a reference to poisons and said that vrviAectien had taught them how to detect murder and crime. After a few remarks by the Chairman and the Rev. T. Collins. a vote of thanks wag acc9rded Dr. Mousey and the proceedings closed.

With the Object of raising funds towards the liquidation of the debt of £l5O, which at present exists on the Runcorn Seamen's Institute, a concert was given in *uncorn Public Hall,on Monday even- ing. Notwithstanding that, a heavy fog prevailed and there were other rttractions in the town, a fairly large audience assembled; and the funds would benefit to some extent. Mr. S. Taylor occupied the chair. A much needed improvement had been effected in the hall. Mr. G. Hitehmough, the ball keeper, had con- structed a " seund board over the platform, with the result that the music, both vocal and instrumental, was heard to greater advantage than iusual. Widnes Sub- scription Brass Band, who had, in fact, arranged the coniaert, held a prominent part in the programme. Under the conductqrship of Mr. W. Rimmer, of South- port, they performed (four-selections in a manner worthy of the reputation the Band has achieved, and the audience signified their appreciation by loud plaudits. Miss F. Lamb gave a pleasing -interpretation of" Shall he upbraid," for which she received an encore' and later on in the evening she contributed " He shall feed his flock." Mr. T. Stanley sang "Four Jolly Smiths" and " Big Ben;" while Mr. Rimmer gave two perform- ances on the cornet,and in each instance his skilful mani- pulation of the instrument secured him an encore. Mr. Wilson Blackledge, of St. Helens, gave his well-known and appreciated humorous sketches, which appeared to strike the audience with as much freshness as ever. During the interval, the Chairman proposed a vote of thanks to th&Band and the other artistes who had pro- vided the concert. He mentioned the excellent work accomplished by the Institute amongst boat people and sailors, and expressed the earnest hope that the debt which at-present burdened the Institute would speedily be cleared off. The motion was carried, and the Chair- man was also thanked for his presence and help, on the motion of Mr. W. Shaw, the missionary.

RUNCORN BRANCH.
