div.head: PE N KETH.
div.p: PE N KETH.
Sr. M MIT'S TEMPARANCHIVSOCLETY.

On Friday night last the members of the St. Mary's Temperance Society held their first annual tea meeting in the Infants'School. The scholars to the numbes of 120 sat down to a substantial Lea at 6 30. After tea singing. &c., was indulged in and fireworks were set off for the amusement of the children in the school yard. The ladies and gentle- men who had charge of ths tea party were Mr. and Mrs. Aitken, Mismes Tinsley and Bolton, Rev. J. R. Jonem, and Mr. E. Foster. The children enjoyed themselves very much. Mr. James Woodward pre- sided over the firework display. ,

- DONFIRB NIGHT. • Bonfire night, this year has been celebrated with more than usual .enthusiasm, by the people of Penketh. The number of fires, large and small, in the neighbourhood was sUrpriling. But the chief interest was centered in the monster bonfire in the Penketh ,Park. The arrangements have been carried out under the direction of Mr. C. B. Parker. the Chairman of the Company. The Penketh Brass Band head by a torchlight procession, was in attendance, and enlivened the proceedings with lively music. The fire was lit at 6.30 by Alias Fanny Garnett. A rather startling feature was the frequent boom of klr. T. Gandy's cannon placed in a field near by. The fireworks were subscribed for by the Yenketh public,and were of a very gorgeous description. Hot coffee was also provided gratis The crowd dispersed about 10 p.m. The flreiwas still burning on Sunday. rlMr. R.. E. Garnett, and Mr. T. Gandy•bad charge f. the fireworks.

• TIM AMERICAN PRESIDENIIAL ELECTIONS. RETURN -OF MR. CLEVELAND. Mr. Grower Cleveland has received a large majority of votes, and will be the next President of the United States. The reports show that the Democrats made large gains in many important States, California and Indiana giving their votes to the party of Tariff Reform. Mr. Stevenson, rice President-elect, says that the result of the election marks the revolt of the farmers and pro- ducers against the fd‘fiinley Tariff; and an important member of the Democratic Campaign Committee has put the same construction on the vote. The Republican partx is said to be in a "state of prostration," and the Presitlent-elect has received innumerable messages con- gratulating him on the result of the election. Mr. Cleveland's electors saamber 277. against 125 who have been returned to support Mr. Harrison; and Mr. Weaver, the candidate of the " People's Party," obtained only 32 votes in the Electoral College. The number necessary for election is 225. The latest reports show that the Senate will remain under the .control of the Republican party. and therefore hostile to any radical reform of the tariff. A :New York telegram says it is believed there that the ,State of Ohio, which has heretofore been Republican, gave Mr. Cleveland a majority of votes on Tuesday. Later returns as to the senatorial elections favour the belief that the representatives of the People's Party will kW the balance of power in that House, and will pro- bable vote with the Democrats. Since the war the Re- pubileans here always controlled the Senate,
OnSlturday the celebrated Besses-&-th%Barn Brass Band gave two concerts in the Town Hall, St. Helens, under the auspices of the Sutton-road Wesleyan Brass Band. Merewrkige attendances.

div.head: ON THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: ON THE SHIP CANAL.
PROGRESS OF THE WORK.

Tom Payne's Bridge, Stockton Heath, forms the starting point to a section on the Ship Cinal which has probably now become more fertile with in- teresting suljects than any other section. We allude to that portion of the work extending from the Bridge to the Locks at Latchford. Around the present bridge itself there are several points well worthy of the visitor's attention. The first is the nevt swing bridge which is being constructed, to take the place of the present stene bridge. It is of the same style ot structure as most of the other bridges—girdered, whale backed, and turned upon the pivit system by hydraulic prersure. There will be about 20,000 tons of iron used in its construction altogether. It is not completed yet, but from dawn until twilight there is quite a troop of mechanics constantly working at it, and as one stands on the present bridge and hetens to the clang of the ham- mers, the ring of the iron, and the puff of engines, it seems to him that a new forge has been opened there. The brick-work foundations anti v alls for the bridge are almost completed and preparations are now being made for

div.head: CARRYING OUT THE DIVERSION
div.p: CARRYING OUT THE DIVERSION

of the road. This diversion will not be of a very exten- sive character. Instead of continuing straight from St. Thomas's Church over the present bridge, the road will branch off to the right for about 30 yards, cross the new swing bridge, and continue over the site now occupied by the row of bay windowed villas on the right hand side of the road immediately, over the present bridge. This means that the demolition of those houses will have to. commence shortly. The property, we believe, has cost the company some £7,000 or £B,OOO. It looks a large sum when the shortness of the diverSion is taken into consideration, for it only extends to the Brewery. , Another feature of interest about the work at this spot is the construction of three subways kto. convey the sewage, gas, and, water, beneath the canal. They are constructed in what is known as the semi-circular style. They are about 12 feet itidiameter, and sink down: to a depth of 70ft., gradually proCeeding beneath the bottom of the canal in a circular or divex fashion, and ascending to the other side of the canal. The mouths of the subways at one side are slightly.lower than at he other. This ferms the

div.head: VITAL PART OF THE PRINCIPLE
div.p: VITAL PART OF THE PRINCIPLE

by which the subways become means of conveyance. By the strength of their own decent down the highest mouth, the gas, water, and sewage will enhance a force of movement which will impel them up to the mouth ef the subway at the other side, which, to accommodate the engineering calculations has had to be built some feet lower than the other mouth. The engineer has had a difficult task with this work, which has taken many months to complete. Glancing over the palacaded road away in the direction of Latchford, the visitor will observe a sight, which is at once impressive and ani- mated. After many months of delay, the excavating and completion of the banks in this section have been attacked. And, now, where but a few weeks ago the spot looked deserted and desolate,it is all life. Where ,the cuttings were filled with sleepers and stagnant water, they are now an exciting conglomoratio& of shreeking locomotives and steam navvies; and more im- pressive and noticeable than all are the banks. But a few weeks ago they were jagged and unfinished pre- cipices ; now they are reclining slopes all alive with two or three hundred men. Granting, however, that, the reader has armed himself with a pass, we persuade him to _

div.head: "TAE A .R.AMBLE
div.p: "TAE A .R.AMBLE

along the embankment. For some distance he will have very little opportunity to look around, in consequence of having to dodge small engines which constantly tush along the track he is walking upon. Presently he comes to an open space, close by some 50 !men who are engaged in finishing the slope of the bank. Standing by and delivering orders in a loud voice, occasioally embellished with an oath, is a Bohemian looking overseer. It takes a few moments before you can get him into conversation. But he's go- ing along well ROW, and says knowingly :—" Yas. This 'ere has bin a difficult section. The sandy natur of the soil was an almighty source of trouble. It w,ern't safe. Lumps of the bank kept sliming down, and it wasn't long before this sloping had to be resorted to. That is to leave no weight on the top of the banks. The banks are chiefly sand, and if they have weight on them this 'ere section would become a series of small landslips. When the slopes are finished the cutting about here will be as wide again as any other spot.' Proceeding for about half a mile, the cutting comes to a short break at Wash-lane. You . • , •

LEAVN TUE CANAL AND MUNN TDB LAND' which leads you to Wash Lane Railway Crossing.: You pass over this and immediately find yourself in the midst of a busy scene. About 40 yards the other side of the crossing the road is being deviated. It is carried up an incline some 300 yards long, at the top of this it will cross a large stome bridge which is being constructed over the Ship Canal. The bridge is scarcely half com- pleted yet, but you can see that it will be a ponderous structure, with four small arches and the large span across the Ship Canal. Wash-lane will continue over nem- and Nu in an almost, straight line to Long-isrovic Bridge. This will dispense with the present rural road which runs over the railway crossings, between two high lines of hedgerows, and, round the Ackers pits. Close by the bridge, however, stands the new Latbhford station. It is now practically completed. Following a deviation of the new road at the bridge you find your- self in the station yard. Prrieeeding along this yard you come to a subway running

div.head: BNNEATH-THE STATION.
div.p: BNNEATH-THE STATION.

At the entrance to it is the booking office. You can ascend a fight of stairs opposite this office, and find yourself on the platform for the Warrington trains. , The subviity leads to the other platform, and does away with any necessity for crossing the lines. An in- spection of the station shows it to be a large, well. fitted place in every way, very muck like the high level sta- tion at Bank Quay. The place stands a considerable height above the level of the surrounding ground, and consequently when you look horn the platform, the present station is seen below. But it can bear no com- parison. It sinks into insignificance in contrast to the fine new place, which is certainly a great acquisition to the railway company. Leaving this place, the new Latchford locks, with their accessGries, and the new railway bridges, are reached. The locks have teen practically finished, for some Mite and the two remaining features of the works there, to which the attention of the engineers is particuiarly turned, are the new bridge and the hydraulic pressure house. The latter place is a large building three parts completed, from which the hydraulic power for working

div.head: AIL MB SW- LNG BRIDGES
div.p: AIL MB SW- LNG BRIDGES

from Acton Grange i;id:tchford, will be supplied. The same place will supply the motive power for opening , the lock gates. Turning to the new bridge we find that the final comfoletions are being bestowed upon it, slid that there ' is a prospect of the new line which is conveyed over it, from Thelwall to Arpley, being opened within a few weeks. 1 This particular bridge appears to be the chief cause of the delay, although there are yet several minor items in the new length which are not yet completed. One of them is worthy of mention. It is the removal of the present signal box at Wilderspool-road crossing from its position on the side of the line, onto a'bridge over the line. The bridge is now being constiucted over the rails on the side of the crossings nearest the station. The object of this removal is to give more power in con- trolling the points. It is a desirable arrangement as the new line descends upon the crossings by a stiff decline' which will cause trains entering Warrington to sweep down with greater speed than formerly. The section of the canal named is remarkable for its number of new bridges ; and caretakers and pointsmen, whom Providence has

div.head: DEPRIVED OR OE REM_
div.p: DEPRIVED OR OE REM_

or leg, and endowed with a weakness which only "neat whisky" will dispel. The men are obeli:ly the remnants of some of the late Mr. Walker's finest foreign contract- ing gangs. It is interesting to listen to their narrations until they come to the point at which their missing mem- ber goes. Then it isn't interesting, because all their " doctors' prescriptions" about whisky are the same, at this juncture. The extension of the hand and the plead• ing look in the eyes are all so very much alike ! And the soft breathing of the words, " A glass is always wel- come, sir," becomes obnoxious because of its palpable frequency in Ship Canal tales. The visitor likes some- thing new. It would be new if one of the narrators said a glass wasn't welcome, and hadn't been recommended to take whisky in consequence of the loss of the limb.

div.head: NO HOPE FOR THE POISONER.
div.p: NO HOPE FOR THE POISONER.

The Home Secretary, after consideration of the evi- dence from Canada and the United States in regard to the poisoner Thomas Neill Cream, sees no reason for interfering with the capital sentence, which will there- fore be carried into effect next Tuesday morning.
RESIGNATION OF kORD EGERTON.

At a meeting of the Cheshire County Council on Thursday, Lord Egerton of Tatton resigned his seat for the Knutsford division. In his letter he said the recur- rence of the serious illness from which he suffered last spring and the continued illness of Lady Egerton ren- dered it necessary that they should pass the winter in the South of, England. The council accepted the resignation with regret.

div.head: RUSH FOR FREE EDUCATION.
div.p: A RUSH FOR FREE EDUCATION.

Much dissatisfaction has been caused by the Barrow School Board in their attempts to carry out a free educa- tion policy. The number of th •se who sought to avail themselves of a resolution passed in freeing the schools was so large that the Board became rather alarmed at the prospect, and are now proposing to charge for stationery to make up for the loss of fees. To this No- posal very great opposition is shown, and the Board will be called upon to abandon it.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
TUE DIRECFORS_AND MR. MOULTON, Q.C.

The directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company on Monday, issued a protest directed to the Mayor of the city against an opinion expressed by Mr. Moulton, Q.C.. and contained in the Report of the Special Com- mittee, to the effect that there was much of the condition of the Ship Canal which was not known to the Man- chester Corporation when it took practical interest in the undertaking. A sufficient admission of this, ccunsel stated, was found in the fact that the Ship Canal Com- pany conceded to the corporation the practical control of their expenditure in the interim. The directors emphatically drew attention to this, because if uncon- tradicted it gives colour to other statements made public in the newspapers which are unjust to the directors, and are not founded on fact. The "Times" for instance, stated on November Ist that the work had been conducted wastefully, and work which had been reported as done proved on investigation to be no more than half done. The directors deny that anything was withheld from the knowledge of the corporation, and ' also that the statement by the " Times "was correct. The company conceded to the corporation the practical nr•ntrnl tho .nmprutllt,ulits to aud harmonious working. Had they not given way, the necessary funds would not have heen foithcoming from the corporation, a.:,11 the works culd, have been stopped.
OLDHAM AND THE SHIP CANAL.
THE PROPOSAL TO LEND A QUARTER OF A MIL-
LION REJECTED.

On Wednesday night, at the meeting of the oldhain Town Council, Alderman Emmett, the ex-Mayer. moved the confirmation of the resolution passed in committee recommending the Council to lend £250,000 to the Man- chester Ship Canal Company. He said a great advan- tage had already accrued to the town from the reduction in rates by the railway companies, from the knowledge that the ship canal would probably rurthur materially reduce rates of carriage. If the wish of the whole of the directors of the canal was to .ler carried out, there was little deubt that Oldham would get a director by lending £250,000. If they borrowed the money at per cent and had to repay it in 50 years, the amount which would be required for payment of interest and for making a sinking fund would be £10,182. The amount they would receive from the Ship Canal would be £11,250 per year, leaviag a safe working margin. The amount, however, they would receive from the Ship Canal, would be sufficient within £5 to repay the loan in 40 years, after allowing for the charges to complete the sinking fund. If the canal was a financial success they would in all probability, be paid out by money borrow- ed in the mark. t. If they lent the money they would be in a position of a third mortgagee, the first nd second mortgagees, with the amount of two millions of money, being practically secured by the revenue by the Bridge- water Canal.—Alderman Hall seconded the resolution, which was supported by Ccuncillor Whittaker, who said It was a question which ought to go befo; e the rate- payers.—On the proposition. 'being put to the vote it received only-13 votes, while there were 21 against. It was therefore lost.
TIIE EXPLOSION ON THE SHIP CANAL WORKS.
BOARD OF TRADE INQUIRY.

On Wednesday Mr. Howard Smith and Mr. J. H. Hallett,C.E., of the Board of Trade, inquired into the circumstances of the explosion of the boiler of the loco- motive Kenyon, on the 3rd ult., at Frodsham, upon the Runcorn section of the Manchester Ship Canal,by which five perso‘s were ivjured. The inquiry was held in the Town Hall. Runcorn. Mr. Gough, from the solicitors' department of the Board of Trade, and Mr. Newman (of Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., Manchester), repre- sented t h.. Manchester Ship Canal Company. The evi- dence showed that the engine in questien was cne of ' three constructed by the Vulcan Foundry Company, Newton-le-Willows, in 1888. In 1891 it developed cer- tain defects, and was sent back to thebuilders for repaid: These having been effected, its working was resumed. During the present year further defects made themselves apparent, and Mr. Marsh, the foreman, fitter in the employ of the Manchester Ship Canal Co. was asked to examine and report upon the condition of the engine and boiler. He did so, and recommended certain work, to cost £350. Mr. Jones, the manager of the section, thinking this a large sum, asked Mr. Fox, . the mechanical engineer of the company, to make fur- ther examination. The result was that he recommended a lesser amount of work should be done, the cost of which—the company themselvas having the materials in stock —would be that of labour only, and would be about £5O. These repairs were effected, but the boiler upon its first trial trip exploded, with the result that five persons were seriously injured. Evidence having been ' given at great length, the court Sound that there had ' been negligence in the examination of the boiler, and as the officials in fault were responsible officials of the Canal Company, the company itself must be held res- ponsible for their serVants.—On the application of Mr. Gough that the company should be ordered to pay a sum towards the cost of the inquiry, they ordered that they pay £5O, which would be about half the expenses.

div.head: MA YBRICK CASE.
div.p: THE MA YBRICK CASE.
SINGULAR INCIDENT IN THE HIGH COURT.

In the High Court of Justice, on Thursday, a man- giving the name of Alexander Robertson applied that the case of Mrs. Maybrick might be brought before the. courts. Replying to questions, he said he had no affi- davits, and was neither a solicitor nor barrister. Be appeared as a British citizen. Baron Pollock said the court could not hear him, and the applicant replied that he would not leave the court until put out. On the usher, however, going to him to remove him, he quietly' walked out of the building

THE UNEMPLOYED INTERVIEW AN EDITOR. After the usual meeting of" unemployed" on Tower Hill on Tuesday, a procession of about three hundred men, headed by a red banner, proceeded to the office or - the" St. James's Gazette" to call the editor to account for having described the Trafalgar Square meeting of Saturday, as composed partly of loafers and lads. The scene at the newspaper office was at one time a very threatening one. The editor at length gave an inter- view to a portion of the men, one of whom, describing himself and his companions as "representing the whole of the 2,000,000 organised working-men in the country." asked for an apology. The editor insisted that not a • word in his journal had been directed against the genuine unemployed, and said he could not withdraw the statement that these meetings were composod to some extent of loafers and lads. Nothing further occurred werthy of note

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, It was my earnest desire to have been one of the first elected Councillors to represent your Ward, but as the con- test developed I conceived it to be for the interests of the electors that I should withdraw in 'favour of a man of more experience than myself. One of your representatives having been made an Alder: man, I no w beg to offer -myself as a candidate for your suffrages at this bye-election. If-elected, I shall do all in my power to'improve the general sanitary condtiion of the Town, knowing this to be most important for the Health-of the Inhabitants; to keep up the present high efficiency of the Gas and Water undertakings with due economy ; to see that the streets are well lighted, and to do all in my power to increase the welfare of the Town, especially West Bank Ward. I am your obediett servant, WILLIAM WINWOOD GOSSAGE.

B 0 ROUG II 0 F WIDNES ELECHON. TO THE ELECTORS OF WEST BANK WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— I have felt honoured in being chosen by my fellow-towns- men to serve them on the Local Board for so many years in the past (my first election being in 3573), and claim to have discharged my trust conscientiously, and am persuaded that all my actions have met with your approval a fact which gives me much encouragement in responding to the hearty invitation extended to me by the ratepayers of West Bank Ward to come forward as a candidate for election to the Municipal Council. As a representative of large interests in the town, I am deeply and earnestly concerned In all matters aft ecting its welfare. The roads have been placed in a very fair state of efficiency, and very many of the streets which were a disgrace tout have been sewered, made, and lighted at a reasonable cost to the property owners, whereby geed value has been obtained ; and, whilst I am in favour of continuing this policy in the immediate future, I pledge myself that, if elected, I will Aceep .a vigilant eye on the spending department of the Council, and will especially watch the interests of this im- portantiWard by doing all in my power to further any pro- .;ject which in my judgment will advance the comfort and welfare of the inhabitants. lam. Ladies and gentlemen. Your faithful and obedient servant, JOSHUA MIDWOOD.

THE NATIONAL L IBE RAL FEDERATION A MANIFESTO. A manifesto has been issued by the National Liberal Federation in view of its approaching annual meeting. Referring to the general position and outlook of the party, it says that the result of the general election offers abundant proof of the steady growth of public opinion In favour of the policy of justice and conciliation towards Ireland, and it disputes the contention of the 1 Unionist party that the opponents of Home Rule secured a moral victory in Great Britain at that election. That Horne Rule still holds the field is universally admitted, aid it will be the duty of the new majority in the House of Commons to support Mr. Gladstone in giving practi- eal effect to the verdict of the country, so that this Parliament may 'ay the foundation of a permanent re- conciliation and real union between Great Britain and Ireland. But beyond the Irish. question are many pro- blems which demand attention, and the Federation believes that the policy which the federated associa- tions have embodied in the document known as the Newcastle programme is that which the Liberal party must necessarily follow, in the immediate future. The party is pledged to deal with Welsh Disestablishment after Home Rule has been attained, and the demand for popular local control of the liquor traffic can no longer be postponed by the Legislature. 411. GORED TO DEATH BY OXEN. An inquest was held at Leamington yesterday, on a cowman named Sutton, aged seventy years, who was gored to death by two oxen. A verdict of "Acciden- tal death "was returned. BUFFALO BILL'S HUN TING EXPEDITION. ILE FLAGSTAFF, ARIZONA, FRIDAY MORNlNG.—Buffalo Bill and the gentlemen accompanying him on his shoot- ing expedition, including Colonel Mackinnon and Major Mildmav, of the Grenadier Guards passed here this morning on their way to the Grand Canyon of the Colorado. All was well with the party.

ORMONDE'S RETURN TO ENGLAND. Ormonde, who was recently sold to a Californian millionaire for £30,000, Is to visit England for a season before being sent to Sill Francisco. E. A. Day, who has been engaged to bring Ormonde to this country, sails in a few days to Buenos Ayres, and is expected to arrive in Southampton with 116 valuable charge in January next. -111, THE BLACKBURN MURDER. THE POLICE STILL WITHOUT & CLUE. Popular excitement over the murder of Alice Barnes was intensified late on Thursday night by a report that the murderer had been captured. The street in front of the police station was quickly thronged with an excited crowd, loud in their execrations, but it turned out a false report, and after a while the crowd dispersed. The police deny the statement that a house at Witton is being watched, and asserts° far they are utterly with- out a clue to carry them a step nearer the solution of the mystery. AN. IRISH PRIEST IMPRISONED FOR CONTEMPT. Yesterday an application was made to the Queen's Bench Division, Dublin, for an order to attach the Rev. John Feir, P.P., of Summerhill, Meath, for having, as alleged, used language on Sunday last from the altar calculated to intimidate witnesses from giving evidence at the hearing of the South Meath election petition. Among other things the rev, gentleman stated .that he would be at the hearing, and would prove that every witness who would come up against his party was a black-dyed scamp. The court held that the language was a contempt of court, and ordered the rev. gentleman to be imprisoned for one calendar month.
